CodeLength.caption: Why a recovery code has twelve words rather than any other number. The standard adds one checksum bit for every thirty-two bits of entropy and then cuts the result into eleven-bit pieces, one word each, so the word count follows from the entropy and nothing is chosen.

The bars group the two thousand and forty-eight words into eight blocks of two hundred and fifty-six, and they are level because every word must be as likely as every other - a code whose first word were predictable would have less entropy than its length claims.

ALPHABET = '123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz'
def b58(data):

    zeros = len(data) - len(data.lstrip(b'\x00'))

title: Wallet recovery: chapter 5 of the 3rd edition recomputed from the standards and checked against Bitcoin Core 31.1

nodes.label: Wallet keys
nodes.body: This first branch of the chapter asks what a Bitcoin wallet really contains and where its keys come from. The chapter begins by correcting a common belief. Wallets for physical cash hold the cash, so many people assume that a Bitcoin wallet holds bitcoins. The book says instead that what many people call a Bitcoin wallet, which it calls a wallet database to tell it apart from the wallet applications that use it, contains only keys, and that those keys are associated with bitcoins recorded on the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This first branch of the chapter asks what a Bitcoin wallet really contains and where its keys come from. The chapter begins by correcting a common belief. Wallets for physical cash hold the cash, so many people assume that a Bitcoin wallet holds bitcoins. The book says instead that what many people call a Bitcoin wallet, which it calls a wallet database to tell it apart from the wallet applications that use it, contains only keys, and that those keys are associated with bitcoins recorded on the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The correction has a practical consequence that shapes the whole chapter. Bitcoin does not store coins in a place that a person can lose; it stores outputs on the blockchain, and a person is the owner of an output only as long as she can prove control of the keys that guard it. The book opens with exactly this warning: losing access to a private key can make it impossible for anyone to spend the bitcoins that were received to the matching public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Every technique in the chapter, from seeds to recovery codes to derivation paths, is an attempt to stop the loss of data from turning into a loss of money without weakening security at other times.

Everything in this branch is met in the wallet application that a reader uses. Chapter 1 introduced the wallet as the software through which people use Bitcoin and explained who holds the keys in a custodial and in a noncustodial wallet. Chapter 3 showed the wallet of Bitcoin Core, and Chapter 4 explained how a single private key becomes a public key and an address. The present chapter takes the next step: a real wallet needs many keys, not one, and it has to make them, store them and restore them in a way that survives the loss of a phone, a computer or a hardware signing device.

The branch has two sections. The first, wallet contents, separates the wallet database from the wallet application, shows that a database may hold only some of the keys that a spending transaction needs, and explains why a wallet application may have to work with an external device to produce a signature. The second, key generation methods, follows the history of how keys are made: first independently, one random key at a time, then from a single seed by a deterministic rule, then with key tweaks that let a public key be derived without the private key, and finally as a whole tree of keys under the hierarchical deterministic standard.

Two cautions apply from the start. The word wallet is used loosely, for the database, for the application and for the hardware device, so a statement about wallets should always be read with the question in mind which of the three is meant. And the safe handling of keys is not a one-time decision: the chapter says that the solutions with almost no downsides are simply recommended, while the others have advantages and disadvantages on which wallet authors make different trade-offs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A learner should expect to meet more than one correct answer.

nodes.label: Wallet contents
nodes.body: Wallet contents is the group of ideas that answer a simple question: what is inside a Bitcoin wallet, and what is not? It collects three concepts. The wallet database is the stored collection of keys that a wallet application works with. Some databases hold only public keys, or only some of the private keys that a spending transaction needs. And the signatures that such incomplete databases cannot produce are obtained by external signing, from a hardware device or from other wallets in a multisignature arrangement (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Wallet contents is the group of ideas that answer a simple question: what is inside a Bitcoin wallet, and what is not? It collects three concepts. The wallet database is the stored collection of keys that a wallet application works with. Some databases hold only public keys, or only some of the private keys that a spending transaction needs. And the signatures that such incomplete databases cannot produce are obtained by external signing, from a hardware device or from other wallets in a multisignature arrangement (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The distinction matters because security and convenience pull in opposite directions. A wallet application that sits on a phone or a web server is exposed to theft and mistakes, while a device that keeps the private keys offline is safer and clumsier to use. Splitting the contents of the wallet between a part that can see payments and a part that can sign them lets a design obtain most of the convenience and most of the safety. The same split is what later sections use for cold storage and for the web store whose server holds no private keys.

The split works because the two things a wallet does need different materials. Recognising a payment needs only public material: from a public key, or from an extended public key and a chain code, a program can derive every address the wallet will ever hand out and watch the chain for payments to them. Authorising a spend needs the private key, and nothing else will do. So a design can put the public material where it is convenient - a phone, a web server, a shop till - and keep the private material somewhere awkward and safe, and the awkward part is then asked for a signature only at the moment of spending. External signing is the message that crosses that boundary: the application builds the unsigned transaction, the holder of the keys signs it, and the signature comes back without the key ever leaving (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets the split in almost every wallet in current use. A hardware signing device is one side of it and the application on the computer the other; a multisignature arrangement is the same shape with several signers; the web store later in this chapter is the same shape again, with a server that can see its takings and cannot spend them. Bitcoin Core shows it directly, because a descriptor wallet can be created from public descriptors alone, and the run of release 31.1 saved with this chapter reports such a wallet as one that holds no private keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Two cautions. The word wallet names three different things here - the stored keys, the program that reads them, and the device that holds the secret half - and a sentence about wallets is ambiguous until one of the three is meant. And a wallet that cannot spend is not therefore harmless: an extended public key reveals every address the wallet will ever use, so whoever obtains it can watch the whole balance and history, which is a privacy loss rather than a theft but a loss all the same (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Wallet database
nodes.body: A wallet database is the stored collection of keys that a wallet application uses. The book introduces the term on purpose: it observes that many people call this thing a Bitcoin wallet, and it prefers the name wallet database so that the data can be told apart from the wallet applications, the programs that read and write it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book states the central fact in one sentence: the database contains only keys, and those keys are associated with bitcoins that are recorded on the blockchain.

paras.text: A wallet database is the stored collection of keys that a wallet application uses. The book introduces the term on purpose: it observes that many people call this thing a Bitcoin wallet, and it prefers the name wallet database so that the data can be told apart from the wallet applications, the programs that read and write it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book states the central fact in one sentence: the database contains only keys, and those keys are associated with bitcoins that are recorded on the blockchain.

This definition corrects an intuition borrowed from cash. A leather wallet that is lost takes its banknotes with it, but a Bitcoin wallet database never contained the bitcoins. What it contains is the ability to prove to Bitcoin full nodes that its owner controls certain keys, and the book says that by proving this to the nodes a person can spend the associated bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Control is therefore a matter of knowledge, and the consequences follow directly: whoever copies the keys obtains the ability to spend, and whoever loses every copy of the keys loses it, even though the outputs remain on the blockchain for everybody to see.

Every wallet application has such a database, though it rarely shows it. In Bitcoin Core the database is a file that the program creates for each wallet; the release 31.1 created for this course reported the wallet format as sqlite and the wallet as a descriptor wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Its documentation describes the command backupwallet as one that safely copies the current wallet file to a destination (Bitcoin Core, 2026), which is how a user obtains a copy of the database. Simple databases hold both the public keys to which bitcoins are received and the private keys that make the signatures to spend them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The database is a long list of entries, and each entry ties a key to what it was created for. In the oldest wallets that was all there was: a private key and its public key, one after another. Modern databases also keep information about how the keys were derived, notes that the user typed, and settings. What matters for recovery is the split between data that can be recomputed and data that cannot. Keys derived from a seed can be recomputed from the seed, while the user's notes cannot, and the later sections of this chapter treat the two cases separately.

The word wallet is still used for the database, so a sentence such as the wallet holds the coins is shorthand that hides the real situation. The same hidden assumption leads people to protect the application, which can be reinstalled, and to neglect the database or the seed, which cannot be replaced. A good habit is to ask of any backup what exactly was saved: the program, the database, the keys or a seed from which the keys can be computed again.

nodes.example: a file of keys, not coins
nodes.definition: The wallet database is the stored collection of keys (and the notes about them) that a wallet application reads and writes; it holds the means to prove control of bitcoins, not the bitcoins themselves.

nodes.label: Wallet with public keys only
nodes.body: Not every wallet database holds everything that a spending transaction needs. The book points out that some databases contain only public keys, and others only some of the private keys that are necessary to authorize a spending transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet application that works with such a database can see the funds sent to its public keys and can show them to the user, but it cannot make the signatures that spending requires. The standard on hierarchical deterministic wallets describes the same idea as sharing a wallet with or without the ability to spend coins (Wuille, 2012).

paras.text: Not every wallet database holds everything that a spending transaction needs. The book points out that some databases contain only public keys, and others only some of the private keys that are necessary to authorize a spending transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet application that works with such a database can see the funds sent to its public keys and can show them to the user, but it cannot make the signatures that spending requires. The standard on hierarchical deterministic wallets describes the same idea as sharing a wallet with or without the ability to spend coins (Wuille, 2012).

The arrangement is useful because the dangerous part of a wallet is the private key and the convenient part is the knowledge of which payments have arrived. A merchant's web server needs the second and must not have the first, because a server that is hacked can then lose only the funds that arrive later and not those received before. An accountant who audits a business needs to see every incoming and outgoing payment but should not be able to move the money. The standard lists audits and per-office balances among its use cases for exactly this reason (Wuille, 2012).

Public-key-only wallets appear in three common places. A web store keeps an extended public key on its server so that it can give each customer a fresh address, a case developed later in this chapter. A hardware signing device is paired with a phone or a computer that holds only the public side. And a multisignature wallet is made of several databases, each of which holds only the keys of one participant, so that no single database can spend alone.

The mechanism rests on the one-way relationship between the two keys of a pair. A public key is computed from a private key by elliptic curve multiplication, a calculation that Chapter 4 explained and that cannot be run backwards. A database that keeps only the public keys, or only an extended public key from which further public keys can be derived, has therefore no way to recover the private keys. The standard calls the extended public key that results from removing the private part the neutered version of the extended private key, because it removes the ability to sign transactions (Wuille, 2012).

A database without private keys is not worthless to an attacker. The standard warns that leaking a public key can mean the loss of privacy, because anyone who holds an extended public key can derive all the addresses below it and so can see the complete history of payments they received (Wuille, 2012). Such a database must therefore be protected like private information, even though it cannot be used to spend.

nodes.example: receiving without the power to spend
nodes.definition: A wallet database that holds public keys but not the private keys can recognise payments and create receiving addresses but cannot sign a spending transaction.

nodes.label: External signing
nodes.body: External signing means that the program which prepares a transaction is not the one that signs it. The book describes the situation in its discussion of databases without private keys: their wallet applications produce the necessary signatures by working with external tools, such as hardware signing devices or other wallets in a multisignature scheme (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A hardware signing device, which the book notes is sometimes confusingly called a hardware wallet, is a separate device that securely stores a private key and does nothing except sign what it is asked to sign.

paras.text: External signing means that the program which prepares a transaction is not the one that signs it. The book describes the situation in its discussion of databases without private keys: their wallet applications produce the necessary signatures by working with external tools, such as hardware signing devices or other wallets in a multisignature scheme (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A hardware signing device, which the book notes is sometimes confusingly called a hardware wallet, is a separate device that securely stores a private key and does nothing except sign what it is asked to sign.

The reason for the separation is the difference in exposure. A phone or a laptop connects to the internet, installs software of uncertain origin and gets infected; a device built only to sign is a much smaller target. The book adds that most hardware signing devices never export private keys, which always remain on the device (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A multisignature scheme goes one step further and spreads the authority itself: Chapter 7 describes a multisignature script as one in which t of k listed public keys must provide signatures before the funds can move (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

In the book's example, Alice's wallet frontend gives out her public keys to the people who want to pay her. When she wants to spend, she supplies to the hardware signing device the key tweaks that she used, the device derives the needed child private keys, signs the transaction and returns it to the less secure frontend for broadcast to the Bitcoin network (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same pattern appears in the web store of Gabriel and in every cold storage arrangement that this chapter describes.

The flow has three steps. The application, which knows only public data, assembles an unsigned transaction. The signer receives it, together with enough information to find the right key, and checks what it is asked to sign. Finally the signature is returned and placed in the transaction, which the application broadcasts. At no point does a private key travel to the application, and that is the property that makes the arrangement worth its inconvenience.

External signing protects the keys but not the user's judgement. A signer can only sign what it is shown, so the transaction details displayed by the device must be checked by the user, because a compromised application may have built a transaction that pays someone else. Nor does a hardware signing device remove the need for a backup: if the device is lost, its keys can be restored only from the seed or recovery code that the following sections describe.

nodes.example: the application builds, the device signs
nodes.definition: In external signing the wallet application builds a transaction and another party, a hardware signing device or the other signers of a multisignature scheme, holds the private keys and returns the signature.

nodes.label: Key generation methods
nodes.body: Key generation methods are the ways a wallet application produces the key pairs that it will later distribute and use. The book separates two ways. In independent key generation, every key is created on its own from random data, and the application must store each one. In deterministic key generation, a single random value, the seed, is expanded by a fixed algorithm into as many keys as needed, so that the same seed always gives the same keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Key generation methods are the ways a wallet application produces the key pairs that it will later distribute and use. The book separates two ways. In independent key generation, every key is created on its own from random data, and the application must store each one. In deterministic key generation, a single random value, the seed, is expanded by a fixed algorithm into as many keys as needed, so that the same seed always gives the same keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The choice decides what a user has to back up. With independent keys, every new key makes the old backup out of date; with a seed, a single record made once covers all keys that will ever be derived from it. The history of wallets can be told as the discovery of this fact, followed by a series of refinements: keys whose public halves can be derived on a machine that has no private keys, and a tree of keys in which a branch can be given a purpose, a department or an account.

The history is a sequence of answers to one question: how can many keys be made so that one record restores them all? The first answer made no attempt - each key was drawn at random, so the set of keys had no structure and a backup was a copy of every key made so far. The second answer replaced the randomness with a rule: keep one random value, the seed, and derive key number n from the seed and from n, so that the same seed always gives the same keys in the same order and the backup is the seed alone. The third answer noticed that on an elliptic curve a public key can be shifted by the same amount as its private key, so a derived public key can be computed without the private one - which is what lets a watching wallet exist. The fourth answer arranges the derivation as a tree rather than a list, giving each branch its own chain code so that a branch can be shared without sharing its neighbours (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012).

The reader meets all four, but only one of them in new software. Independent generation is met in old wallet files and in the import path of current wallets, which must still accept a loose key; the seed is met as the recovery code a wallet shows on first use; the tweak is met whenever a server derives addresses it cannot spend; and the tree is met as the paths of the next branch and as the descriptors of the branch after. Bitcoin Core's own list of implemented proposals names the tree standard and the path conventions built on it, which is how a learner can check that the history ends where this chapter says it does (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is that a deterministic scheme moves the risk rather than removing it. One record now restores everything, which is the benefit; one record now also loses everything, and one leak of it gives away every key the wallet will ever have, including keys not yet derived. That is why the rest of the chapter is about the handling of that single record, and why the chapter's own closing advice is to write it down and to test the restoration rather than to trust that it will work (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Independent key generation
nodes.body: Independent key generation is the method in which a wallet application creates each of the keys that it plans to use independently of the others. Each is a fresh random number with no connection to the rest, and the wallet database is simply the collection of them. The book calls this the earliest design, illustrated as a collection of independently generated keys stored in a wallet database, and notes that all early Bitcoin wallet applications worked this way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The figure that illustrates it is captioned nondeterministic key generation.

paras.text: Independent key generation is the method in which a wallet application creates each of the keys that it plans to use independently of the others. Each is a fresh random number with no connection to the rest, and the wallet database is simply the collection of them. The book calls this the earliest design, illustrated as a collection of independently generated keys stored in a wallet database, and notes that all early Bitcoin wallet applications worked this way (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The figure that illustrates it is captioned nondeterministic key generation.

The method is simple, and its weakness is the backup. The book explains that users had to back up the wallet database each time they generated and distributed new keys, which could be as often as each time they created an address for a new payment. A failure to back up in time meant losing access to any funds received to keys that had not yet been saved. For each independently generated key the user has to back up about 32 bytes plus overhead, a figure that is small for one key and large for a wallet that is used the way privacy advises (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The design left a mark on user behaviour that the book describes. Some users and applications tried to minimise the data to be backed up by using a single key, which can be secure but severely reduces the privacy of that user and of everyone who transacts with them. People who valued privacy created a new key pair for each transaction, and their wallet databases could only reasonably be backed up on digital media (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The owner's course notes of 2021, written after the second edition, treat the same design under the headings nondeterministic wallet, random wallet and its disadvantages (Altunel, 2021).

A private key is a 256-bit number, which is 32 bytes. A wallet that holds a thousand independent keys therefore needs at least 32 times 1,000, that is 32,000 bytes, of fresh backup data, and every additional key adds 32 more. The cost grows linearly with the number of keys, and the real burden is not the size but the frequency, because the backup must be repeated whenever the database changes. The standard on hierarchical deterministic wallets records a workaround of the Bitcoin reference client of its time: by default 100 keys were cached in a pool of reserve keys, so that a backup stayed valid for a while (Wuille, 2012).

Independent keys are not obsolete only in theory: a database that contains them can still be restored only from a backup of the database itself, and no recovery code can regenerate them. Anyone who inherits an old wallet file should check whether its keys were derived from a seed or are independent, because the answer decides whether a seed is enough. The book's closing sentence for the method is a recommendation: modern wallet applications do not generate keys independently but derive them from a single random seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 1,000 keys, 32,000 bytes to back up
nodes.definition: In independent key generation every key is created separately from random data, so every key has to be saved on its own and the backup is out of date after each new key.

nodes.label: Seed
nodes.body: A seed is the starting value of a deterministic wallet. The book defines it in the course of its explanation of hash functions: using the same hash function with the same input, which it calls a seed, will produce the same seemingly random values (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In practice a seed is a large random number, usually 128 to 256 bits according to the book, although the standard on hierarchical deterministic wallets allows between 128 and 512 bits and advises 256 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023)[B32].

paras.text: A seed is the starting value of a deterministic wallet. The book defines it in the course of its explanation of hash functions: using the same hash function with the same input, which it calls a seed, will produce the same seemingly random values (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In practice a seed is a large random number, usually 128 to 256 bits according to the book, although the standard on hierarchical deterministic wallets allows between 128 and 512 bits and advises 256 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023)[B32].

The seed is the single secret on which all the other keys depend, and this concentrates both the benefit and the risk. The benefit is the backup: a user of deterministic key generation can back up every key in the wallet by recording the seed and a reference to the algorithm. The book illustrates this with Alice, who has received bitcoins to a million different addresses and needs to back up only 64 hexadecimal digits to recover access to all of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The risk is symmetric: whoever obtains the seed can generate every private key.

A seed is met whenever a wallet application asks the user to write something down at creation. The words, or the other recovery code that the application shows, are an encoding of the seed or of the value from which it is computed. The root seed of a hierarchical deterministic wallet, which a later concept describes, is the seed in this sense. In this chapter the seed is usually produced from a recovery code, and the next branch explains how.

The book's example seed is the 64-digit hexadecimal number f1cc3bc0 followed by the rest of the value, and it was obtained by hashing some random data from the operating system, a command the book prints. A hexadecimal digit stands for four bits, so 64 digits make 256 bits, or 32 bytes. The seed does not need to look special: its only requirement is that nobody could have predicted it, which means that it must come from a good source of randomness, the entropy that Chapter 4 discussed.

A seed is only as strong as its randomness. The book sets this out when it contrasts recovery codes with brainwallets: humans are very poor sources of randomness, which is why a seed should be created randomly by the wallet application and not chosen by the user (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A second caution is that the seed alone is not always enough to recover everything. The following branches show that a user may also need the derivation paths, a passphrase and the wallet's notes.

nodes.example: a 256-bit random value
nodes.definition: A seed is the random value from which a deterministic wallet derives all its keys; the same seed, with the same algorithm, always gives the same keys.

nodes.label: Deterministic key generation
nodes.body: Deterministic key generation is the creation of keys by a repeatable algorithm. Where independent generation draws a new random number each time, the deterministic method draws one random number, the seed, and computes everything else from it. The book builds the idea on a property of hash functions: a cryptographic hash function always produces the same output for the same input, changes its output unpredictably if the input changes even slightly, and does not let anyone predict the new output even when the new input is known (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Deterministic key generation is the creation of keys by a repeatable algorithm. Where independent generation draws a new random number each time, the deterministic method draws one random number, the seed, and computes everything else from it. The book builds the idea on a property of hash functions: a cryptographic hash function always produces the same output for the same input, changes its output unpredictably if the input changes even slightly, and does not let anyone predict the new output even when the new input is known (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The property turns one random value into a practically unlimited number of seemingly random values, and, more usefully, makes them reproducible. If the derived values are used as private keys, the same keys can be generated again whenever the seed and the algorithm are available. The book concludes that a user can back up every key in the wallet by simply recording the seed and a reference to the algorithm that was used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This is the idea on which every wallet recovery scheme of the chapter rests.

The book shows the rule on the command line. A random value is collected and hashed with SHA-256, giving the seed f1cc3bc0 and so on; then a loop hashes the text made of the seed, a plus sign and a counter, for the counters 0, 1 and 2, and prints three values that begin 50b18e0b, a965dbcd and 19580c97 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Python program in the worked example does the same calculation. A real wallet does not hash text in this way, but the structure is the same: a secret, a counter, a one-way function and a derived value.

The rule in the book's example is the SHA-256 hash of the text made of the seed, a space, a plus sign, a space, the counter and a line break; the book's command pipes the output of echo into sha256sum, and echo ends its line with a line break that is therefore part of what is hashed. For the counter 0 the result begins 50b18e0b, and the program in the worked example reproduces the whole value. Hashing the same text without the line break gives a different value, which the checks of this chapter confirm. Each derived value is 256 bits, which is the size of a private key. The values are independent in the sense that knowing one gives no practical way to find the seed or the others, because a hash function cannot be run backwards.

This simple scheme is a teaching device, not a wallet standard. It produces a single sequence of keys, and it does not allow public keys to be derived separately from the private ones, which is the flexibility that modern wallets need; the book remarks that modern wallet applications have a more cunning way of achieving this (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A secret seed must be protected as carefully as before, and one more warning applies: the algorithm is part of the backup, so a seed without the name of the rule that was applied cannot be turned back into keys.

nodes.example: sha256 of seed plus 0, 1, 2
nodes.definition: Deterministic key generation computes keys from a seed by a fixed rule, such as hashing the seed with a counter, so the same seed always yields the same keys.

nodes.label: Key tweak
nodes.body: A key tweak is a number that is added to a key to produce a related key. The book introduces it through the equation that relates a public key to a private key: the public key is the private key multiplied by the generator point of the curve. The book notes that operations on an elliptic curve are not intuitive but are analogous to the addition, subtraction and multiplication of regular arithmetic, and that it is therefore possible to create a derived key pair by adding the same value to both sides of the equation: adding 123 times the generator to a public key gives the public key of the private key increased by 123 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The value that is added is known as a key tweak.

paras.text: A key tweak is a number that is added to a key to produce a related key. The book introduces it through the equation that relates a public key to a private key: the public key is the private key multiplied by the generator point of the curve. The book notes that operations on an elliptic curve are not intuitive but are analogous to the addition, subtraction and multiplication of regular arithmetic, and that it is therefore possible to create a derived key pair by adding the same value to both sides of the equation: adding 123 times the generator to a public key gives the public key of the private key increased by 123 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The value that is added is known as a key tweak.

The tweak makes it possible to derive child public keys by somebody who knows nothing about the parent private key. The book's story is that Alice generates a public key and gives it to Bob. Bob does not know the private key but knows the global constant, the generator, so he can add any value to Alice's public key. If he then tells Alice the value, she can add the same value to her private key and obtain the private key that matches the public key Bob created (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). If a deterministic algorithm generates the tweaks, someone without the private key can derive an essentially unlimited sequence of public keys, and the owner can derive the matching private keys.

The technique is the foundation of the separation between the frontend and the signer that the previous section described. Alice's frontend distributes public keys to those who want to pay her, and when she wants to spend she gives the tweaks to a hardware signing device. The same arithmetic, with a different tweak rule, is behind the extended public keys of the standard, the web store example and the taproot output key of the segwit version 1 addresses in Chapter 4.

Let k be a private key and K = k times G its public key. For any tweak t, K plus t times G equals the point (k plus t) times G, which is the public key of the private key k plus t. The worked checks of this chapter confirm it for the book's private key from Chapter 4, 1E99423A, and for the tweak 123: adding the public key of 123 to K gives the same point as the public key of the key increased by 123. The arithmetic of the private keys is performed modulo the order of the curve, a number that the section on child keys explains.

A tweak is only as private as the rule that produces it. If the tweaks are publicly known, anyone who holds the parent public key can compute all the child public keys, and anyone who learns a child private key can subtract the tweak and obtain the parent private key; the checks of this chapter show the subtraction at work. The standard states the general version of the warning: knowledge of a parent extended public key plus any non-hardened private key descending from it is equivalent to knowing the parent extended private key (Wuille, 2012). This weakness is the reason for hardened derivation, which a later concept presents.

nodes.example: K plus 123 times G
nodes.definition: A key tweak is a value added to a public key, and in the same way to its private key, so that the child public key can be computed by someone who does not know the private key.

nodes.label: Hierarchical deterministic key generation
nodes.body: Hierarchical deterministic key generation, usually shortened to HD, is the standard way to derive keys from a seed. It is defined in BIP32, a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal by Pieter Wuille that has the status Deployed (Wuille, 2012). The book describes it as deterministic key generation combined with optional public child key derivation, using an algorithm that produces a tree of keys: any key can be the parent of a sequence of child keys, and any child can in turn be the parent of grandchildren, with no arbitrary limit on the depth (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Hierarchical deterministic key generation, usually shortened to HD, is the standard way to derive keys from a seed. It is defined in BIP32, a Bitcoin Improvement Proposal by Pieter Wuille that has the status Deployed (Wuille, 2012). The book describes it as deterministic key generation combined with optional public child key derivation, using an algorithm that produces a tree of keys: any key can be the parent of a sequence of child keys, and any child can in turn be the parent of grandchildren, with no arbitrary limit on the depth (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The standard exists because a single sequence of keys shares everything or nothing. The proposal explains that deterministic wallets typically consist of one chain of key pairs, so that sharing happens on an all-or-nothing basis, while an owner often wants to share only some public keys. Its example is a web shop whose server needs the addresses that receive customer payments, but not the change addresses that are generated when the merchant spends (Wuille, 2012). A tree lets one branch be shared and another kept private.

The book states that every modern Bitcoin wallet of which its authors are aware uses hierarchical deterministic key generation by default (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Bitcoin Core's documentation lists BIP32 as implemented since version 0.13.0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026), and the wallet that the release 31.1 created for this chapter reported key paths such as m/84h/0h/0h/0/0 for its first address, a position in such a tree (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The tree can be given a meaning: the book mentions a branch for incoming payments and another for change, and in corporate settings branches for departments, subsidiaries, functions or accounting categories (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Every key in the tree has an index, and an extended key can have 2 to the power 31 normal children and 2 to the power 31 hardened children, which together are the 2 to the power 32, about four billion, children that the book mentions (Wuille, 2012)[AH]. The details of how a child is computed, what an extended key is and how a path is written are developed in the second half of the chapter. At this point it is enough to know that the tree is built from a single starting value, so that a seed again suffices to rebuild all of it.

A tree has a freedom that a list does not: two wallets can place the same keys at different positions, and a recovery then needs to know which positions were used. This is the derivation path problem that the second branch of the chapter treats at length. A second caution concerns the word standard. The header of BIP32 gives its type as Informational, and many details of real wallets, such as which paths to use, come from further proposals that this chapter introduces one by one (Wuille, 2012).

nodes.example: a tree of keys under one seed
nodes.definition: Hierarchical deterministic (HD) key generation, the standard BIP32, derives a tree of keys from one seed; any key can be the parent of further keys, and public keys can be derived without private keys.

nodes.label: Recovery codes
nodes.body: A recovery code is the short, written form of a wallet's seed: a sequence of words, or in one case a string of letters and digits, from which every key of a deterministic wallet can be computed again. The chapter introduces the term in its section on seeds and recovery codes, where it says that recovery codes are intended to make backups easier and safer, and it notes that although seeds are large random numbers, usually 128 to 256 bits, most recovery codes use human-language words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This branch is about the codes themselves: the schemes in wide use, what each adds, and the decisions a user makes when they write one down.

paras.text: A recovery code is the short, written form of a wallet's seed: a sequence of words, or in one case a string of letters and digits, from which every key of a deterministic wallet can be computed again. The chapter introduces the term in its section on seeds and recovery codes, where it says that recovery codes are intended to make backups easier and safer, and it notes that although seeds are large random numbers, usually 128 to 256 bits, most recovery codes use human-language words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This branch is about the codes themselves: the schemes in wide use, what each adds, and the decisions a user makes when they write one down.

The branch matters because the recovery code is the one thing a user is asked to keep, and keeping it is the whole of the backup. The chapter states both sides of that plainly: if a wallet database is corrupted or lost, every private key can be regenerated from the original seed, but if someone else obtains the seed they can generate the same private keys and steal all the bitcoins from a single-signature wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A code is therefore a single object that has to survive fire, flood and forgetfulness while resisting theft and coercion, and those requirements pull against each other.

Recovery codes are met the first time a modern wallet application is started. The chapter says that a wallet implementing deterministic wallets with a BIP39 recovery code shows the user a sequence of 12 to 24 words when the wallet is first created, and that this sequence of words is the wallet backup (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Other applications show other kinds: the Electrum wallet from version 2.0 on, the lnd wallet with its 24-word cipher seed, the Muun wallet with a code that accompanies a printed kit, and hardware signing devices that offer the shares of a split code (Electrum Technologies, 2026) (Lightning Labs, 2026a) (Muun, 2026) (Rusnak et al., 2017).

The branch is organised in two groups. The first group, the recovery code schemes, takes the five kinds the chapter lists as in wide use, BIP39, Electrum version 2, Aezeed, Muun and SLIP39, and adds the proposal the chapter mentions in a note, codex32; each section says what the scheme encodes, what it adds over BIP39, and what it costs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Olsson Curr et al., 2023). The second group collects the choices that cut across the schemes: whether to use a passphrase, what plausible deniability buys and costs, why a chosen phrase is not a recovery code, what memory can and cannot be trusted with, what a code is worth to someone willing to use force, and what a wallet birthday saves during a restoration.

Two confusions should be cleared away before the detail begins. The first is that a recovery code is not a password: it is not chosen by the user, it is generated from randomness by the wallet, and it cannot be changed without moving the money, except in the one scheme that enciphers its own seed (Lightning Labs, 2026a). The second is that the schemes are not interchangeable. The chapter says that some solutions have almost no downsides and are universally adopted, while others involve trade-offs on which wallet authors differ, and it recommends only the first kind as best practice (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); which code a user holds therefore determines which software can read it.

nodes.label: Recovery code schemes
nodes.body: This group describes the recovery code schemes themselves. The chapter lists five as being in wide use at the time of writing, BIP39, Electrum version 2, Aezeed, Muun and SLIP39, and adds a note on a sixth proposal, codex32, which appeared while the book was being written (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each section of the group explains what the scheme turns into words, what defect of BIP39 it was designed to repair, and what it asks of the software that has to read the code back.

paras.text: This group describes the recovery code schemes themselves. The chapter lists five as being in wide use at the time of writing, BIP39, Electrum version 2, Aezeed, Muun and SLIP39, and adds a note on a sixth proposal, codex32, which appeared while the book was being written (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each section of the group explains what the scheme turns into words, what defect of BIP39 it was designed to repair, and what it asks of the software that has to read the code back.

A student who learns only one scheme will misread the others. The schemes differ in whether the words encode the seed itself or a ciphertext, in whether the code carries a version number, in whether its checksum covers the passphrase, and in whether one code is enough or several must be collected. Those differences decide what happens in the one situation that matters, the restoration, and they explain why a code written by one wallet is sometimes refused by another.

All six schemes work by turning a secret into words that a person can copy without error, and they differ in three choices. The first is what the words encode: the entropy behind a seed, as in the scheme the rest of the chapter uses, or a ciphertext, or a share of a secret that has been split. The second is what protects the words against a copying mistake: a checksum computed from the secret itself, which is how the first scheme works, or a longer checksum that also identifies the scheme, which is how the version-prefix designs work. The third is what the words carry besides the secret - a version number, a creation date, a share index - because whatever is not in the words has to be remembered separately. Those three choices explain every difference a learner will meet, including why one code can be restored by any wallet and another needs the software that made it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013) (Electrum Technologies, 2026) (Lightning Labs, 2026a) (Rusnak et al., 2017) (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

The reader meets a scheme as a list of words shown once, when a wallet is created, and then never again unless something has gone wrong. That is the difficulty with this group: the only moment at which the differences matter is a restoration, by which time the wallet that made the code may be gone. The schemes are met in their own documents, which this course fetched and saved so they can be compared side by side, and the differences are met in the one place they are visible without a restoration - the number of words, their checksum behaviour, and whether the first word reveals which scheme is in use (Palatinus et al., 2013) (Electrum Technologies, 2026) (Lightning Labs, 2026a) (Rusnak et al., 2017) (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

The caution is that a word list is not a format marker. Several schemes draw their words from the same English list, so a code can look exactly like a code of another scheme and derive a different seed, and a learner who assumes that twelve English words mean one particular scheme will restore an empty wallet and conclude that the funds are gone. The record of which scheme a code belongs to is part of the backup, and the chapter's own recommendation about writing the code down should be read as including it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: BIP39 recovery code
nodes.body: A BIP39 recovery code is a word sequence that represents, that is encodes, a random number used as a seed from which a deterministic wallet is derived (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard that defines it, BIP39, describes the implementation of a mnemonic code or mnemonic sentence, a group of easy-to-remember words, for the generation of deterministic wallets, and says that it consists of two parts: generating the mnemonic and converting it into a binary seed (Palatinus et al., 2013). The chapter sums up the procedure in one line: the wallet generates a random sequence of bytes, adds a checksum to it, and encodes the data into a series of 12 to 24 words, which may be localised to the user's language (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A BIP39 recovery code is a word sequence that represents, that is encodes, a random number used as a seed from which a deterministic wallet is derived (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard that defines it, BIP39, describes the implementation of a mnemonic code or mnemonic sentence, a group of easy-to-remember words, for the generation of deterministic wallets, and says that it consists of two parts: generating the mnemonic and converting it into a binary seed (Palatinus et al., 2013). The chapter sums up the procedure in one line: the wallet generates a random sequence of bytes, adds a checksum to it, and encodes the data into a series of 12 to 24 words, which may be localised to the user's language (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The scheme exists because people transcribe words better than hexadecimal. The standard's own motivation says that a mnemonic sentence is superior for human interaction compared with the handling of raw binary or hexadecimal representations of a wallet seed, and that such a sentence could be written on paper or spoken over the telephone (Palatinus et al., 2013). The chapter adds the practical consequence: recovery codes make it easier for users to back up because they are easy to read and correctly transcribe (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The hexadecimal and word forms of the same code, printed side by side in the chapter, make the point better than any argument.

A reader meets BIP39 in nearly every wallet application and in several places in this course. The chapter chooses it, together with BIP32 derivation and BIP44-style paths, as the stack of technologies it thinks most widely used in wallets, and the second half of the chapter is about that stack (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The lnd wallet documentation notes that its own cipher seed and a BIP39 phrase look similar and share only the English word list (Lightning Labs, 2026b). Bitcoin Core, by contrast, does not implement BIP39 at all: its list of implemented proposals names BIP 32, 43, 44, 49, 84 and 86 but no BIP 39, and the wallet that release 31.1 created for this chapter has descriptors with extended keys and no recovery code (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The arithmetic of the code is fixed by two rules. The entropy must be a multiple of 32 bits and between 128 and 256 bits; the checksum is the first entropy-length over 32 bits of the SHA-256 hash of that entropy, appended to it; and the result is cut into groups of 11 bits, each group an index into a list of 2,048 words (Palatinus et al., 2013). For the smallest allowed size this gives the worked example: 128 bits of entropy plus 128 divided by 32, that is 4, checksum bits make 132 bits, and 132 divided by 11 is the 12 words that a wallet shows. The rest of the mechanism, the word list, the key-stretching function and the optional passphrase, has its own group later in this chapter.

BIP39 has shortcomings that the standard itself lists, and they are the reason the other schemes exist. The seed depends on the word list used, because the conversion hashes the sentence rather than the entropy, so translating a code to another language gives a different seed; the conversion is one-way, so an arbitrary BIP32 seed cannot be written as a BIP39 sentence; the checksum is short, so about one random error in 256 is missed and no correction is possible; and there is no versioning scheme, which the standard says is now largely mitigated by descriptor wallets (Palatinus et al., 2013). The chapter is blunter: BIP39 recovery codes have several shortcomings which later schemes attempt to address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 12 words for 128 bits of entropy
nodes.definition: A BIP39 recovery code is a sequence of 12 to 24 words that encodes a random number together with a short checksum, from which a 512-bit seed is derived; the standard was published in 2013 and is the most widely used scheme.

nodes.label: Electrum version 2 recovery code
nodes.body: The Electrum version 2 recovery code is the word-based scheme used in the Electrum wallet from version 2.0 onwards. The chapter says that it has several advantages over BIP39: it does not rely on a global word list that every version of every compatible program must implement, and its codes include a version number that improves reliability and efficiency; like BIP39 it supports an optional passphrase, which Electrum calls a seed extension, and it uses the same key-stretching function (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Electrum's own document is the source for the mechanism and calls the scheme its Seed Version System (Electrum Technologies, 2026).

paras.text: The Electrum version 2 recovery code is the word-based scheme used in the Electrum wallet from version 2.0 onwards. The chapter says that it has several advantages over BIP39: it does not rely on a global word list that every version of every compatible program must implement, and its codes include a version number that improves reliability and efficiency; like BIP39 it supports an optional passphrase, which Electrum calls a seed extension, and it uses the same key-stretching function (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Electrum's own document is the source for the mechanism and calls the scheme its Seed Version System (Electrum Technologies, 2026).

Both advantages answer a real failure. A fixed word list means that every future version of every wallet has to ship the same list in order to read an old code, and Electrum's document says that this threatens the portability of BIP39 phrases, a problem made worse by one list per language (Electrum Technologies, 2026). A missing version number means that software cannot tell which derivation a code belongs to; the document warns that a wallet which has dropped a deprecated derivation cannot detect that a phrase is unsupported and will return an empty wallet instead, which threatens users' funds (Electrum Technologies, 2026).

A reader meets this scheme whenever an Electrum phrase has to be restored, and it is the reason Electrum refuses to generate BIP39 codes at all (Electrum Technologies, 2026). The chapter's sidebar on how much entropy is needed records Electrum's figure among the others: BIP32 allows seeds of 128 to 512 bits, BIP39 accepts 128 to 256 bits of entropy, Electrum version 2 accepts 132 bits, Aezeed accepts 128, and SLIP39 either 128 or 256 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example is that figure in words: 132 bits of entropy divided by 11 bits a word is the 12 words of a typical Electrum phrase, which the document confirms when it says that a typical seed has 12 words, giving 132 bits of entropy in the choice of the seed (Electrum Technologies, 2026).

The version number is read out of a keyed hash of the phrase. The document gives the procedure: the phrase is normalised, reduced to single spaces between words with diacritics removed, then hashed with HMAC-SHA512 under the key 'Seed version'; the first hexadecimal digit of the result says how long the version prefix is, and the prefix itself is the version number (Electrum Technologies, 2026). Three numbers are registered: 0x01 for standard pay-to-public-key-hash and multisignature wallets, 0x100 for segwit, and 0x101 for two-factor wallets (Electrum Technologies, 2026). Generation works backwards from this rule: a nonce, a number varied for the purpose, is enumerated and the phrase re-hashed until the hash begins with the wanted prefix, so a phrase that produces no registered number is not a valid Electrum seed, which is how the version doubles as an integrity check (Electrum Technologies, 2026).

The scheme's own document is careful about what the prefix costs. Imposing a prefix does not reduce the entropy of the seed, because an attacker gains no knowledge of the phrase, but it does let an attacker reject a wrong candidate before doing the key stretching, which reduces the strength that stretching adds; with Electrum's values the document works the cost out as 2 to the 132 plus 11 minus 8, that is about 2 to the 135 hashes (Electrum Technologies, 2026). The scheme also shares BIP39's deeper limitation: its optional passphrase is not covered by any checksum, so a mistyped passphrase cannot be detected (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 132 bits of entropy in 12 words
nodes.definition: The Electrum version 2 scheme derives both the master private key and a version number from a hash of the normalised phrase, so it needs no fixed word list and can tell an old code from a new one.

nodes.label: Aezeed cipher seed
nodes.body: Aezeed is the word-based recovery code of the lnd wallet, and the chapter presents it as another scheme offering improvements over BIP39. It says that Aezeed includes two version numbers, one internal, which removes several problems with upgrading wallet applications, and one external, which can be incremented to change the underlying cryptographic properties of the code; that it includes a wallet birthday, a reference to the date on which the wallet database was created; and that it supports changing the passphrase or other aspects of the code without moving funds to a new seed, the user needing only to back up a new code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The package's own document calls it the aezeed cipher seed scheme (Lightning Labs, 2026a).

paras.text: Aezeed is the word-based recovery code of the lnd wallet, and the chapter presents it as another scheme offering improvements over BIP39. It says that Aezeed includes two version numbers, one internal, which removes several problems with upgrading wallet applications, and one external, which can be incremented to change the underlying cryptographic properties of the code; that it includes a wallet birthday, a reference to the date on which the wallet database was created; and that it supports changing the passphrase or other aspects of the code without moving funds to a new seed, the user needing only to back up a new code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The package's own document calls it the aezeed cipher seed scheme (Lightning Labs, 2026a).

The scheme was written to fix exactly the two gaps the chapter names. Its document says that the new scheme aims to address two major features lacking in BIP39, versioning and a wallet birthday: without a version, wallets may not know how to re-derive addresses during recovery; without a birthday, they do not know how far back in the chain to look to derive all of the user's addresses (Lightning Labs, 2026a). It adds a third complaint, that BIP39 uses a very weak key derivation function, and uses scrypt with the parameters n equal to 32,768, r equal to 8 and p equal to 1 instead (Lightning Labs, 2026a). The chapter repeats the figure when it compares key-stretching parameters (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The scheme is met by anyone recovering an lnd node. The recovery document says that fund recovery requires two pieces of data, the 24-word cipher seed and the encrypted static channel backup file, and that only the first is needed if just the on-chain funds are wanted (Lightning Labs, 2026b). It also warns that a BIP39 phrase and a cipher seed look similar but share only the default English word list of BIP39 (Lightning Labs, 2026b). The worked example is the plaintext the scheme starts from, which its document gives as one byte of internal version, two bytes of timestamp and sixteen bytes of entropy: 1 plus 2 plus 16 is the 19 bytes that are then enciphered (Lightning Labs, 2026a).

The enciphering is what distinguishes the scheme. The document describes the steps: the external version is put at the front; scrypt with the version's parameters derives a 32-byte key from the user's passphrase with a five-byte salt, which it says makes the precomputation of keys infeasible, the purpose the salt section of this chapter describes; the 19-byte plaintext is enciphered with aez, an authenticated cipher whose checksum length is configurable and is set to 8 bytes, that is a 64-bit checksum, with the version and salt as associated data; and the resulting 33 bytes are encoded as 24 English words from BIP39's list (Lightning Labs, 2026a). If no passphrase is given, the string 'aezeed' is used instead (Lightning Labs, 2026a). Because the words are a ciphertext, the same seed can be re-enciphered under a new passphrase or new parameters, which is what upgrading a code means.

Authentication changes the trade-offs in a way the chapter discusses at length. Unlike the other schemes, Aezeed authenticates its optional passphrase and returns an error for a wrong value, which the chapter says eliminates plausible deniability, adds error detection and makes it possible to prove that the passphrase has been revealed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The scheme's document points the other way on the same fact: because the mnemonic is itself a ciphertext, leaving it in plaintext is advisable only if a passphrase is also set, in contrast with BIP39, where the words alone may be enough to steal funds (Lightning Labs, 2026a). The chapter also names the cost the scheme shares with BIP39: like it, Aezeed depends on both the backup and the recovery software supporting the same word list (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 19 plaintext bytes before enciphering
nodes.definition: The Aezeed scheme of the lnd wallet enciphers a plaintext of version, timestamp and entropy into a 24-word code, so the passphrase is authenticated and the code can be upgraded or re-enciphered.

nodes.label: Muun recovery code
nodes.body: The Muun recovery code is the odd one in the chapter's list. The chapter describes it as a nonword code, used in the Muun wallet, which defaults to requiring that spending transactions be signed by multiple keys; the code must be accompanied by additional information, which Muun provides in a document, and the code is unrelated to the seed and is instead used to decrypt the private keys contained in that document (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Everything a user needs is therefore in two parts that are useless apart.

paras.text: The Muun recovery code is the odd one in the chapter's list. The chapter describes it as a nonword code, used in the Muun wallet, which defaults to requiring that spending transactions be signed by multiple keys; the code must be accompanied by additional information, which Muun provides in a document, and the code is unrelated to the seed and is instead used to decrypt the private keys contained in that document (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Everything a user needs is therefore in two parts that are useless apart.

The arrangement follows from what the wallet is. A wallet whose spending requires several keys cannot be restored from one seed alone, because the other participants' public keys are not derivable from it, a point the chapter makes in its discussion of explicit paths (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Packing the keys into a document and protecting them with a separate code solves that problem without asking the user to understand it. The chapter is honest about the price: this is unwieldy compared with the BIP39, Electrum version 2 and Aezeed codes, but it provides support for newer technologies and standards that are becoming more common in new wallets, such as the Lightning Network, output script descriptors and miniscript (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The scheme is met through Muun's own recovery tool, whose document says that the tool can be used to transfer all funds out of a Muun account to an address of the user's choosing, and that the process requires no collaboration from Muun to work (Muun, 2026). The instructions show how the two parts come together: the tool is run with the path to the user's kit document as its argument (Muun, 2026). The document also states that the tool is open source so that auditors can inspect the code, build their own binaries and verify them (Muun, 2026).

The mechanism is encryption rather than derivation. The private keys exist already; the document carries them in encrypted form; and the recovery code is the secret from which the decryption key is obtained. A user who holds both can decrypt the keys and sign a transaction that moves the funds elsewhere, which is why the recovery tool's single purpose is to sweep an account rather than to restore a working wallet. Because the keys are not derived from the code, changing the code means re-encrypting the document, not moving the money.

The scheme's weakness is the one its shape implies: two objects must both survive, and losing either loses the funds. Keeping the kit and the code in the same place also defeats the separation, exactly as the chapter warns for a passphrase kept with its recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And because the code is specific to one wallet's design, it cannot be read by other software, so this is the clearest case of the lock-in that standards such as BIP39 and descriptors exist to prevent.

nodes.example: a code that decrypts a printed kit
nodes.definition: The Muun recovery code is not words and is not the seed: it is a key that decrypts the private keys held in a document the wallet gives the user, which suits a wallet whose spending needs several signatures.

nodes.label: SLIP39 share set
nodes.body: SLIP39 is a successor to BIP39 with some of the same authors, and the chapter describes what it adds: a single seed can be distributed using multiple recovery codes that can be stored in different places or by different people, and when the codes are created the user specifies how many will be required to recover the seed, so that five codes may be made of which only three are needed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard itself describes an interoperable implementation of Shamir's secret sharing and a specification for its use in backing up hierarchical deterministic wallets (Rusnak et al., 2017).

paras.text: SLIP39 is a successor to BIP39 with some of the same authors, and the chapter describes what it adds: a single seed can be distributed using multiple recovery codes that can be stored in different places or by different people, and when the codes are created the user specifies how many will be required to recover the seed, so that five codes may be made of which only three are needed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard itself describes an interoperable implementation of Shamir's secret sharing and a specification for its use in backing up hierarchical deterministic wallets (Rusnak et al., 2017).

The scheme answers a tension that no single code can resolve. The standard puts it as the usual approach of redundant backups set against the risk that a backup holder absconds with an asset of significant and liquidable value, and says that secret sharing distributes custodianship among a number of trusted parties in a manner that can prevent loss even if one or a few of those parties are compromised (Rusnak et al., 2017). The chapter's own closing advice points the same way: either keep recovery codes very safe or use a method such as SLIP39 that lets a code be distributed across several locations without relying on the safety of any one of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The scheme is met in hardware signing devices from the company whose employees wrote it, and in the chapter's list of schemes in wide use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A reader also meets its structure in the standard's own example, in which a user splits an encrypted master secret two-of-four at the group level, keeps two group shares, splits one further three-of-five among friends and another two-of-six among family, so that even all six family members cannot recover the secret without three friends or one of the user's own shares (Rusnak et al., 2017). The worked example is the smallest standard size: the standard's table gives a 128-bit master secret a share value of 200 bits, which at ten bits a word, with a list of exactly 1,024 words, is the 20 words of one share (Rusnak et al., 2017).

The mathematics is polynomial interpolation over a finite field. The standard explains that a polynomial of degree less than the threshold is constructed and each party is given a point, an input and the matching output, so that any threshold-many points define the polynomial exactly; it stores the shared secret as the value at 255 and a digest of it at 254, so that a correct recovery can be verified (Rusnak et al., 2017). The sharing is applied to each byte of the secret separately in the field of 256 elements (Rusnak et al., 2017). Before splitting, the master secret is encrypted with the user's passphrase by a four-round Feistel network whose round function is PBKDF2, a construction the standard notes is invertible, so that an existing BIP39 wallet can be migrated into the scheme (Rusnak et al., 2017).

A threshold scheme moves risk rather than removing it. Too low a threshold makes theft easier, too high makes loss easier, and the chapter notes that SLIP39 depends on a global word list and does not directly provide versioning, the two complaints it also makes of BIP39 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard adds that there is no way to verify that the correct passphrase was used, which is deliberate, since it lets one encrypted secret yield several master secrets under different passphrases (Rusnak et al., 2017); the consequence for a user is the same lack of error detection the chapter describes for BIP39.

nodes.example: 20 words for a 128-bit master secret
nodes.definition: SLIP39 splits one seed into several word codes with a threshold, so that any sufficient subset recovers the seed and any smaller subset reveals nothing about it.

nodes.label: Codex32 recovery code
nodes.body: codex32 is the proposal the chapter adds in a note beside the five schemes. It describes a new system for distributing recovery codes with similarities to SLIP39, which allows creating and validating codes with nothing except printed instructions, scissors, a precision knife, brass fasteners and a pen, plus privacy and a few hours of spare time, while those who trust computers can do it instantly in software; up to 31 codes can be created with a stated number required to recover the seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The proposal itself, BIP93, calls the format a checksummed base32 format and a standard for backing up and restoring the master seed of a BIP32 hierarchical deterministic wallet (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

paras.text: codex32 is the proposal the chapter adds in a note beside the five schemes. It describes a new system for distributing recovery codes with similarities to SLIP39, which allows creating and validating codes with nothing except printed instructions, scissors, a precision knife, brass fasteners and a pen, plus privacy and a few hours of spare time, while those who trust computers can do it instantly in software; up to 31 codes can be created with a stated number required to recover the seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The proposal itself, BIP93, calls the format a checksummed base32 format and a standard for backing up and restoring the master seed of a BIP32 hierarchical deterministic wallet (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

The proposal exists for the kind of user who does not want to trust a device at all. Its motivation says that safely storing the master seed is the hardest and most important part of self-custody, and that there is a tension between security, which demands limiting the number of backups, and resilience, which demands widely replicated backups, which encrypting the seed does not resolve because the encryption key raises the same problem (Olsson Curr et al., 2023). Because all computations can be done with simple lookup tables, it states in so many words that checksums can be computed and verified, and seeds split and recovered, entirely using pen and paper (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

A reader meets codex32 first as a string. The worked example counts the characters of the standard's own first test vector, ms10testsxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx4nzvca9cmczlw, and finds 48: three for the prefix, one threshold character, four identifier characters, one share index, 26 data characters and 13 of checksum (Olsson Curr et al., 2023). The chapter asks readers interested in distributed recovery codes to investigate the proposal's current status, because details might change significantly before the book was published (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the BIPs repository still gives BIP93 the status Draft (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

The checksum is what makes the hand computation possible. The standard uses the bech32 alphabet rather than a word list, giving fixed-length compact encodings, and a BCH error-correcting checksum rather than a hash; the ability to compute properties by hand comes, it says, from the choice of a small field and the use of linear error-correcting codes, and comes with no reduction in security as long as users use high-quality randomness (Olsson Curr et al., 2023). The price of that choice is stated as plainly: because hand computation must be supported, the standard does not support passphrases or key hardening, and it does not support splitting shares further (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

The proposal is explicitly not a finished standard, and a course should treat it as one more point on the trade-off curve rather than as a recommendation. Its own comparison with BIP39 is the sharpest summary of why such proposals exist: BIP39 has no error-correcting ability, cannot sensibly be extended to support secret sharing, has no support for versioning or other metadata, and has technical design decisions that make interoperability difficult, among them the use of SHA-512 to derive seeds and the use of 11-bit words (Olsson Curr et al., 2023). Every one of those sentences is a design decision a student can now recognise in the earlier sections.

nodes.example: 48 characters in the standard's own example
nodes.definition: codex32 writes a BIP32 master seed in the bech32 alphabet with an error-correcting checksum that can be verified by hand, and can split the seed into up to 31 shares with a threshold between 2 and 9.

nodes.label: Choices behind a recovery code
nodes.body: This group gathers the decisions that are not settled by choosing a scheme. Whether to add a passphrase, whether plausible deniability is a feature or a trap, why a phrase a person invents is not a recovery code, how far memory can be trusted, what a code is worth to someone prepared to use force, and whether the code records when the wallet was created: each of these is discussed in the chapter, and each applies across several of the schemes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group gathers the decisions that are not settled by choosing a scheme. Whether to add a passphrase, whether plausible deniability is a feature or a trap, why a phrase a person invents is not a recovery code, how far memory can be trusted, what a code is worth to someone prepared to use force, and whether the code records when the wallet was created: each of these is discussed in the chapter, and each applies across several of the schemes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The decisions matter because they are the ones a user actually makes, and because they cannot all be made well at once. The chapter's sidebar on recovery code passphrases says that many users and developers disagree about which approach is better, with some strongly in favour of plausible deniability and others preferring the increased safety that error detection gives novice users and those under duress, and it expects the debate to continue as long as recovery codes are widely used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A course that presented one answer would misrepresent the field.

These decisions work against one another, and the mechanism that creates the tension is the passphrase. A passphrase is mixed into the derivation as part of the salt, so each passphrase produces a different seed and therefore a different wallet from the same words; no checksum covers it, so a mistyped passphrase does not fail but silently opens an empty wallet. From that single fact the whole group follows. Deniability is the same property seen from the other side: because every passphrase is a valid wallet, no observer can show that a particular one was intended. Memory is the cost: the words are protected by a checksum and the passphrase is not, so remembering it is the weakest link in a chain the rest of which is written down. And coercion is the risk that makes deniability look attractive and the reason the chapter treats it as a trap rather than a feature (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The reader meets these decisions at the one moment a wallet asks whether to set a passphrase, usually with a sentence of explanation and no account of the consequences. They are met again in the published record of what goes wrong: the list of physical attacks that this chapter reads and counts, which its own source says is not comprehensive, and the recurring reports of wallets restored correctly from the words and found empty because the passphrase was not quite the one used. The wallet birthday is met in the opposite way, as the field a restoration asks for and a user cannot answer (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lopp, 2026).

The caution is that a second secret is a second thing to lose, and the arithmetic of that is bad. A code written down and a passphrase in a person's head is not two defences but one defence and one single point of failure, because the loss of either loses the funds while the theft of both is needed to take them.
