That is the reasoning behind the chapter's blunt preference for a written record over a memorised one, and a learner should separate the question of what protects against theft from the question of what protects against loss, because almost every recommendation in this group answers only one of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Recovery code passphrase
nodes.body: A passphrase, in the context of a recovery code, is an additional secret that the user supplies and that enters the computation of the seed. The chapter says that the BIP39, Electrum version 2, Aezeed and SLIP39 schemes may all be used with an optional passphrase, and that if the only place the passphrase is kept is the user's memory it has the same advantages and disadvantages as memorising the code itself (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In BIP39 the passphrase is appended to a fixed string to form the salt of the key-stretching function, which the seed derivation group explains in detail (Palatinus et al., 2013).

paras.text: A passphrase, in the context of a recovery code, is an additional secret that the user supplies and that enters the computation of the seed. The chapter says that the BIP39, Electrum version 2, Aezeed and SLIP39 schemes may all be used with an optional passphrase, and that if the only place the passphrase is kept is the user's memory it has the same advantages and disadvantages as memorising the code itself (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In BIP39 the passphrase is appended to a fixed string to form the salt of the key-stretching function, which the seed derivation group explains in detail (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The passphrase exists to make a stolen code useless. The chapter names the two features it creates: a second factor, something memorised, which protects a recovery code from compromise by a casual thief, though protection from a tech-savvy thief needs a very strong passphrase; and a form of plausible deniability or duress wallet, where a chosen passphrase leads to a wallet with a small amount of funds that distracts an attacker from the real one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first of these is the reason a passphrase is worth considering at all; the second is the subject of its own section.

A user meets the passphrase at two moments: when a wallet offers one at creation, and when a restoration asks for it. The chapter's own tables show what it changes: the same 12-word code gives the seed beginning 5b56c417 with no passphrase and the seed beginning 3b5df16d with the passphrase SuperDuperSecret (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example extends the same computation to a passphrase of four letters, typo, and gets a third, unrelated seed, which is the point of the next paragraph.

The mechanism is that the passphrase is an input and not a check. In BIP39 the key-stretching function takes the words as its password and the string 'mnemonic' followed by the passphrase as its salt, so any passphrase at all produces some 512-bit seed (Palatinus et al., 2013). The chapter draws the conclusion for the user: given a single recovery code, every possible passphrase leads to a different seed, so there is essentially no wrong passphrase, all passphrases are valid and they all lead to different seeds, forming a vast set of possible uninitialised wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Three of the four schemes do not include the passphrase in the checksum they use against data-entry mistakes, so a wrong passphrase cannot be detected; Aezeed, which authenticates its passphrase, is the exception (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The passphrase introduces a new way to lose everything, which the chapter states twice. If the wallet owner is incapacitated or dead and nobody else knows the passphrase, the seed is useless and the funds are lost forever; and if the owner backs the passphrase up in the same place as the code, the second factor is defeated (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's conclusion is that passphrases should be used only together with a carefully planned process for backup and recovery, one that considers the possibility of outliving the owner and allowing the family to recover the estate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A further cost is the reduced error detection: a slightly wrong passphrase shows a zero balance, which a novice may read as permanent loss, or may not notice for years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a different seed for every passphrase
nodes.definition: A passphrase is an extra secret that is mixed into the derivation of the seed, so that one recovery code yields a different wallet for every passphrase and the code alone is not enough to spend.

nodes.label: Plausible deniability
nodes.body: Plausible deniability is the chapter's name for the ability to create multiple passphrases for the same recovery code that all look valid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because every passphrase yields a working tree of keys, a user who hands over a code, with or without a passphrase, cannot be proved to have handed over the one that holds the money. BIP39's own text claims the property in the same words, saying that the method provides plausible deniability because every passphrase generates a valid seed, and thus a deterministic wallet, but only the correct one makes the desired wallet available (Palatinus et al., 2013).

paras.text: Plausible deniability is the chapter's name for the ability to create multiple passphrases for the same recovery code that all look valid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because every passphrase yields a working tree of keys, a user who hands over a code, with or without a passphrase, cannot be proved to have handed over the one that holds the money. BIP39's own text claims the property in the same words, saying that the method provides plausible deniability because every passphrase generates a valid seed, and thus a deterministic wallet, but only the correct one makes the desired wallet available (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The property matters because recovery codes are sometimes taken by force rather than stolen quietly. The chapter sets out the positive case: if someone obtains a code but not the passphrase, they see a valid tree of keys, and a user who prepared for that contingency by sending some bitcoins to the passphrase-free tree will have that money stolen, which is a bad thing in itself but also a warning that the code has been compromised, allowing the user to investigate and take corrective measures (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A learner meets the idea under two names. As a feature of a scheme, it follows from a passphrase that is not authenticated, which is the case in BIP39, Electrum version 2 and SLIP39; SLIP39's standard says explicitly that there is no way to verify that the correct passphrase was used, which allows the user to obtain multiple master secrets from a single encrypted secret (Rusnak et al., 2017). As a wallet design, it is the duress wallet the chapter names among the features a passphrase creates: a chosen passphrase that leads to a wallet holding a small amount intended to distract an attacker from the real one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mechanism is the absence of a check, so the property cannot be had together with error detection. Aezeed shows the trade-off from the other side: because it authenticates the passphrase and returns an error for a wrong one, the chapter says it eliminates plausible deniability, adds error detection and makes it possible to prove that the passphrase has been revealed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Which of those three is an advantage depends entirely on who is asking for the passphrase, and that is why the chapter presents the question as an open disagreement among users and developers rather than as a solved problem (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The danger of the property is as concrete as its benefit, and the chapter states it without softening: if a user is coerced into giving an attacker a code and it does not yield the amount of bitcoins the attacker expected, the attacker may go on coercing them until a different passphrase with access to more money is given, and designing for deniability means there is no way to prove that everything has been revealed, so coercion may continue even after it has (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A learner should take from this that deniability is a defence against a thief who has left, not against one who is still present.

nodes.example: a valid tree under every passphrase
nodes.definition: Plausible deniability is the property that a revealed recovery code or passphrase always looks valid, so a holder cannot be shown to have withheld anything - which protects and endangers them at the same time.

nodes.label: Brainwallet
nodes.body: A brainwallet is a wallet whose seed comes from a phrase that the user thought up. The chapter raises the term only to separate it from a recovery code: recovery codes are often confused with brainwallets, it says, and they are not the same, the primary difference being that a brainwallet consists of words chosen by the user whereas recovery codes are created randomly by the wallet and presented to the user (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP39 makes the same separation in its motivation, saying that the guide is a way to transport computer-generated randomness with a human-readable transcription and not a way to process user-created sentences, also known as brainwallets, into a wallet seed (Palatinus et al., 2013).

paras.text: A brainwallet is a wallet whose seed comes from a phrase that the user thought up. The chapter raises the term only to separate it from a recovery code: recovery codes are often confused with brainwallets, it says, and they are not the same, the primary difference being that a brainwallet consists of words chosen by the user whereas recovery codes are created randomly by the wallet and presented to the user (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP39 makes the same separation in its motivation, saying that the guide is a way to transport computer-generated randomness with a human-readable transcription and not a way to process user-created sentences, also known as brainwallets, into a wallet seed (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The distinction decides whether the keys can be guessed. The chapter gives the reason in one clause: the difference makes recovery codes much more secure because humans are very poor sources of randomness (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A phrase a person invents is drawn from a small space of memorable phrases that an attacker can enumerate, and an attacker who can enumerate it needs no access to the user at all, because the public blockchain shows which addresses hold money. The entropy group of this chapter returns to this as a general rule about where randomness must come from.

The term is met mostly as a historical warning, in older guides that invited users to remember a sentence, and in the chapter's tip that separates the two ideas (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is also met implicitly whenever a wallet refuses to let a user type their own words: that refusal is the scheme protecting the user from themselves. The owner's course notes for this chapter devote a slide pair to the same comparison, under the heading brainwallets against mnemonics (Altunel, 2021).

The worked example measures what the wallet's randomness buys. A 12-word BIP39 code is chosen from a list of 2,048 words, so a code drawn uniformly stands for one of 2,048 to the twelfth possibilities, and that number has 132 bits, of which 128 are entropy and 4 the checksum (Palatinus et al., 2013). A phrase that a person composes has no such guarantee: its space is whatever an attacker's dictionary and grammar can generate, which is many orders of magnitude smaller, and no key-stretching function closes a gap of that size, as the chapter notes when it says that key stretching helps only when an attacker already has to search a large space (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The term is sometimes used loosely for memorising a recovery code, and the two should not be mixed up: memorising a code the wallet generated keeps the wallet's randomness and risks only forgetting, whereas inventing a phrase destroys the randomness. The chapter's recommendation covers both cases from the other side, strongly encouraging a reader to write the code down even when the scheme was designed for easy memorisation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 132 bits in twelve random words
nodes.definition: A brainwallet is a wallet whose keys come from a phrase the user chose, which is insecure because people are poor sources of randomness; a recovery code is generated by the wallet instead.

nodes.label: Memorising a recovery code
nodes.body: Memorising a recovery code means keeping it only in one's head. The chapter says that a large part of the motivation for using words was to make a recovery code easy to remember, and it prints the same code in hexadecimal and in English words so that a reader can judge which they would rather memorise (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The ability is therefore a side effect of the encoding, not a recommended practice.

paras.text: Memorising a recovery code means keeping it only in one's head. The chapter says that a large part of the motivation for using words was to make a recovery code easy to remember, and it prints the same code in hexadecimal and in English words so that a reader can judge which they would rather memorise (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The ability is therefore a side effect of the encoding, not a recommended practice.

There is one situation in which it is genuinely valuable, and the chapter names it: there may be cases where remembering a code is a powerful feature, such as when a person cannot transport physical belongings, like a code written on paper, without their being seized or inspected by an outside party that might steal the bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For a reader in a stable situation this is an edge case; for a reader crossing a border under pressure it may be the only option.

The question is met whenever a wallet shows its words for the first time and asks the user to confirm them. It is also met in the schemes themselves: Electrum calls its optional extra secret a seed extension and the chapter notes that keeping a passphrase only in memory has the same advantages and disadvantages as memorising the code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Electrum Technologies, 2026). The worked example of this section is the comparison the chapter prints: 32 hexadecimal groups against 12 ordinary English words for the same 128 bits.

The mechanism is simply that 12 to 24 dictionary words are within the reach of ordinary rote learning, where 32 hexadecimal digits are not, and that the word list was designed to help: BIP39 says an ideal word list is chosen so that the first four letters identify a word unambiguously, avoids similar pairs such as build and built or woman and women, which make a sentence harder to remember and more error-prone, and is sorted so that implementations can search it efficiently (Palatinus et al., 2013). None of this makes the memory itself reliable.

The chapter lists three failure modes, and they are the reason it advises against relying on memory alone. If the code is forgotten and the original wallet database is lost, the bitcoins are lost forever; if the owner dies or is severely injured and the heirs have no access to the wallet database, they cannot inherit; and if someone believes that a code is memorised, they may try to coerce the user into disclosing it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Its own conclusion is explicit: even with a scheme designed for easy memorisation, the authors very strongly encourage a reader to consider writing the code down (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: words instead of hexadecimal
nodes.definition: Memorising a code is possible because the code is words, and is dangerous because memory fails, cannot be inherited and can be coerced; the chapter recommends writing the code down as well.

nodes.label: Coercion and physical risk
nodes.body: Coercion is the risk that someone obtains a recovery code by threatening its holder rather than by breaking anything. The chapter raises it in the list of reasons not to rely on memory: if someone thinks a user has a code memorised that will give them access to bitcoins, they may attempt to coerce that user into disclosing it, and the chapter supports the point by citing a record kept by the Bitcoin contributor Jameson Lopp, documenting over 100 physical attacks against suspected owners of bitcoin and other digital assets, including at least three deaths and numerous occasions where someone was tortured, held hostage, or had their family threatened (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lopp, 2026).

paras.text: Coercion is the risk that someone obtains a recovery code by threatening its holder rather than by breaking anything. The chapter raises it in the list of reasons not to rely on memory: if someone thinks a user has a code memorised that will give them access to bitcoins, they may attempt to coerce that user into disclosing it, and the chapter supports the point by citing a record kept by the Bitcoin contributor Jameson Lopp, documenting over 100 physical attacks against suspected owners of bitcoin and other digital assets, including at least three deaths and numerous occasions where someone was tortured, held hostage, or had their family threatened (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lopp, 2026).

The risk belongs in a technical chapter because it follows from a technical fact. Bitcoin payments are irreversible and a key cannot be frozen or reissued, so a code is a bearer instrument: whoever can state it can spend. Every design decision in this branch therefore has a human consequence as well as a cryptographic one, and the chapter treats the two together, which is why it discusses deniability as a safety question and not only as a property of a hash function.

A learner meets the subject in the chapter's cautions and in the list the chapter points to, whose saved copy for this course describes itself as a list of known attacks against Bitcoin and crypto-asset owning entities that occurred in meatspace, and notes that it is not comprehensive because many attacks are not publicly reported (Lopp, 2026). The copy read for this chapter is longer than the figure the book printed: its table holds 364 rows, which is checked by a claim of this chapter that counts them, so the chapter's over 100 is a floor and not a current count (Lopp, 2026).

The defences available are organisational rather than mathematical, and the chapter names them in passing. A duress wallet with a small balance can satisfy a casual attacker, at the risk the deniability section describes; distributing a code with SLIP39 or codex32 means that no one place and no one person can be made to produce the whole secret; and not being believed to hold a code at all is the most effective defence of the three, which is why the chapter treats privacy and recovery as related subjects (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Rusnak et al., 2017) (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

Two things should be said carefully. The first is that the published figures are a lower bound on reported cases and not a measurement of risk for any individual, since the list itself says it is incomplete (Lopp, 2026). The second is that a scheme chosen for resistance to coercion can increase the danger, as the chapter's own analysis of deniability shows: when nothing can be proved to have been fully revealed, there is also nothing that ends the demand (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a published record of attacks
nodes.definition: Because a recovery code is all that is needed to spend, people who are believed to hold one have been attacked in person; the chapter cites a public list of such cases and the list has grown since.

nodes.label: Wallet birthday
nodes.body: A wallet birthday is the date on which the wallet database was created, stored inside the recovery code itself. The chapter names it as one of the two features Aezeed adds over BIP39: a reference to the date when the user created the wallet database, which allows a restoration process to find all of the funds associated with a wallet without scanning the entire blockchain, something it says is especially useful for privacy-focused lightweight clients (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The idea is metadata rather than cryptography: nothing is protected by it, and a restoration is simply made cheaper.

paras.text: A wallet birthday is the date on which the wallet database was created, stored inside the recovery code itself. The chapter names it as one of the two features Aezeed adds over BIP39: a reference to the date when the user created the wallet database, which allows a restoration process to find all of the funds associated with a wallet without scanning the entire blockchain, something it says is especially useful for privacy-focused lightweight clients (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The idea is metadata rather than cryptography: nothing is protected by it, and a restoration is simply made cheaper.

Without it, a restoration has to assume the worst. A wallet that does not know when its keys were first used must examine the whole chain, which for a lightweight client means either downloading a great deal of data or asking a server questions that reveal which addresses are of interest. The Aezeed document gives the same reason from the implementer's side: without a birthday, wallets do not know how far back to look in the chain to ensure that they derive all of the proper user addresses (Lightning Labs, 2026a).

A reader meets the birthday during an lnd recovery, where the log line the recovery document prints says that the seed birthday has been surpassed and that recovery of the wallet is starting from a particular height with a recovery window, and the document notes that the rescan's duration depends on how old the wallet is, because the cipher seed stores the wallet's birthday (Lightning Labs, 2026b). The same document says that without a birthday a wallet would have to be rescanned back to the genesis block (Lightning Labs, 2026b).

The field is small because the resolution needed is coarse. Aezeed's plaintext is one byte of internal version, two bytes of timestamp and sixteen bytes of entropy, and the document explains that the two-byte timestamp is expressed in Bitcoin days genesis, the number of days since the timestamp in Bitcoin's genesis block, which saves space and avoids a wasteful level of granularity; it adds that this can currently express time up until 2188 (Lightning Labs, 2026a). The worked example checks that claim: two bytes hold 65,536 values, which at 365 days a year is 179 years, and 2009 plus 179 is 2188.

A birthday is a privacy hazard as well as a convenience: it narrows the window in which a wallet's transactions can be looked for, and a code that carries it tells anyone who reads the code roughly when its owner started. It is also absent from the schemes in widest use, so a BIP39 restoration still has to scan broadly; the gap limit section of this chapter describes the other half of that problem, which is not when to start scanning but how far to go.

nodes.example: a date in two bytes
nodes.definition: A wallet birthday is the creation date recorded inside a recovery code, so that a restoration can scan the blockchain from that date instead of from the beginning.

nodes.label: The BIP39 stack
nodes.body: This branch opens the second half of the chapter, in which the book stops surveying the options and works through one stack of technologies in detail. It names the three parts of that stack: BIP39 recovery codes, BIP32 hierarchical deterministic key derivation and BIP44-style implicit paths, and says that all of these standards have been around since 2014 or earlier, so a reader will have no problem finding additional resources for using them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The present branch covers the first part, the path from a random number to a recovery code and from the code to the seed.

paras.text: This branch opens the second half of the chapter, in which the book stops surveying the options and works through one stack of technologies in detail. It names the three parts of that stack: BIP39 recovery codes, BIP32 hierarchical deterministic key derivation and BIP44-style implicit paths, and says that all of these standards have been around since 2014 or earlier, so a reader will have no problem finding additional resources for using them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The present branch covers the first part, the path from a random number to a recovery code and from the code to the seed.

The branch matters because this is where the abstract words of the first two branches become arithmetic a student can carry out. The chapter describes BIP39 in nine numbered steps, split into two halves: steps one to six generate the code, steps seven to nine turn the code into a seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Everything a wallet shows the user, the twelve or twenty-four words, and everything it keeps, the 512-bit seed, is produced by those nine steps, and each of them is short enough to be checked by hand.

The reader has already met the results of these steps. The chapter's three tables print a 128-bit entropy value with its twelve words and the resulting seed, the same words with the passphrase SuperDuperSecret and a different seed, and a 256-bit entropy value with twenty-four words and its seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked examples of this branch recompute those tables from their inputs, which is possible because every function involved, SHA-256 and PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512, is in Python's standard library (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The same functions are what a wallet application uses.

The branch has two groups, matching the two halves of the standard. Generating a recovery code covers the random input, the checksum that is appended to it, the word list the bits are read against, the eleven-bit segments that index into it, the fixed relation between entropy size and word count, and the text normalisation that makes the words comparable across systems. From the code to the seed covers the key-stretching function, the particular function PBKDF2 and its salt, the 512-bit root seed that comes out, the optional passphrase that changes it, and the question of how much entropy is actually needed.

One point of order will save a reader confusion later. The standard's text calls the words a mnemonic and the chapter calls them a recovery code; they are the same thing, and this course uses the chapter's term except when quoting (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013). A second point is that the two halves are independent: the standard says that the conversion of the sentence to a seed is completely independent of generating the sentence, which is why a wallet can derive a seed from words it did not generate and why software must compute the checksum itself and warn if it is invalid (Palatinus et al., 2013).

nodes.label: Generating a recovery code
nodes.body: This group follows the first six steps of BIP39. The chapter states them as a list: create a random sequence, that is entropy, of 128 to 256 bits; create a checksum of it by taking the first entropy-length over 32 bits of its SHA-256 hash; add the checksum to the end of the random sequence; split the result into segments 11 bits long; map each 11-bit value to a word from the predefined dictionary of 2,048 words; and the recovery code is the sequence of words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each section of the group is one of the ideas those steps rely on.

paras.text: This group follows the first six steps of BIP39. The chapter states them as a list: create a random sequence, that is entropy, of 128 to 256 bits; create a checksum of it by taking the first entropy-length over 32 bits of its SHA-256 hash; add the checksum to the end of the random sequence; split the result into segments 11 bits long; map each 11-bit value to a word from the predefined dictionary of 2,048 words; and the recovery code is the sequence of words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each section of the group is one of the ideas those steps rely on.

The order of the steps is not arbitrary, and understanding it answers questions that otherwise look like magic. Why 2,048 words and not 1,000? Because 2,048 is 2 to the 11th, so a word is exactly 11 bits. Why is a code always a multiple of three words? Because the entropy is a multiple of 32 bits and the checksum is a thirty-second of it, so the total is a multiple of 33 bits, that is of three words. Why can a wallet detect a mistyped word at all? Because the last few bits are not entropy but a hash of the rest.

The six steps work as one arithmetic chain with no choices left in it. The entropy is a whole number of bits, and the standard allows only lengths that are multiples of thirty-two. The checksum is the first bits of a digest of that entropy, one bit for every thirty-two bits of it, appended to the end. The total is then cut into pieces of eleven bits, each piece read as a number between zero and two thousand and forty-seven, and each number replaced by the word at that position in a list of exactly that many words. Because eleven bits address the list exactly, no number is wasted and no word is unreachable; and because the number of pieces is the total divided by eleven, the word count is decided by the entropy rather than chosen. Normalising the text is the last rule in the chain: the same words written with different accents or spacing must produce the same bytes, or the same code would give two different seeds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The reader meets these steps the first time a wallet is created, and this chapter's own figures let them be followed by hand: the entropy the chapter works with, its four checksum bits, the first three word numbers its bits give, and the table of every entropy length with its checksum and word count. The same steps are met in the published test vectors, which this course runs rather than quotes, and in the chapter's own visual for the word count, where the figures are computed on every build rather than written down (Palatinus et al., 2013) (Trezor, 2026).

Two cautions. The checksum protects the words and not the user's intention: it catches a mistyped word, which is its purpose, but it cannot tell that the code written down belongs to a different wallet. And the entropy is the only secret in the chain, so the strength of everything that follows is the strength of that one draw; a code generated from a source a person chose, rather than from the wallet's own generator, has the length of a strong code and the strength of a guess, which is why the chapter gives that mistake a section of its own (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013).

nodes.label: Entropy
nodes.body: Entropy, in this chapter, is the amount of unpredictability in a value, counted in bits: a value with 128 bits of entropy is one that an attacker could only find by searching among 2 to the 128 equally likely possibilities. The chapter uses the word for the random input of the process, saying that the wallet starts from a source of entropy, adds a checksum and then maps the entropy to a word list, and that step one is to create a random sequence, which it glosses as entropy, of 128 to 256 bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard requires that this entropy be a multiple of 32 bits and says that with more entropy security is improved but the sentence length increases (Palatinus et al., 2013).

paras.text: Entropy, in this chapter, is the amount of unpredictability in a value, counted in bits: a value with 128 bits of entropy is one that an attacker could only find by searching among 2 to the 128 equally likely possibilities. The chapter uses the word for the random input of the process, saying that the wallet starts from a source of entropy, adds a checksum and then maps the entropy to a word list, and that step one is to create a random sequence, which it glosses as entropy, of 128 to 256 bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard requires that this entropy be a multiple of 32 bits and says that with more entropy security is improved but the sentence length increases (Palatinus et al., 2013).

Entropy is the one quantity that decides whether a wallet can be guessed, and it cannot be added later. The chapter's opening example makes the point about repeatability rather than secrecy: a hash function always produces the same output for the same input, but if the input changes even slightly the output is different, and if the function is cryptographically secure nobody should be able to predict the new output, not even if they know the new input (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). All of that holds only if the first value was unpredictable; a seed derived from a guessable value is guessable however many times it is hashed.

A reader meets entropy at the first moment a wallet is created, usually invisibly. The chapter's own demonstration reads bytes from the operating system's random device and hashes them to produce a seed, printing the 64 hexadecimal digits of the result (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example takes the chapter's own 128-bit entropy value and counts it: sixteen bytes, each of eight bits, make the 128 bits that the first table of the chapter labels entropy input (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 4 of the book discussed the same requirement for a single private key, where the entropy comes from a cryptographically secure random source.

The mechanism of interest is how little entropy is needed to produce a great deal of key material. The chapter explains that a hash function lets one take one random value and transform it into a practically unlimited number of seemingly random values, and that using the same function with the same input, called a seed, produces the same seemingly random values again (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The entropy of the seed is therefore the entropy of the whole wallet: no derivation step adds any, because every later value is a function of the seed. The sidebar on how much entropy is needed works through the consequences of that fact in numbers.

Two misconceptions are worth naming. The first is that longer is always better: the chapter's sidebar concludes that there is no apparent benefit to using more than 128 bits of entropy, because the security strength of a Bitcoin public key is 128 bits, while noting one secondary benefit of more entropy if part of a code is seen by an attacker (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is that entropy is a property of the value: it is a property of how the value was produced, so a 128-bit number a person invented has far less than 128 bits of entropy, which is the point of the brainwallet section of the previous branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013).

nodes.example: 128 random bits in sixteen bytes
nodes.definition: Entropy is the unpredictability of a value, measured in bits; a BIP39 code encodes 128 to 256 bits of it, drawn by the wallet from a source of randomness and not chosen by a person.

nodes.label: BIP39 checksum
nodes.body: A checksum is a short value computed from data and stored with it, so that a later reader can recompute it and notice if the data has changed. The BIP39 checksum is defined exactly: create a checksum of the random sequence by taking the first entropy-length divided by 32 bits of its SHA-256 hash, and add the checksum to the end of the random sequence (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013). For the 128-bit entropy of the chapter's table that is 128 over 32, four bits, and the worked example computes them: the first byte of the hash written in binary, cut to four digits, is 0111.

paras.text: A checksum is a short value computed from data and stored with it, so that a later reader can recompute it and notice if the data has changed. The BIP39 checksum is defined exactly: create a checksum of the random sequence by taking the first entropy-length divided by 32 bits of its SHA-256 hash, and add the checksum to the end of the random sequence (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013). For the 128-bit entropy of the chapter's table that is 128 over 32, four bits, and the worked example computes them: the first byte of the hash written in binary, cut to four digits, is 0111.

The checksum is what turns a long string of words from a secret into a secret that can be typed back. Without it, any twelve words from the list would be a valid code and a single wrong word would silently produce a different wallet. With it, software can tell the user that the code is wrong before deriving anything, and the standard requires exactly that: although using a sentence not generated by the standard's own procedure is possible, this is not advised, and software must compute a checksum for the sentence using a word list and issue a warning if it is invalid (Palatinus et al., 2013).

A reader meets the checksum in two places. The first is the arithmetic of the chapter's table, where the checksum column grows with the entropy: 4 bits for 128, 5 for 160, 6 for 192, 7 for 224 and 8 for 256 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is a wallet's refusal to accept a code that was typed wrongly. Because the checksum is computed from the entropy and not from the words, and because its own bits become part of the last word, the detection is of the whole code and not of one word in isolation.

The mechanism is a hash function used as a compressor. SHA-256 maps the entropy to 32 bytes; the leading bits of that output are taken, however many are needed; and they are appended so that the total length is a multiple of 11. For the 12-word case the entropy contributes 128 bits, which is 11 segments of 11 bits plus 7 bits left over, and the four checksum bits complete the twelfth segment, so the last word of a 12-word code carries 7 bits of entropy and 4 bits of checksum. A wrong word therefore changes both the data and the value being checked, which is why the error is noticed.

The standard is candid that this checksum is weak, and the reason is its length. It lists as a shortcoming that the checksum is short, so it gives only modest odds of catching random errors, with about one error in 256 missed, and that it is not able to provide any assistance in correcting errors (Palatinus et al., 2013). Four bits for a 12-word code are weaker still. A student should therefore not treat a valid checksum as proof that a code is the right one, only as evidence that it was probably typed correctly; and should notice that this is precisely the gap that codex32's error-correcting checksum was designed to close (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

nodes.example: the first four bits of a SHA-256 hash
nodes.definition: The BIP39 checksum is the first entropy-length over 32 bits of the SHA-256 hash of the entropy, appended to it, so that a mistyped code can be detected but not corrected.

nodes.label: Word list
nodes.body: The word list is the dictionary against which the bits of a code are read. The chapter's step five says to map each 11-bit value to a word from the predefined dictionary of 2,048 words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The number is not a round decimal but a round binary one: the worked example shows that 2 to the 11th is 2,048, so one word carries exactly 11 bits and no bits are wasted. The list used by every English BIP39 wallet is the one in the standard's repository, a copy of which is saved for this chapter and read by its claims (Palatinus et al., 2013).

paras.text: The word list is the dictionary against which the bits of a code are read. The chapter's step five says to map each 11-bit value to a word from the predefined dictionary of 2,048 words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The number is not a round decimal but a round binary one: the worked example shows that 2 to the 11th is 2,048, so one word carries exactly 11 bits and no bits are wasted. The list used by every English BIP39 wallet is the one in the standard's repository, a copy of which is saved for this chapter and read by its claims (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The list is what makes the code transcribable, and its design decides how often transcription fails. The standard sets out the criteria of an ideal list: a smart selection of words such that the first four letters identify a word unambiguously; similar words avoided, because pairs such as build and built, woman and women, or quick and quickly are harder to remember and more error-prone and easier to guess; and a sorted list, which lets implementations use binary search and allows a prefix tree to be used (Palatinus et al., 2013). Each criterion is a defence against a human error rather than an attacker.

A reader meets the list every time a wallet shows or accepts words. The chapter's example code, army van defense carry jealous true garbage claim echo media make crunch, is twelve of its entries, and the worked examples of this branch look them up by index: 96 is army and 423 is crunch, the first and last words of that code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013). The list is shared beyond BIP39: SLIP39 uses its own list of 1,024 words with its own criteria, while Aezeed encodes its ciphertext with the default BIP39 English list (Rusnak et al., 2017) (Lightning Labs, 2026a).

The mechanism is a plain lookup in both directions. To write a code, the bits are cut into 11-bit groups and each group's value, a number from 0 to 2,047, selects the word at that position; to read a code, each word's position is found and written back as 11 bits (Palatinus et al., 2013). Because the list is a fixed, ordered sequence, the mapping is exact and reversible, and because the first four letters are unique, a wallet can accept abbreviations and still recover the full word. The list must be encoded in UTF-8 using normalisation form compatibility decomposition, which the normalisation section explains (Palatinus et al., 2013).

Dependence on the list is the scheme's best-known weakness. The standard says that because the words rather than the entropy are hashed to make the seed, translating a code to a different list necessarily creates a completely different seed, and therefore strongly discourages non-English lists, adding that if one is needed an existing list should be used rather than a new one invented (Palatinus et al., 2013). Electrum's document calls the requirement plainly inconsistent, since BIP39 still needs the list in order to compute its checksum even though keys and addresses were deliberately made independent of it (Electrum Technologies, 2026). A learner should treat the English list as part of the backup.

nodes.example: 2,048 words, eleven bits each
nodes.definition: The BIP39 word list holds exactly 2,048 words, so that each word stands for 11 bits; the list is sorted, has unique four-letter prefixes and avoids similar pairs.

nodes.label: Eleven-bit segment
nodes.body: An eleven-bit segment is one group of the bit string that becomes one word. The chapter's step four is to split the result, meaning the entropy with its checksum appended, into 11-bit length segments, and step five maps each segment's value to a word (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard says the same with the arithmetic attached: the concatenated bits are split into groups of 11 bits, each encoding a number from 0 to 2,047, serving as an index into a word list (Palatinus et al., 2013).

paras.text: An eleven-bit segment is one group of the bit string that becomes one word. The chapter's step four is to split the result, meaning the entropy with its checksum appended, into 11-bit length segments, and step five maps each segment's value to a word (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard says the same with the arithmetic attached: the concatenated bits are split into groups of 11 bits, each encoding a number from 0 to 2,047, serving as an index into a word list (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The segment is where a reader can see that a recovery code is not a sentence but a number written in a strange base. Each word is a digit in base 2,048, and the whole code is one large integer, the entropy, with a few check digits at the end. Seeing this removes the temptation to think of the words as independently meaningful, which matters because it explains why the order of the words is as important as the words themselves and why one wrong word invalidates the code.

A reader meets the segments when checking a code by hand, which the worked example does for the book's own code: the 128 bits of the entropy 0c1e24e5917779d297e14d45f14e1a1a begin 00001100000, 11110001000, 00100111001, and those three values, 96, 1929 and 459, select army, van and defense, the first three words the chapter prints (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013). The same bit-slicing appears in the other schemes with different widths: SLIP39 uses 10-bit segments against a list of 1,024 words, and codex32 uses 5-bit characters of the bech32 alphabet (Rusnak et al., 2017) (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

The mechanism is positional, and the boundaries do not respect byte boundaries. Eleven does not divide eight, so a segment generally straddles two bytes of the entropy, which is why an implementation works on a bit string rather than on bytes. For a 12-word code the first 11 segments use 121 of the 128 entropy bits and the twelfth segment takes the remaining 7 entropy bits together with the 4 checksum bits, which is the arithmetic the checksum section describes from the other side.

Two traps are common here. The first is to assume that each word corresponds to a fixed part of the entropy in a way that lets a single word be corrected independently: it does not, because the segments overlap byte boundaries and the last segment mixes entropy with checksum. The second is to read the segments from the hexadecimal digits directly: hexadecimal digits are four bits and a segment is eleven, so the conversion has to go through the full bit string, which is what the worked example does.

nodes.example: the first three segments of the book's code
nodes.definition: The entropy and checksum are read as consecutive groups of 11 bits, each group a number from 0 to 2,047 that selects one word of the list.

nodes.label: Code length
nodes.body: The length of a recovery code is not a free choice: it is determined by the amount of entropy. The chapter prints the relation as a table with four columns, entropy in bits, checksum in bits, entropy plus checksum, and recovery code words, whose five rows run from 128 bits and 12 words to 256 bits and 24 words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard gives the same table with two formulas above it: the checksum length is the entropy over 32, and the number of words is the entropy plus the checksum over 11 (Palatinus et al., 2013).

paras.text: The length of a recovery code is not a free choice: it is determined by the amount of entropy. The chapter prints the relation as a table with four columns, entropy in bits, checksum in bits, entropy plus checksum, and recovery code words, whose five rows run from 128 bits and 12 words to 256 bits and 24 words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard gives the same table with two formulas above it: the checksum length is the entropy over 32, and the number of words is the entropy plus the checksum over 11 (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The table answers the question a user actually asks, which is what the number of words tells them. A 12-word code means 128 bits of entropy; a 24-word code means 256. Because the formulas are fixed, the word count is a reliable statement about the strength of the backup, and a code of a length not in the table is not a BIP39 code at all. For software the same arithmetic is a cheap validity test before any hashing is done.

A reader meets the lengths as wallet options. The chapter says that a wallet shows a sequence of 12 to 24 words when first creating a wallet, and its own tables use 12 words for the 128-bit example and 24 for the 256-bit one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The figures also appear in the comparison with the other schemes: Electrum version 2 accepts 132 bits, which is 12 words of 11 bits with no checksum of its own; Aezeed encodes 33 bytes as 24 words; SLIP39's 128-bit secret becomes 20 words of 10 bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Electrum Technologies, 2026) (Lightning Labs, 2026a) (Rusnak et al., 2017).

The worked example computes the chapter's whole table from the two formulas, and the agreement is exact for all five rows. The reason the word counts come out whole is that the entropy is a multiple of 32: if the entropy is 32 times some number k, the checksum is k bits and the total is 33k, which 11 divides. That is also why codes grow in steps of three words, from 12 to 15 to 18 to 21 to 24, and why no 13-word BIP39 code exists.

A longer code is not automatically a better one. The chapter's sidebar explains that BIP32 extended private keys consist of a 256-bit key and a 256-bit chain code, so at most 512 bits of entropy can be held, that only slightly fewer than 2 to the 256 regular private keys exist, and that the security strength of a Bitcoin public key is 128 bits, from which it concludes that there is no apparent benefit beyond 128 bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It also reports that as of 2023 most modern wallets generate 128 bits, or a value near it such as Electrum's 132 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The practical consequence is that a 12-word code is not a weak backup.

nodes.example: the chapter's entropy and word-length table
nodes.definition: Entropy length, checksum length and word count are tied together: the checksum is a thirty-second of the entropy and the total divided by 11 is the number of words, so codes have 12, 15, 18, 21 or 24 words.

nodes.label: Text normalisation
nodes.body: Text normalisation is the operation that rewrites a piece of text in one agreed form before it is used as data. It is needed because the same visible characters can be stored in more than one way: the worked example takes the single character e with an acute accent, which is one code point, and shows that after normalisation form compatibility decomposition it is two, a plain e followed by a combining accent. BIP39 requires exactly this form, saying that the word list may contain native characters but they must be encoded in UTF-8 using normalisation form compatibility decomposition, abbreviated NFKD (Palatinus et al., 2013).

paras.text: Text normalisation is the operation that rewrites a piece of text in one agreed form before it is used as data. It is needed because the same visible characters can be stored in more than one way: the worked example takes the single character e with an acute accent, which is one code point, and shows that after normalisation form compatibility decomposition it is two, a plain e followed by a combining accent. BIP39 requires exactly this form, saying that the word list may contain native characters but they must be encoded in UTF-8 using normalisation form compatibility decomposition, abbreviated NFKD (Palatinus et al., 2013).

Without the rule, two wallets could disagree about a code that looks identical on both screens. The seed is derived by hashing the text of the words and the text of the passphrase, and a hash function gives a different output for different bytes, however similar they look. The requirement therefore protects the one property the whole scheme rests on, that the same words always give the same seed, and it matters most for the localised word lists and for passphrases, which may contain any characters at all.

A reader meets normalisation in the derivation step: the standard says that the sentence, in UTF-8 NFKD, is used as the password and the string mnemonic plus passphrase, again in UTF-8 NFKD, as the salt (Palatinus et al., 2013). Electrum has a rule of its own with the same purpose and a different shape: its preparation function removes all but one space between words, removes diacritics, and removes spaces between Asian characters before the phrase is hashed (Electrum Technologies, 2026). SLIP39 avoids the problem for passphrases by requiring them to contain only printable ASCII characters (Rusnak et al., 2017).

The mechanism is a standard mapping applied character by character. Compatibility decomposition replaces each precomposed character by its parts and rewrites compatibility characters into their ordinary equivalents, and the result is a sequence of code points that is the same whatever form the input took. In Python the operation is one call in the standard library's unicodedata module, which the worked example uses; a wallet applies it to the words and to the passphrase just before they are given to the key-stretching function.

The rule is easy to forget and its failures are silent, because a wrong normalisation gives a valid-looking seed for an empty wallet, exactly like a mistyped passphrase. The checksum does not help, since it is computed over the entropy rather than the text. For a course the safe habit is the one BIP39's own test vectors enforce: the Japanese vectors exist specifically to test heavily normalised symbols in the passphrase, and any implementation that passes them has got the rule right (Palatinus et al., 2013).

nodes.example: one character, two code points
nodes.definition: Normalisation rewrites text in a single canonical form before it is hashed, so that two spellings a person cannot distinguish produce the same bytes and therefore the same seed.

nodes.label: From the code to the seed
nodes.body: This group covers the last three of BIP39's nine steps, the ones that turn words back into the number a wallet actually uses. The chapter states them in order: the first parameter to the PBKDF2 key-stretching function is the entropy produced from step six; the second is a salt composed of the string constant mnemonic concatenated with an optional user-supplied passphrase; and PBKDF2 stretches these using 2,048 rounds of hashing with the HMAC-SHA512 algorithm, producing a 512-bit value as its final output, which is the seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group covers the last three of BIP39's nine steps, the ones that turn words back into the number a wallet actually uses. The chapter states them in order: the first parameter to the PBKDF2 key-stretching function is the entropy produced from step six; the second is a salt composed of the string constant mnemonic concatenated with an optional user-supplied passphrase; and PBKDF2 stretches these using 2,048 rounds of hashing with the HMAC-SHA512 algorithm, producing a 512-bit value as its final output, which is the seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because this is the step at which a passphrase can be added, and because it is the step most often misunderstood. The output is not the entropy that went in: it is 512 bits derived from it, and the derivation is one-way, which is why an arbitrary BIP32 seed cannot be written as a BIP39 code (Palatinus et al., 2013). The number of rounds is also the only defence against an attacker who knows part of a code, and the chapter is careful about how much that defence is worth.

The last steps work by making the derivation deliberately expensive. The words, normalised, become the password; the fixed text of the standard, followed by the passphrase if there is one, becomes the salt; and the two are fed to a key-stretching function which applies a keyed hash two thousand and forty-eight times over, each round taking the previous round's output, so that the cost of trying one candidate is two thousand and forty-eight times the cost of one hash. The result is sixty-four bytes, and those bytes are the seed. Two properties of the construction matter. The output is longer than the entropy that went in, which adds no strength and is not meant to: stretching protects a weak password against a search, and the seed's real strength stays that of the original draw. And the passphrase enters through the salt rather than through the password, which is why no checksum can cover it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013) (Moriarty et al., 2017) (Krawczyk et al., 1997).

The reader meets this step as the pause when a wallet is restored, and as the three seeds the chapter prints: one from its words with no passphrase, one from the same words with a passphrase, and one from its longer code. This course recomputes all three from the standard rather than copying them, and checks them against the published vectors of an independent implementation. The step is met again in chapter 4's discussion of how keys are protected, and in any wallet that offers to encrypt a backup, because the same stretching is what stands between a short password and the data behind it (Palatinus et al., 2013) (Trezor, 2026).

The caution is that the passphrase has no safety net at all. Every passphrase produces a valid seed, so a typo produces a working wallet that is simply the wrong one, with no error and no clue; the only test is to look for the funds. The second caution is about the stretching count itself: two thousand and forty-eight rounds was modest when the standard was written and is more modest now, which is why one of the alternative schemes in this chapter uses a function with a far higher cost, and why this number should be read as a historical choice rather than a recommendation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013) (Lightning Labs, 2026a).

nodes.label: Key-stretching function
nodes.body: A key-stretching function is a function that turns a secret, typically one with limited entropy, into a key, and that is made deliberately expensive to compute. The chapter introduces it when it says that the entropy is used to derive a longer, 512-bit seed through the use of the key-stretching function PBKDF2, and that the function takes two parameters, the entropy and a salt (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word stretching refers to the cost rather than to the length: the output could be produced far more cheaply, and is not.

paras.text: A key-stretching function is a function that turns a secret, typically one with limited entropy, into a key, and that is made deliberately expensive to compute. The chapter introduces it when it says that the entropy is used to derive a longer, 512-bit seed through the use of the key-stretching function PBKDF2, and that the function takes two parameters, the entropy and a salt (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The word stretching refers to the cost rather than to the length: the output could be produced far more cheaply, and is not.

The purpose is to raise the price of guessing. The chapter explains what this does and does not buy: the function, with its 2,048 rounds of hashing, makes it slightly harder to brute-force the recovery code using software, while special-purpose hardware is not significantly affected; for an attacker who must guess an entire code, the 128-bit minimum length already provides more than sufficient security; but where an attacker learns a small part of a user's code, key stretching adds some security by slowing down how fast combinations can be checked (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Stretching is therefore a defence for the partially-compromised case.

A reader meets stretching in every scheme of the first branch, with different parameters, and the differences are the chapter's own comparison. BIP39 uses 2,048 rounds and the chapter says its parameters were considered weak by modern standards even when it was published almost a decade earlier, likely a consequence of being designed for compatibility with hardware signing devices with low-powered processors; some alternatives use stronger parameters, such as Aezeed's 32,768 rounds of the more complex scrypt algorithm, although these may be less convenient on such devices (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example is that ratio: 32,768 over 2,048 is 16 times the work.

The mechanism is iteration. A single hash is cheap, so the function applies the underlying operation again and again, each round depending on the previous one, so that the total cost is the number of rounds times the cost of one round, for the defender once and for the attacker once per guess. Newer functions add a second dimension: scrypt is specified as a password-based key derivation function based on memory-hard functions, which its specification says offer added protection against attacks using custom hardware, the very hardware the chapter says BIP39's round count does not slow down (Percival and Josefsson, 2016) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Stretching cannot rescue a weak secret, and the chapter's own figures show why: multiplying an attacker's work by 2,048 is worth about 11 bits of entropy, which is useful beside 64 bits of a half-seen code and irrelevant beside 128 bits of a full one. It also costs the honest user time on every restoration, which is the reason the parameters were chosen low. A learner should read a round count as a statement about the designers' expectations of the attacker's hardware, and should notice that codex32 omits stretching entirely so that the scheme can be computed by hand (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

nodes.example: 2,048 rounds against 32,768
nodes.definition: A key-stretching function derives a key from a secret deliberately slowly, by repeating a hash many times, so that each guess an attacker makes costs more.

nodes.label: PBKDF2
nodes.body: PBKDF2 is the second password-based key derivation function of the PKCS #5 standard, and it is the particular key-stretching function BIP39 names. Its specification defines it as applying a pseudorandom function to derive keys, with four inputs: a password, a salt, an iteration count and the intended length of the derived key in octets, and says it is recommended for new applications (Moriarty et al., 2017). BIP39 fixes all four: the sentence is the password, the string mnemonic followed by the passphrase is the salt, the iteration count is 2,048, HMAC-SHA512 is the pseudorandom function, and the derived key is 512 bits, that is 64 bytes (Palatinus et al., 2013).

paras.text: PBKDF2 is the second password-based key derivation function of the PKCS #5 standard, and it is the particular key-stretching function BIP39 names. Its specification defines it as applying a pseudorandom function to derive keys, with four inputs: a password, a salt, an iteration count and the intended length of the derived key in octets, and says it is recommended for new applications (Moriarty et al., 2017). BIP39 fixes all four: the sentence is the password, the string mnemonic followed by the passphrase is the salt, the iteration count is 2,048, HMAC-SHA512 is the pseudorandom function, and the derived key is 512 bits, that is 64 bytes (Palatinus et al., 2013).

Naming a standard function rather than inventing one is what makes a recovery code portable. Any implementation with a correct PBKDF2 produces the same seed from the same words, which is why a code written by one wallet can be read by another, and why this course can reproduce the book's tables with nothing but Python's standard library. Python's documentation describes its own function in the same terms, as providing the PKCS #5 password-based key derivation function 2, using HMAC as a pseudorandom function (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The worked example is the chapter's first table, recomputed: the twelve words army van defense carry jealous true garbage claim echo media make crunch, with the salt mnemonic and 2,048 iterations of HMAC-SHA512, give a seed that begins 5b56c417303faa3f, exactly the value the chapter prints (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The claims of this chapter check all 64 bytes of that seed and of the chapter's other two tables, and they also reproduce the example in Python's own documentation, which uses SHA-256, a different salt and 500,000 iterations (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The mechanism is HMAC applied in a chain. HMAC is the keyed hash of RFC 2104, which computes its output as the hash of the key combined with an outer pad together with the hash of the key combined with an inner pad and the message (Krawczyk et al., 1997). PBKDF2 computes the first HMAC over the salt and a block counter, then applies HMAC repeatedly to the previous output, and combines all the intermediate values by exclusive-or; the result is as long as the hash, and further blocks are produced for longer keys. With SHA-512 one block is 64 bytes, which is exactly the length BIP39 wants, so a BIP39 seed is one such chain of 2,048 links. The worked example writes that chain out with the keyed hash rather than calling the standard library's own function for it, because the Python of the course's browser pages is built without that function; a claim of this chapter checks that the two give the same seed.

Two details matter in practice. The first is the order of the arguments: the words are the password and the salted constant is the salt, and swapping them produces a valid-looking but wrong seed, which no checksum will catch. The second is that PBKDF2's security rests on the password: its specification notes that the salt's purpose is to make precomputation infeasible, not to add secrecy, since the salt is assumed to be known (Moriarty et al., 2017). The chapter's own judgement on the parameters, that they were weak even when published, applies to the iteration count and not to the function (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the book's first seed, recomputed
nodes.definition: PBKDF2 is the standard password-based key derivation function that BIP39 uses: it applies HMAC-SHA512 2,048 times to the words and the salt and returns 64 bytes.
