nodes.label: Salt
nodes.body: A salt is a value that is combined with a secret before a key is derived from it, in order to make the derivation specific to that salt. The chapter explains the general purpose first: the purpose of a salt in a key-stretching function is to make it difficult to build a lookup table enabling a brute-force attack; and then the particular use BIP39 makes of it: in this standard the salt has another purpose, as it allows the introduction of a passphrase that serves as an additional security factor protecting the seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard states the value exactly: the salt is the string mnemonic plus the passphrase, both in normalised UTF-8 (Palatinus et al., 2013).

paras.text: A salt is a value that is combined with a secret before a key is derived from it, in order to make the derivation specific to that salt. The chapter explains the general purpose first: the purpose of a salt in a key-stretching function is to make it difficult to build a lookup table enabling a brute-force attack; and then the particular use BIP39 makes of it: in this standard the salt has another purpose, as it allows the introduction of a passphrase that serves as an additional security factor protecting the seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard states the value exactly: the salt is the string mnemonic plus the passphrase, both in normalised UTF-8 (Palatinus et al., 2013).

The first purpose is the classical one. The specification of PBKDF2 explains it with a number: a salt serves to produce a large set of keys for a given password, one of which is selected at random according to the salt, so that it is difficult for an opponent to precompute all the keys, or even the most likely keys, corresponding to a dictionary of passwords; with a 64-bit salt there are as many as 2 to the 64 keys for each password (Moriarty et al., 2017). The second purpose, carrying the passphrase, is BIP39's own and is what makes a single code able to stand for many wallets.

A reader meets the salt as a string that is almost always the same. With no passphrase it is the eight characters mnemonic, which the chapter says produces a specific 512-bit seed from any given recovery code; with a passphrase it is mnemonic followed by that passphrase, and the chapter says the stretching function then produces a different seed from the same code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example shows the effect with the chapter's own passphrase: the same password under the two salts gives two different outputs, so the comparison is false.

Mechanically the salt is simply the second argument, and PBKDF2 feeds it into the first HMAC of its chain together with a block counter (Moriarty et al., 2017). Because it enters the first link, a change of one character changes every later link and therefore the whole output: there is no part of the seed that depends only on the words. That is why the chapter can say that every possible passphrase leads to a different seed, and why the set of wallets reachable from one code is as large as the set of possible passphrases (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

BIP39's use of the salt breaks one of the salt's usual properties, and a reader should notice it. A classical salt is random and stored beside the derived key, so that two users with the same password get different keys; BIP39's salt is a fixed constant when no passphrase is used, so every wallet in the world uses the same salt, and the protection against precomputed tables comes from the 128 bits of entropy in the words rather than from the salt. The specification's recommendation that a salt should be at least eight random octets is therefore not met, and does not need to be met, in this one special case (Moriarty et al., 2017).

nodes.example: the constant mnemonic, with or without a passphrase
nodes.definition: A salt is the second, non-secret input of a key derivation function; BIP39's salt is the string mnemonic followed by the optional passphrase, which is how the passphrase changes the seed.

nodes.label: Root seed
nodes.body: The root seed is the single number that stands for a whole wallet. The chapter introduces it at the head of the section on creating a hierarchical deterministic wallet: such wallets are created from a single root seed, which is a 128-, 256- or 512-bit random number, and most commonly this seed is generated by or decrypted from a recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's glossary gives the same definition in one line, calling the HD wallet seed or root seed a potentially short value used as a seed to generate the master private key and master chain code for an HD wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The root seed is the single number that stands for a whole wallet. The chapter introduces it at the head of the section on creating a hierarchical deterministic wallet: such wallets are created from a single root seed, which is a 128-, 256- or 512-bit random number, and most commonly this seed is generated by or decrypted from a recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's glossary gives the same definition in one line, calling the HD wallet seed or root seed a potentially short value used as a seed to generate the master private key and master chain code for an HD wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The seed is the object that backups are really about. The chapter says that every key in the wallet is deterministically derived from this root seed, which makes it possible to re-create the entire wallet from that seed in any compatible wallet, and so makes it easy to back up, restore, export and import wallets containing thousands or even millions of keys by transferring only the recovery code that the seed is derived from (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). One short number therefore replaces an unbounded list of keys, which is the whole gain of determinism.

A reader meets the seed as the output of the previous sections and the input of the next branch. BIP39 always produces 512 bits of it, which the worked example counts as 64 bytes, and BIP32 is more permissive: it asks for a seed of a chosen length between 128 and 512 bits, advising 256, generated from a random number generator (Wuille, 2012). The chapter's sidebar notes that BIP32 allows seeds from 128 to 512 bits while the schemes feed it between 128 and 256 bits of entropy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

What happens to the seed is the subject of the next branch, and one sentence of it belongs here: the root seed is given to HMAC-SHA512 and the resulting hash is used to create a master private key and a master chain code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012). Nothing else in the wallet is random. The seed's length matters only up to the size of that one operation's input, which is why BIP32 observes that the total number of possible extended key pairs is almost 2 to the 512 while the keys themselves are only 256 bits long and offer about half of that in terms of security, and concludes that master keys are generated from a potentially short seed value instead (Wuille, 2012).

The seed and the recovery code are not the same object, and the difference matters when software is chosen. The code is an encoding of the entropy; the seed is the stretched result; the mapping from code to seed is one-way, so a wallet that imports a seed directly cannot show the user words for it (Palatinus et al., 2013). A wallet that asks for a seed in hexadecimal and a wallet that asks for words are therefore asking for different things, and giving the wrong one produces an empty wallet with no warning.

nodes.example: 512 bits, that is 64 bytes
nodes.definition: The root seed is the value from which every key of a hierarchical deterministic wallet is derived; BIP39 produces one of 512 bits, and BIP32 accepts 128 to 512.

nodes.label: Optional passphrase in BIP39
nodes.body: The optional passphrase of BIP39 is a user-supplied string that is appended to the salt of the key derivation. The chapter devotes a section to it: the standard allows the use of an optional passphrase in the derivation of the seed, and if none is used the code is stretched with a salt consisting of the constant string mnemonic, producing a specific 512-bit seed from any given code; if a passphrase is used, the stretching function produces a different seed from that same code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The previous branch discussed the choice; this section is about the mechanism and its arithmetic.

paras.text: The optional passphrase of BIP39 is a user-supplied string that is appended to the salt of the key derivation. The chapter devotes a section to it: the standard allows the use of an optional passphrase in the derivation of the seed, and if none is used the code is stretched with a salt consisting of the constant string mnemonic, producing a specific 512-bit seed from any given code; if a passphrase is used, the stretching function produces a different seed from that same code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The previous branch discussed the choice; this section is about the mechanism and its arithmetic.

The consequence the chapter emphasises is that the passphrase cannot be validated. Given a single recovery code, every possible passphrase leads to a different seed; essentially there is no wrong passphrase; all passphrases are valid and they all lead to different seeds, forming a vast set of possible uninitialised wallets, and the set is so large, 2 to the 512, that there is no practical possibility of brute-forcing or accidentally guessing one that is in use (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter repeats the point as a tip: every passphrase leads to some wallet, which unless previously used will be empty (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example is the chapter's second table, recomputed from its inputs: the same twelve words, with the passphrase SuperDuperSecret appended to the constant salt, give a seed beginning 3b5df16df2157104, where the same words with no passphrase gave 5b56c417303faa3f (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A claim of this chapter checks all 64 bytes of both, and a further claim shows that four different passphrases give four different seeds, none of which is signalled as wrong.

The mechanism is a string concatenation inside the salt and nothing more: the salt is the eight characters mnemonic followed by the passphrase, both normalised, and the words remain the password (Palatinus et al., 2013). No separate field records whether a passphrase was used, and no checksum covers it, which is why the chapter groups BIP39 with Electrum version 2 and SLIP39 as schemes that do not include the passphrase in their checksum (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Aezeed, by enciphering rather than salting, is able to authenticate it instead (Lightning Labs, 2026a).

The risks are the ones the previous branch set out, and they are worth repeating where the mechanism is visible. A forgotten passphrase is an unrecoverable loss, because nothing in the code hints at it; a passphrase stored with the code is no second factor at all; and a mistyped passphrase shows an empty wallet rather than an error (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's closing advice on the subject is that passphrases are very useful but should be used only in combination with a carefully planned process for backup and recovery (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the book's second seed, recomputed
nodes.definition: In BIP39 the optional passphrase is appended to the constant salt, so any passphrase yields a different valid seed from the same words and none of them is wrong.

nodes.label: Security strength
nodes.body: Security strength is the amount of work an attacker needs in order to break something, expressed as a number of bits: a strength of 128 bits means about 2 to the 128 operations. The chapter's sidebar asks how much entropy a user needs and answers it with three such numbers. Extended private keys consist of a 256-bit key and a 256-bit chain code, for a total of 512 bits, so there are at most 2 to the 512 different extended private keys; there are only slightly fewer than 2 to the 256 regular private keys, and it is those that secure the bitcoins; and the security strength of a Bitcoin public key is 128 bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Security strength is the amount of work an attacker needs in order to break something, expressed as a number of bits: a strength of 128 bits means about 2 to the 128 operations. The chapter's sidebar asks how much entropy a user needs and answers it with three such numbers. Extended private keys consist of a 256-bit key and a 256-bit chain code, for a total of 512 bits, so there are at most 2 to the 512 different extended private keys; there are only slightly fewer than 2 to the 256 regular private keys, and it is those that secure the bitcoins; and the security strength of a Bitcoin public key is 128 bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The question is practical, because the schemes disagree. The chapter opens the sidebar by noting that the variation in these numbers makes it unclear how much entropy is needed for safety, and promises to demystify it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The answer has consequences a student can act on: a 12-word code is not a compromise, a 24-word code is not twice as strong, and the choice between them is not where attention should go.

The reasoning is met in three steps that the sidebar takes in turn. Starting with more than 512 bits of entropy still gives an extended private key containing 512 bits, so there is no point in more than 512; using more than 256 bits still gives private keys containing only 256 bits of entropy, and the chapter adds that there may be future protocols where extra entropy in the extended keys provides extra security but that this is not currently the case; and because an attacker with a classical computer would need about 2 to the 128 operations on Bitcoin's curve to find a private key for another user's public key, there is no apparent benefit to more than 128 bits of entropy, as long as the generated private keys are selected uniformly from the whole range (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example is those three numbers.

The mechanism behind the 128 is the mathematics of the curve, which chapter 4 of the book introduced: the best known attacks on the discrete logarithm problem for a 256-bit curve cost about the square root of the group size, that is about 2 to the 128 operations, and BIP32 repeats the figure when it states its own assumptions, saying that given a public key an attacker cannot find the private key more efficiently than by solving the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, assumed to require 2 to the 128 group operations (Wuille, 2012). A seed with more than 128 bits of entropy therefore protects a key whose public form can be attacked with 2 to the 128 work.

The sidebar names one real benefit of more entropy and warns against relying on it: if a fixed percentage of a code, but not the whole code, is seen by an attacker, more entropy makes the unseen part harder, so half of a 128-bit code, 64 bits, is plausibly brute-forcible while half of a 256-bit code is not; but the chapter does not recommend relying on this defence and advises either keeping codes very safe or distributing them with a scheme such as SLIP39 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The other caution is that these are strengths against computation, not against coercion or data loss, which are the risks the rest of the chapter addresses.

nodes.example: 512, 256 and 128 bits
nodes.definition: Security strength is the work an attacker needs, measured in bits; extended keys hold 512 bits, private keys 256, and the elliptic curve offers about 128, so more than 128 bits of entropy buys little.

nodes.label: Hierarchical deterministic wallet
nodes.body: A hierarchical deterministic wallet, which the chapter and the standards abbreviate to HD wallet, is a wallet whose keys form a tree, every node of which is computed from the seed. The book's glossary calls the hierarchical deterministic protocol the key creation and transfer protocol of BIP32, which allows creating child keys from parent keys in a hierarchy, and an HD wallet a wallet using that protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This branch is the detailed treatment the chapter promised when it first mentioned the idea: how the master keys are made from the seed, and how any key can produce children.

paras.text: A hierarchical deterministic wallet, which the chapter and the standards abbreviate to HD wallet, is a wallet whose keys form a tree, every node of which is computed from the seed. The book's glossary calls the hierarchical deterministic protocol the key creation and transfer protocol of BIP32, which allows creating child keys from parent keys in a hierarchy, and an HD wallet a wallet using that protocol (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This branch is the detailed treatment the chapter promised when it first mentioned the idea: how the master keys are made from the seed, and how any key can produce children.

The branch matters because the tree is what the whole chapter is for. A single seed is a good backup only if everything else can be recomputed from it, and BIP32 is the rule by which it is recomputed. BIP32's own motivation gives the two reasons it exists: deterministic wallets do not require frequent backups, and elliptic curve mathematics permits schemes in which public keys can be calculated without revealing private keys, which lets, for example, a web shop's server generate fresh addresses for each order without having access to the keys needed for spending (Wuille, 2012). The second reason is also why the tree has to be a tree and not a single chain: sharing one chain is all or nothing, whereas a hierarchy allows selective sharing (Wuille, 2012).

The reader has met the tree twice already: in the overview of key generation methods in the first branch, and in the key paths of the wallet that Bitcoin Core 31.1 created for this chapter, whose first address was reported at the path m/84h/0h/0h/0/0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Bitcoin Core's documentation lists BIP32 as implemented since version 0.13.0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter says that every modern Bitcoin wallet of which its authors are aware uses this scheme by default (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch has four groups. The master keys group turns the seed into the root of the tree with one keyed hash. The child derivation group gives the functions that make a child from a parent, in the two private forms, normal and hardened, and in the public form, and explains what a child key can and cannot be used for on its own. The extended keys group explains the pair of key and chain code that is passed around as one object, and how it is written as the xprv and xpub strings a reader will have seen. The tree navigation group gives the path notation and the two standards, BIP43 and BIP44, that fix what the levels of the tree mean.

One warning applies to the whole branch. The tree is enormous and nothing marks which parts of it a wallet used: the chapter points out that in a BIP32 tree there are approximately four billion first-level keys, each with its own four billion children, and so on, so it is not possible for a wallet application to generate even a small fraction of every possible key, which means that recovering from data loss requires knowing more than the recovery code and the algorithms, it also requires knowing which paths were used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That problem is the subject of the next branch, and a reader should keep it in mind while reading this one.

nodes.label: Master keys from the seed
nodes.body: This group covers the one step that turns a seed into the root of a key tree. The chapter states it in three short sentences: the root seed is input into the HMAC-SHA512 algorithm and the resulting hash is used to create a master private key and a master chain code; the master private key then generates a corresponding master public key using the normal elliptic curve multiplication that chapter 4 introduced; and the master chain code is used to introduce entropy in the function that creates child keys from parent keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group covers the one step that turns a seed into the root of a key tree. The chapter states it in three short sentences: the root seed is input into the HMAC-SHA512 algorithm and the resulting hash is used to create a master private key and a master chain code; the master private key then generates a corresponding master public key using the normal elliptic curve multiplication that chapter 4 introduced; and the master chain code is used to introduce entropy in the function that creates child keys from parent keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The step deserves its own group because it is where two objects appear that the rest of the branch keeps together. Everything below the root is derived, so if the master private key and the master chain code are right, the whole tree is right; if either is wrong, nothing below it is recoverable. The group also introduces the keyed hash that does all the work, which is used again at every level of the tree, so understanding it once is enough for the entire standard.

The step works by using a keyed hash as a splitter. The seed is passed to a keyed hash function together with a fixed key, the same text for every wallet in the world, and the function returns sixty-four bytes. The left thirty-two are read as a number and become the master private key; the right thirty-two become the master chain code. Three properties follow. Because the hash key is fixed and public, nothing secret is added at this step - the entire secret is the seed, and the master keys are a deterministic function of it. Because the two halves come from one hash, neither half reveals the other, which is what lets the chain code be shared alongside a public key without exposing the private one. And because the output is defined by the standard, any implementation given the same seed reaches the same root, which is what makes a code restorable in software that did not create it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012) (Krawczyk et al., 1997).

The reader meets the root as the thing a wallet never shows. What a wallet shows is the recovery code at one end and addresses at the other; the master key and chain code sit between them and surface only in an extended key, where the two are carried together. They are met directly in the standard's first test vector, which this course recomputes from the seed so that the arithmetic can be compared with the published values, and in the key origin of a descriptor, whose fingerprint is derived from the master public key (Wuille, 2012) (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

The caution is that this is the single point from which everything hangs. Whoever learns the master private key and the master chain code has every key of the wallet, present and future, in every branch; there is no part of the tree that is out of reach from the root. That is the reason the root is not stored where it can be read, and the reason hardened derivation exists further down - so that a compromise of one branch does not walk back up to the root. A learner should also note that the chain code is not a second secret of the same kind: it is secret in the private form and published in the public form, deliberately (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012).

nodes.label: HMAC-SHA512
nodes.body: HMAC is a way of using an ordinary hash function with a key, so that the output depends on both. Its specification defines the construction exactly: to compute HMAC over the data, one computes the hash of the key combined with an outer pad together with the hash of the key combined with an inner pad and the text, with the key padded with zeros to the hash's block length (Krawczyk et al., 1997). HMAC-SHA512 is that construction with SHA-512 as the hash, so its output is 64 bytes. BIP32 names it as the function used at every derivation and notes that it is specified in an RFC (Wuille, 2012).

paras.text: HMAC is a way of using an ordinary hash function with a key, so that the output depends on both. Its specification defines the construction exactly: to compute HMAC over the data, one computes the hash of the key combined with an outer pad together with the hash of the key combined with an inner pad and the text, with the key padded with zeros to the hash's block length (Krawczyk et al., 1997). HMAC-SHA512 is that construction with SHA-512 as the hash, so its output is 64 bytes. BIP32 names it as the function used at every derivation and notes that it is specified in an RFC (Wuille, 2012).

A keyed hash is needed because a plain hash would not keep the tree private. If children were derived by hashing the parent key alone, anyone who learned a child's position could derive it; by mixing in a second 32-byte value, the chain code, the standard makes the derivation depend on a secret that is not the key itself. BIP32 says this in its own words when it explains why extended keys exist: in order to prevent the derived keys from depending solely on the key itself, both private and public keys are first extended with an extra 256 bits of entropy (Wuille, 2012).

The reader meets this function three times in the chapter: making the master keys, deriving a normal child and deriving a hardened child, where the chapter says the parent public key, chain code and index number are combined and hashed with the HMAC-SHA512 algorithm to produce a 512-bit hash (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is also the function inside PBKDF2 in the previous branch, and the function Electrum uses with the key 'Seed version' to derive its version number (Palatinus et al., 2013) (Electrum Technologies, 2026). The worked example applies it as BIP32's master key generation does: the fixed key is the twelve characters of the text Bitcoin seed, the message is the seed, and the first eight bytes of the result are e8f32e723decf405, which agree with the standard's own first test vector.

The mechanism to remember is the shape of the output and how it is split. HMAC-SHA512 returns 64 bytes, which BIP32 always divides into two 32-byte halves that it calls I-left and I-right; the left half is used as key material and the right half becomes a chain code (Wuille, 2012). Because SHA-512 is a hash function, neither half reveals anything about the inputs, and because the two halves come from one computation, knowing one does not give the other. The key of the HMAC is the chain code at every derivation except the first, where it is the constant 'Bitcoin seed'.

Two confusions arise here. The first is between the two arguments: the chain code is the key and the key material is part of the message, which is the reverse of what the names suggest, and swapping them yields a plausible but incompatible wallet. The second is to treat HMAC as encryption: nothing is recoverable from its output, which is exactly why the derivation is one-way and why a child key cannot be used to find its parent, as the chapter states when it says the derivation function is a one-way function (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the keyed hash of the test vector's seed
nodes.definition: HMAC-SHA512 is a keyed hash: it combines a key and a message into 64 bytes that cannot be produced without the key, and BIP32 uses it both to make the master keys and to derive every child.

nodes.label: Master private key
nodes.body: The master private key is the private key at the root of the tree. The chapter calls it m and says that the root seed is input into HMAC-SHA512 and the resulting hash is used to create a master private key and a master chain code, and that the master private key then generates a corresponding master public key, written M, by the ordinary multiplication by the generator point (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 states the same as a procedure: split the HMAC output into two 32-byte sequences and use the left one, read as a 256-bit number, as the master secret key (Wuille, 2012).

paras.text: The master private key is the private key at the root of the tree. The chapter calls it m and says that the root seed is input into HMAC-SHA512 and the resulting hash is used to create a master private key and a master chain code, and that the master private key then generates a corresponding master public key, written M, by the ordinary multiplication by the generator point (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 states the same as a procedure: split the HMAC output into two 32-byte sequences and use the left one, read as a 256-bit number, as the master secret key (Wuille, 2012).

This key matters because it is the one key from which every other can be reached, and therefore the one key whose loss or leak is total. BIP32 draws the consequence when it discusses what care extended keys need: knowing an extended private key allows reconstruction of all descendant private keys and public keys (Wuille, 2012). The chapter's advice about hardened derivation at the first level follows from the same fact: as a best practice, the level-1 children of the master keys are always derived through hardened derivation to prevent compromise of the master keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets the master private key as the string that begins xprv, which the extended keys group explains, and as the letter m at the head of every path. The worked example computes it from the standard's own first test vector: the left 32 bytes of the keyed hash of the seed 000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f are e8f32e72...c8436b35, and the claims of this chapter check that serialising this number with its chain code gives exactly the xprv string the standard prints for chain m (Wuille, 2012).

The mechanism is a reading of bytes as a number, with one validity test. BIP32 says that if the left half, read as a number, is zero or greater than or equal to the order of the curve, the master key is invalid (Wuille, 2012); the order is the count of points the generator reaches, a number just below 2 to the 256, so the test fails only with vanishing probability. From the master private key the master public key follows by the multiplication of chapter 4, and the pair of key and chain code is what the next sections treat as a single object.

The master private key is not the seed, and the distinction is practical. The seed can be shorter and is what a recovery code encodes; the master key is derived from it and cannot be turned back into it. A wallet that exports an xprv is therefore exporting something that cannot be written as words, and a user who holds only an xprv has a complete wallet but no recovery code. BIP32 also notes that a serialised extended key that mixes up the private and public version bytes is invalid, and its fifth test vector exists to make implementations reject exactly such strings (Wuille, 2012).

nodes.example: the left half of the hash, as a number
nodes.definition: The master private key is the left 32 bytes of HMAC-SHA512 over the seed, read as a 256-bit number; it is the root of the tree and is written m.

nodes.label: Master chain code
nodes.body: The master chain code is the second half of the same hash. The chapter writes it c and says that it is used to introduce entropy in the function that creates child keys from parent keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 says to use the right 32-byte sequence as the master chain code, and explains what a chain code is for: both private and public keys are extended with an extra 256 bits of entropy, an extension called the chain code, which is identical for corresponding private and public keys and consists of 32 bytes (Wuille, 2012).

paras.text: The master chain code is the second half of the same hash. The chapter writes it c and says that it is used to introduce entropy in the function that creates child keys from parent keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 says to use the right 32-byte sequence as the master chain code, and explains what a chain code is for: both private and public keys are extended with an extra 256 bits of entropy, an extension called the chain code, which is identical for corresponding private and public keys and consists of 32 bytes (Wuille, 2012).

Without it, a public key would be enough to enumerate a family. The chapter makes the point when it introduces chain codes generally: the chain code introduces deterministic random data so that knowing the index and a child key is not sufficient to derive other child keys, and knowing a child key does not make it possible to find its siblings unless the chain code is also known (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chain code is therefore a secret in its own right, even though it is not a key and cannot sign anything.

A reader meets the chain code inside every extended key: an xprv or xpub string contains 32 bytes of chain code beside the key, which is why such strings are so much longer than an address (Wuille, 2012). The worked example computes the master chain code of the standard's first test vector, 873dff81...ed37d508, the right half of the hash whose left half was the master private key. The same value is what the claims of this chapter feed into the derivations that reproduce the standard's published keys.

Mechanically the chain code is the HMAC key at the next level. Each derivation calls HMAC-SHA512 with the parent's chain code as the key, and the right half of the result becomes the child's chain code, so each node of the tree has its own (Wuille, 2012). Because the chain code of a private key and of its public counterpart are the same, a holder of the extended public key can carry out the same hash for a normal child, which is what makes public derivation possible; the hardened variant breaks that symmetry deliberately.

The chain code is the part users forget, and forgetting it is fatal to recovery in two ways. A key without its chain code cannot derive anything, which the chapter states for the child case: without the child chain code, the child key cannot be used to derive any grandchildren (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And a chain code that leaks turns a single leaked child private key into a disaster, which is the risk BIP32 calls the weakness that may not be immediately obvious: knowledge of a parent extended public key plus any non-hardened private key descending from it is equivalent to knowing the parent extended private key (Wuille, 2012).

nodes.example: the right half of the hash
nodes.definition: The master chain code is the right 32 bytes of HMAC-SHA512 over the seed: 256 bits of extra entropy that make every derivation depend on more than the key.

nodes.label: Deriving child keys
nodes.body: This group covers the functions that make a child key from a parent. The chapter introduces them as the child key derivation functions, abbreviated CKD, and says that they are based on a one-way hash function that combines three things: a parent private or public key, a seed called a chain code of 256 bits, and an index number of 32 bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 defines three of them: from a private parent to a private child, from a public parent to a public child, and from a private parent to a public child, and states plainly that the fourth, from a public parent to a private child, is not possible (Wuille, 2012).

paras.text: This group covers the functions that make a child key from a parent. The chapter introduces them as the child key derivation functions, abbreviated CKD, and says that they are based on a one-way hash function that combines three things: a parent private or public key, a seed called a chain code of 256 bits, and an index number of 32 bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 defines three of them: from a private parent to a private child, from a public parent to a public child, and from a private parent to a public child, and states plainly that the fourth, from a public parent to a private child, is not possible (Wuille, 2012).

The group is the mathematical centre of the chapter. Everything that makes an HD wallet useful, the ability to hand a server an extended public key, the ability to keep private keys on a device that never sees the internet, the ability to restore a whole wallet from one code, is a consequence of how these three functions relate. The group is also where the one serious hazard of the design lives, the leak that hardened derivation exists to prevent, so a reader who skips it will not understand why paths contain apostrophes.

The derivation works the same way at every node and in both directions. The function takes a key, its chain code and an index number, concatenates them, and passes them to the keyed hash; the left half of the result is added to the parent private key to give the child private key, and the right half becomes the child's chain code. Because adding that left half to the private key corresponds, on the curve, to adding its multiple of the generator point to the public key, the same left half derives the child public key from the parent public key - so a party with only the public key and the chain code can derive public children. The index chooses which child, and the standard splits the four thousand million indices of each node into two halves: the lower half uses the parent public key in the hash and so allows public derivation, while the upper half, called hardened, uses the parent private key instead and therefore cannot be derived publicly at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012).

The reader meets this function at every step of every path in the rest of the chapter: each slash in a path is one application of it, and the apostrophe or the letter h on a level means that the index was taken from the hardened half. It is met in the extended public key a web store is given, which is exactly the parent key and chain code the public form of the function needs, and in this course's own derivations, which reproduce the standard's test vectors chain by chain and the addresses an independent node derived from the same account descriptor (Wuille, 2012) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is the one case where the construction leaks, and the standard names it. If an attacker obtains a parent extended public key and any one non-hardened child private key, the parent private key follows by subtraction, and with it the whole branch. Hardened derivation exists to close exactly that path, which is why the account levels of the standard paths are hardened and the branches below them are not. A learner should also keep in mind that a child key on its own is indistinguishable from a key drawn at random, which is a privacy property and not a security one (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012).

nodes.label: Child key derivation
nodes.body: Child key derivation is the operation that produces one child of one parent. The chapter describes the inputs and the split in two sentences: the parent public key, chain code and index number are combined and hashed with HMAC-SHA512 to produce a 512-bit hash, and this hash is split into two 256-bit halves, of which the right half becomes the chain code for the child while the left half is added to the parent private key to produce the child private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 gives the same in its notation, splitting the output into I-left and I-right (Wuille, 2012).

paras.text: Child key derivation is the operation that produces one child of one parent. The chapter describes the inputs and the split in two sentences: the parent public key, chain code and index number are combined and hashed with HMAC-SHA512 to produce a 512-bit hash, and this hash is split into two 256-bit halves, of which the right half becomes the chain code for the child while the left half is added to the parent private key to produce the child private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 gives the same in its notation, splitting the output into I-left and I-right (Wuille, 2012).

The uniformity is the point. One function, differing only in what is fed to it, generates the whole tree, so an implementation that is correct once is correct everywhere, and a reader who follows it once can follow every path. The split is what makes the recursion work: because each derivation produces a new chain code as well as a new key, the child is itself a complete parent and the tree can be extended to any depth, which the chapter states when it says that each child can in turn become a parent and create its own children, in an infinite number of generations (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets the operation in every path they read: each slash in m/84h/0h/0h/0/0 is one call of this function. The worked example records the arithmetic of the split that every call performs: the 512 bits of the hash divided in two give 256 bits for each half, which is 32 bytes. The claims of this chapter carry out the full derivations of BIP32's first and second test vectors and compare the results with the strings the standard publishes, so the description above is checked at six depths for two different seeds (Wuille, 2012).

The left half is not used directly as the key: it is added to the parent key. BIP32 says that the returned child key is the left half, read as a number, plus the parent key, taken modulo the order of the curve, and that the returned chain code is the right half; it adds the validity rule that if the left half is greater than or equal to the order, or the child key is zero, the result is invalid and the next index should be used, with a probability lower than one in 2 to the 127 (Wuille, 2012). Addition rather than multiplication was a deliberate change made in 2013, which the standard's own change log records as faster and easier to implement (Wuille, 2012).

Two properties of the function should be read carefully. It is one-way, so the chapter can say that because the derivation function is a one-way function the child key cannot be used to find the parent key, nor any siblings (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); but that statement holds for the child key alone, not for a child key together with the parent's extended public key, which is the leak discussed under hardened derivation (Wuille, 2012). And the index is an input, not a property of the key: the same parent gives a completely different child for every index, and nothing in a child shows which index produced it.

nodes.example: 512 bits split into two halves of 32 bytes
nodes.definition: A child is derived by hashing the parent key, the parent chain code and an index with HMAC-SHA512 and splitting the 512-bit result: the left half makes the child key, the right half is the child chain code.

nodes.label: Chain code
nodes.body: A chain code is 32 bytes that travel with a key and take part in deriving its children. The chapter lists it among the three inputs of the derivation function as a seed called a chain code of 256 bits, and explains the name's logic: the initial chain code at the root of the tree is made from the seed, while subsequent child chain codes are derived from each parent chain code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example counts the bytes of the master chain code of BIP32's first test vector and confirms the 256 bits.

paras.text: A chain code is 32 bytes that travel with a key and take part in deriving its children. The chapter lists it among the three inputs of the derivation function as a seed called a chain code of 256 bits, and explains the name's logic: the initial chain code at the root of the tree is made from the seed, while subsequent child chain codes are derived from each parent chain code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example counts the bytes of the master chain code of BIP32's first test vector and confirms the 256 bits.

The chain code is what separates an HD wallet from a mere sequence of hashes. The chapter states the property it provides twice: the chain code is used to introduce deterministic random data to the process, so that knowing the index and a child key is not sufficient to derive other child keys; and knowing a child key does not make it possible to find its siblings unless you also have the chain code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because the same chain code belongs to a private key and to its public counterpart, it is also the reason an extended public key can derive a branch of public keys.

A reader meets the chain code in three forms. It is 32 of the 78 bytes of a serialised extended key (Wuille, 2012); it is the key argument of every HMAC in the derivation; and it is the thing a wallet must store or recompute for every node it uses. The chapter notes the consequence for a child key handled on its own: you need both the child private key and the child chain code to start a new branch and derive grandchildren (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Mechanically a chain code is produced and consumed in the same way at every level: the right half of the derivation's hash becomes the child's chain code, and that chain code is the HMAC key for the child's own children (Wuille, 2012). The root is the only exception, where the chain code comes from the right half of the hash of the seed under the fixed key 'Bitcoin seed'. Nothing else is done to a chain code: it is never hashed on its own, never published, and never used to sign.

The chain code is secret even though it is not a key, and that is the mistake to avoid. BIP32's implications section says that leaking a private key means access to coins while leaking a public key can mean loss of privacy, and that somewhat more care must be taken with extended keys because they correspond to an entire subtree (Wuille, 2012). The chapter adds the sharpest consequence: because an extended public key contains the chain code, a single leaked child private key together with a parent chain code reveals all the private keys of all the children, and can even be used to deduce the parent private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 256 bits beside every key
nodes.definition: A chain code is the 32 bytes of extra entropy carried beside a key so that derivation depends on more than the key; a key's children cannot be found without it.

nodes.label: Index number
nodes.body: The index number is the third input of the derivation function and the one that says which child is wanted. The chapter devotes a section to it: the index number used in the derivation function is a 32-bit integer, and to distinguish keys created through the normal function from those derived through hardened derivation the number is split into two ranges; indices between 0 and 2 to the 31 minus 1, that is 0x0 to 0x7FFFFFFF, are used only for normal derivation, and indices between 2 to the 31 and 2 to the 32 minus 1, that is 0x80000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF, only for hardened derivation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example prints the three boundary values of those ranges.

paras.text: The index number is the third input of the derivation function and the one that says which child is wanted. The chapter devotes a section to it: the index number used in the derivation function is a 32-bit integer, and to distinguish keys created through the normal function from those derived through hardened derivation the number is split into two ranges; indices between 0 and 2 to the 31 minus 1, that is 0x0 to 0x7FFFFFFF, are used only for normal derivation, and indices between 2 to the 31 and 2 to the 32 minus 1, that is 0x80000000 to 0xFFFFFFFF, only for hardened derivation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example prints the three boundary values of those ranges.

The split is a piece of engineering that makes a security property visible in a path. Because the range decides the derivation, a reader can tell from an index alone whether the parent's private key was needed, and therefore whether the branch above can be shared as an extended public key. BIP32 states the counts the split produces: each extended key has 2 to the 31 normal child keys and 2 to the 31 hardened child keys, the normal ones using indices 0 through 2 to the 31 minus 1 (Wuille, 2012).

A reader meets indices in the displayed form rather than the numeric one. The chapter explains the convention: to make the number easier to read, the index for hardened children is displayed starting from zero but with a prime symbol, so the first normal child is 0 and the first hardened child, index 0x80000000, is displayed as 0 followed by a prime; in a sequence the second hardened key has index 0x80000001 and is displayed as 1 with a prime; and when you see an index i with a prime it means 2 to the 31 plus i (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In plain text the prime is written as an apostrophe or as the letter h, and the chapter recommends h where an apostrophe would have a special meaning, as in output script descriptors used in a shell (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mechanism is a comparison and a serialisation. BIP32's derivation first checks whether the index is at least 2 to the 31 and takes the hardened branch if so; the index is then serialised as four bytes, most significant first, and appended to the key material before hashing (Wuille, 2012). The two notations are therefore the same number: 0h is 2147483648 and 1h is 2147483649, which is why the evidence files of this chapter show Bitcoin Core writing paths such as m/84h/0h/0h/0/0 with the letter h where the book writes a prime (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Three slips are common. The first is to read 2147483647 as the number of children of a key: the chapter prints that figure, saying that each parent key can have 2,147,483,647 children and giving 2 to the 31 as the value, but 2 to the 31 is 2147483648, and BIP32 counts 2 to the 31 normal children with indices 0 to 2 to the 31 minus 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012). The second is to read the prime as part of the number; it is a notation for adding 2 to the 31. The third is to assume the two notations are interchangeable everywhere: a descriptor in a shell should use h, because an apostrophe would be consumed by the shell (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: two ranges in 32 bits
nodes.definition: The index is the 32-bit number that selects which child is derived; indices below 2 to the 31 are normal children and those at or above it are hardened, displayed with an apostrophe or an h.

nodes.label: Private child key derivation
nodes.body: Private child key derivation is the function that takes a parent private key with its chain code and an index and returns a child private key with its own chain code. The chapter describes the normal case: the parent public key, the chain code and the index number are combined and hashed with HMAC-SHA512 to produce a 512-bit hash, whose right half becomes the child's chain code and whose left half is added to the parent private key to produce the child private key, illustrated with the index set to zero to produce the first child of the parent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Private child key derivation is the function that takes a parent private key with its chain code and an index and returns a child private key with its own chain code. The chapter describes the normal case: the parent public key, the chain code and the index number are combined and hashed with HMAC-SHA512 to produce a 512-bit hash, whose right half becomes the child's chain code and whose left half is added to the parent private key to produce the child private key, illustrated with the index set to zero to produce the first child of the parent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

This is the function a signing device runs. A wallet that knows a path and holds the master private key with its chain code can reproduce any private key it ever used, which is the whole promise of a seed backup; and because the arithmetic is addition modulo a number, it is cheap enough for a small device to do many times. The chapter adds the organisational gain in the same section: changing the index extends the parent and creates the other children in the sequence, so one parent organises a whole chain of keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example is one step of BIP32's first test vector, done as arithmetic. For the normal child of index 1 below m/0h, the left half of the derivation hash is 4eb9d781...5c5ec4bf and the parent private key is edb2e14f...11a0afea; their sum modulo the order of the curve begins 0x3c6cb8d0f6a264c9, which is the private key the standard publishes for chain m/0h/1 inside its xprv string (Wuille, 2012). The claims of this chapter check the full key and the complete serialised strings for every chain of test vectors 1 and 2.

Two details of the mechanism are worth stating precisely. The first is what goes into the hash: for a normal child it is the compressed serialisation of the parent public key followed by the four bytes of the index, which is why the parent public key can be computed from the parent private key and nothing else is needed; for a hardened child it is a zero byte, the 32 bytes of the parent private key and the index (Wuille, 2012). The second is the arithmetic: the addition is modulo the order of the curve, so the result stays a valid private key, and BIP32 notes that the earlier version of the standard multiplied by the left half instead and was changed to addition in 2013 for speed and ease of implementation (Wuille, 2012).

The chapter's description of the inputs contains a slip a careful reader will notice. In the list of the three combined items it writes a parent private or public key, with the parenthesis uncompressed key, while BIP32 serialises the parent public key in compressed form, the 33 bytes beginning 02 or 03 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012). The claims of this chapter show that using the 65-byte uncompressed form gives a different child key, so the parenthesis has to be read as a slip rather than as an option. The second caution is the same as everywhere in this group: the function needs the chain code, and a private key alone derives nothing.

nodes.example: the left half added to the parent key
nodes.definition: A private child is the sum, modulo the order of the curve, of the parent private key and the left half of the derivation hash; the right half is the child's chain code.

nodes.label: Hardened child key derivation
nodes.body: Hardened derivation is the alternative derivation function that breaks the relationship between the parent public key and the child chain code. The chapter introduces it as a counter to a risk and describes the change in one sentence: the hardened derivation function uses the parent private key to derive the child chain code instead of the parent public key, which creates a firewall in the parent-child sequence, with a chain code that cannot be used to compromise a parent or sibling private key; it adds that the function looks almost identical to normal private derivation except for that substitution (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Hardened derivation is the alternative derivation function that breaks the relationship between the parent public key and the child chain code. The chapter introduces it as a counter to a risk and describes the change in one sentence: the hardened derivation function uses the parent private key to derive the child chain code instead of the parent public key, which creates a firewall in the parent-child sequence, with a chain code that cannot be used to compromise a parent or sibling private key; it adds that the function looks almost identical to normal private derivation except for that substitution (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The risk it answers is the chapter's clearest security argument. Access to an extended public key does not give access to child private keys, but because the extended public key contains the chain code, a child private key that is known or somehow leaked can be used with the chain code to derive all the other child private keys, and worse, together with the parent chain code it can be used to deduce the parent private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 states the same as a property its design deliberately does not have, and says that this is the reason for the existence of hardened keys and why they are used at the account level, so that a leak of account-level or lower private keys never risks compromising the master or other accounts (Wuille, 2012).

A reader meets hardened derivation as the apostrophes and letters h in every standard path: m/44h/0h/0h, m/84h/0h/0h and the rest are hardened at their first three levels (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b) (Rusnak, 2017). The worked example performs one hardened derivation in full, from BIP32's own first test vector: with the master private key and chain code obtained from the seed, hashing a zero byte, the parent private key and the index 2 to the 31, then adding the left half to the parent key, gives a child private key beginning 0xedb2e14f9ee77d26, which is the key inside the xprv the standard publishes for chain m/0h (Wuille, 2012). The claims of this chapter check that the whole serialised string matches.

The mechanism is the change of one input, with a padding byte to keep the length. BIP32 says that for a hardened child the message is a zero byte, the 32-byte parent private key and the four-byte index, and notes that the zero byte pads the private key to make it 33 bytes long, the same length as a compressed public key (Wuille, 2012). Everything else is identical: the chain code is still the HMAC key, the left half is still added to the parent key and the right half still becomes the child's chain code. Because the message now contains a secret, a holder of the extended public key cannot compute it, and BIP32's public derivation function simply returns failure for such an index (Wuille, 2012).

Hardening is not a stronger kind of key and it does not protect the child. The chapter's own summary of when to use it is the practical rule: if you want the convenience of an extended public key to derive branches of public keys without exposing yourself to the risk of a leaked chain code, derive it from a hardened parent rather than a normal one, and as a best practice the level-1 children of the master keys are always derived through hardened derivation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The cost is that nothing above a hardened step can be shared as an extended public key, which is why standard paths harden the first three levels and leave the last two normal.

nodes.example: the first hardened child of a test vector's master key
nodes.definition: Hardened derivation feeds the parent private key, not the parent public key, into the hash, so the resulting chain code cannot be used with a leaked child key to recover the parent.

nodes.label: Public child key derivation
nodes.body: Public child key derivation is the function that produces a child public key from a parent public key and chain code, without any private key. The chapter calls it a very useful characteristic of HD wallets and says it gives two ways to derive a child public key, either from the child private key or directly from the parent public key, so that an extended public key can be used to derive all of the public keys, and only the public keys, in that branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 defines it as CKDpub and says it is only defined for non-hardened child keys (Wuille, 2012).

paras.text: Public child key derivation is the function that produces a child public key from a parent public key and chain code, without any private key. The chapter calls it a very useful characteristic of HD wallets and says it gives two ways to derive a child public key, either from the child private key or directly from the parent public key, so that an extended public key can be used to derive all of the public keys, and only the public keys, in that branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 defines it as CKDpub and says it is only defined for non-hardened child keys (Wuille, 2012).

This function is the reason the standard exists in the form it has. BIP32's motivation gives the use case: elliptic curve mathematics permits schemes where public keys can be calculated without revealing private keys, which lets a web shop let its web server generate fresh addresses for each order or each customer without giving the server access to the keys required for spending (Wuille, 2012). The chapter develops the same example at length in its web store section, and lists the other case, cold storage, where the extended private key stays on paper or on a device while the extended public key is kept online (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader has already met the arithmetic in the first branch, where the chapter adds 123 to a public key and to its private key and gets a matching pair (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example repeats the property on a curve small enough to print: on the curve with the equation y squared equals x cubed plus 7 over the field of 97 elements, with the point (1, 28) as generator, the sum of the points for 13 and 7 equals the point for 20, and the point for 7 is (12, 38). The same identity on Bitcoin's own curve is checked by the claims of this chapter, as are the complete public derivations of BIP32's test vectors.

The mechanism mirrors the private function exactly. BIP32 says that for a normal child the hash is taken over the compressed parent public key and the index, the right half becomes the child chain code, and the child public key is the point for the left half added to the parent public key (Wuille, 2012). Because the point for a sum of numbers is the sum of their points, this gives the same key as deriving the child private key and then multiplying, which BIP32 states as an identity and calls the fact that makes non-hardened keys useful (Wuille, 2012). For a hardened index the message would need the parent private key, so the function returns failure, and the standard adds that from a public parent key to a private child key is not possible at all (Wuille, 2012).

The convenience has the cost that the whole group has been circling. An extended public key lets its holder compute every address of a branch, so BIP32 warns that it must be treated more carefully than a regular public key, both because leaking a public key can mean loss of privacy and because of the leak that a non-hardened child private key makes possible (Wuille, 2012). The chapter's account of the web store notes the benefit that remains even so: a hack of the website can only steal the funds the owner would have received in the future, not those received in the past (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the tweak added on a small curve
nodes.definition: A public child can be derived from a parent public key and chain code alone, because adding a value to a public key gives the public key of the sum, so a server can make addresses without the power to spend.

nodes.label: Using a derived child key
nodes.body: This section answers the question the chapter asks about a child key taken out of the tree: what can it be used for on its own? The chapter's answer is short: it can be used to make a public key and a Bitcoin address, and then to sign transactions to spend anything paid to that address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Everything else it might seem to offer is excluded by the surrounding sentences, which say that the child key cannot be used to find the parent key, cannot be used to find any siblings, such as the key before or after it, and without the child chain code cannot derive any grandchildren either (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This section answers the question the chapter asks about a child key taken out of the tree: what can it be used for on its own? The chapter's answer is short: it can be used to make a public key and a Bitcoin address, and then to sign transactions to spend anything paid to that address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Everything else it might seem to offer is excluded by the surrounding sentences, which say that the child key cannot be used to find the parent key, cannot be used to find any siblings, such as the key before or after it, and without the child chain code cannot derive any grandchildren either (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The property matters for privacy and for operational safety. The chapter puts it in a tip: a child private key, the corresponding public key and the Bitcoin address are all indistinguishable from keys and addresses created randomly, and the fact that they are part of a sequence is not visible outside the wallet function that created them, so once created they operate exactly as normal keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A payer therefore learns nothing about the receiver's wallet from an address, and a wallet can hand out a key without handing out a position in a tree.

A reader meets this independence whenever a single key is exported or imported. A signing device that is given a key and a path returns a signature and nothing else; a descriptor that names a single public key, as in the Bitcoin Core evidence of this chapter where one address is described by a descriptor over one 33-byte key with its origin recorded, works without any chain code (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The worked example is the number of siblings a normal child cannot reach: 2 to the 31 minus 1, that is 2147483647 other normal children of the same parent.

The mechanism behind each prohibition is one of the facts already established. The parent cannot be recovered because the derivation runs through a one-way hash and because the subtraction that would undo it needs the left half of the hash, which needs the chain code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012). Siblings cannot be reached because each index gives an unrelated hash, and grandchildren cannot be derived because the child chain code is missing. BIP32 confirms the first of these as an intended security property: given a child extended private key and the index, an attacker cannot find the parent private key more efficiently than a brute force of 2 to the 256 over HMAC-SHA512 (Wuille, 2012).

The independence holds for the child key alone, and the exception is the one this group has repeated: a non-hardened child private key together with the parent extended public key does reveal the parent extended private key, which BIP32 lists among the properties its scheme does not have (Wuille, 2012). A second caution concerns what independence does not buy: because the chain of a wallet's addresses can often be linked on the blockchain by how outputs are spent, the indistinguishability of a single key is not privacy for the wallet as a whole, which is why chapter 2 of the book treats address reuse and change outputs as privacy questions.

nodes.example: 2,147,483,647 siblings it cannot reach
nodes.definition: A child key on its own behaves exactly like a randomly generated key: it can make a public key, an address and signatures, but it cannot find its parent, its siblings or its own children.

nodes.label: Extended keys
nodes.body: This group is about the object a wallet actually passes around. The chapter introduces it from the derivation function: the function needs a key, a chain code and an index, of which the two essential ingredients are the key and the chain code, and combined these are called an extended key; the term could also be thought of as extensible key, because such a key can be used to derive children (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group covers the idea, its two forms, the way it is written as text and the short identifier that points back to a parent.

paras.text: This group is about the object a wallet actually passes around. The chapter introduces it from the derivation function: the function needs a key, a chain code and an index, of which the two essential ingredients are the key and the chain code, and combined these are called an extended key; the term could also be thought of as extensible key, because such a key can be used to derive children (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group covers the idea, its two forms, the way it is written as text and the short identifier that points back to a parent.

The group matters because extended keys are what users copy and paste, and because what they can do is easy to misjudge. The chapter gives the right picture: think of an extended key as the root of a branch in the tree structure, with which the rest of the branch can be derived, where the extended private key can create a complete branch and the extended public key can only create a branch of public keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A reader who understands that sentence can tell, of any string beginning xprv or xpub, what has been handed over.

An extended key works by packaging exactly what the derivation function needs. The function needs a key and a chain code, so an extended key is the two joined together, and once a program holds one it can derive the whole subtree below it without asking anybody. Written down, the package is seventy-eight bytes: version bytes that say which form and which network, the depth in the tree, the four-byte fingerprint of the parent, the index this key was derived at, the chain code, and the key itself - with the private form padded by a zero byte so that both forms are the same length. Those bytes are then written in the checksummed text of chapter 4, which is why the two forms are distinguishable at a glance by the letters they begin with. The fingerprint is what lets software recognise which parent a key came from without holding the parent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012).

The reader meets extended keys as the long strings that are copied and pasted - into a watching wallet, into a payment processor, into a descriptor's key origin. They are met in this chapter's own figures, where the public form is printed beside the private form it was neutered from, both of the same length and differing in their version bytes; and in a real node, whose descriptors carry an extended key with its origin and its ranged child path, as the run saved with this chapter shows (Wuille, 2012) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

The caution is that the public form is far more powerful than its name suggests. It cannot spend, but it can derive every address of its subtree, which means that handing one out discloses the whole history and the whole future of that branch to its holder. And a leaked public form becomes a leaked private form the moment any non-hardened child private key from the same branch also leaks, as the previous section's warning describes. A learner should treat an extended public key as sensitive data that merely cannot be stolen from (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012).

nodes.label: Extended key
nodes.body: An extended key is the pair consisting of a key and a chain code. The chapter says that extended keys are stored and represented simply as the concatenation of the key and the chain code, and that there are two types, the extended private key, which is a private key with a chain code and can derive child private keys and from them child public keys, and the extended public key, which is a public key with a chain code and can create child public keys only (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 writes the private pair as k with c and the public pair as K with c, where K is the point for k (Wuille, 2012).

paras.text: An extended key is the pair consisting of a key and a chain code. The chapter says that extended keys are stored and represented simply as the concatenation of the key and the chain code, and that there are two types, the extended private key, which is a private key with a chain code and can derive child private keys and from them child public keys, and the extended public key, which is a public key with a chain code and can create child public keys only (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 writes the private pair as k with c and the public pair as K with c, where K is the point for k (Wuille, 2012).

The pairing is necessary because neither half derives anything alone. The chain code is the key of the HMAC and the key is part of its message, so a derivation needs both, which is why the standard introduced the chain code in the first place: to stop derived keys depending solely on the key itself (Wuille, 2012). Treating the pair as one object also makes the tree easy to talk about, since every node of the tree is exactly one extended key.

A reader meets extended keys in text form, which the serialisation section explains, and in the structure the chapter describes as a branch root. The worked example counts the bytes of BIP32's serialisation before the checksum: four version bytes, one of depth, four of parent fingerprint, four of child number, 32 of chain code and 33 of key data make 78, which the standard calls this 78-byte structure (Wuille, 2012). The key data is 33 bytes in both forms, which is why the two are the same length: a compressed public key is 33 bytes, and a private key is padded with a leading zero byte to match (Wuille, 2012).

The depth and the child number in that layout are what let software place a key in the tree: the depth is zero for a master node, one for a level-1 derived key and so on, and the child number is the index with which this key was derived, zero for a master key (Wuille, 2012). Neither is needed for the arithmetic of derivation; both are recorded so that an extended key can be interpreted without being told where it came from. BIP32 also requires an importing implementation to check that the public key data corresponds to a point on the curve, and declares the key invalid if it does not (Wuille, 2012).

The chapter's own phrase, that extended keys are stored simply as the concatenation of the key and the chain code, describes the pair and not the serialised string, which carries five more fields and a checksum (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012). A second caution is that an extended key is not a wallet: it says nothing about which script types or which paths were used, which is the gap that descriptors fill in the next branch (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

nodes.example: 78 bytes before encoding
nodes.definition: An extended key is a key together with its chain code, stored as the two concatenated; it is the root of a branch and is what a derivation function needs.

nodes.label: Extended private key
nodes.body: An extended private key is the extended key whose key half is private. The chapter says it is the combination of a private key and chain code and can be used to derive child private keys, and from them child public keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 adds what that implies for the whole subtree: knowing an extended private key allows reconstruction of all descendant private keys and public keys (Wuille, 2012). The chapter prints an example, a 111-character string beginning xprv9tyUQ, and the worked example decodes exactly that string.

paras.text: An extended private key is the extended key whose key half is private. The chapter says it is the combination of a private key and chain code and can be used to derive child private keys, and from them child public keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 adds what that implies for the whole subtree: knowing an extended private key allows reconstruction of all descendant private keys and public keys (Wuille, 2012). The chapter prints an example, a 111-character string beginning xprv9tyUQ, and the worked example decodes exactly that string.

Such a key is the most dangerous object in a wallet after the seed, and the most useful. It is what a signing device holds, what a cold backup contains and what has to be kept offline; BIP32's use cases list full wallet sharing as the case in which two systems both need to spend and therefore the master private extended key must be shared (Wuille, 2012). Because one such key stands for an unbounded number of future keys, losing control of it cannot be repaired by generating new addresses.

The worked example takes the chapter's printed xprv and decodes it with nothing but base58 arithmetic and SHA-256: the checksum is correct, the version bytes are 0488ade4, the depth is 1, and the 33 bytes of key data begin with a zero byte, the padding BIP32 prescribes for a private key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012). The depth of 1 is worth noticing: the key the chapter prints as an example is not a master key but a level-1 child, and its parent fingerprint is not zero.

The operations the key permits follow from the previous group. With the chain code it derives any child, normal or hardened; by multiplication it gives the matching public key; by discarding the private half it gives the extended public key, which BIP32 calls the neutered version, since it removes the ability to sign transactions (Wuille, 2012). The claims of this chapter check that the extended public key the chapter prints beside its xprv is exactly the neutered form of it, which is how a reader can confirm the two strings are a pair.

Two warnings belong here. The first is that an extended private key is not protected by being long or unfamiliar: anyone who copies the string has the subtree. The second is about the prefix: the version bytes are chosen so that base58 encoding yields xprv on mainnet and tprv on testnet, and BIP49 and BIP84 define further version bytes that give yprv and zprv for their own script types, so a string that does not begin xprv may still be an extended private key (Wuille, 2012) (Weigl, 2016) (Rusnak, 2017). BIP43 recommends against that practice, suggesting that the xpub and xprv prefixes always be used and the purpose level carry the meaning instead (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a).

nodes.example: the book's xprv, decoded
nodes.definition: An extended private key is a private key with its chain code; it can derive every descendant key, private and public, and is written with the prefix xprv.
