nodes.label: Extended public key
nodes.body: An extended public key is the extended key whose key half is public. The chapter says it is a public key and chain code which can be used to create child public keys, public only, and that an extended public key can therefore be used to derive all of the public keys, and only the public keys, in that branch of the wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is abbreviated xpub after its prefix, and the worked example counts the characters of the chapter's own example: 111, the length BIP32 says the encoding always has (Wuille, 2012).

paras.text: An extended public key is the extended key whose key half is public. The chapter says it is a public key and chain code which can be used to create child public keys, public only, and that an extended public key can therefore be used to derive all of the public keys, and only the public keys, in that branch of the wallet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is abbreviated xpub after its prefix, and the worked example counts the characters of the chapter's own example: 111, the length BIP32 says the encoding always has (Wuille, 2012).

This is the object that makes the standard worth having, and the chapter gives its two classic uses. One is to install an extended public key on a web server serving an online shop, so that the server can create a new address for every transaction while holding no private keys that could be stolen (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The other is cold storage: the extended private key is kept on paper or on a hardware device while the extended public key is kept online, so that receive addresses can be created at will while the private keys stay offline (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32's own use cases add audits, where all account public keys are shared so that an auditor can see every payment but no secret key (Wuille, 2012).

A reader meets xpubs in several concrete places in this course. The chapter's web store section has Gabriel export one from a hardware signing device and copy it into his payment processing software (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The descriptors of the wallet created by Bitcoin Core 31.1 for this chapter each contain an xpub with its key origin, for example an account at m/84h/0h/0h followed by the branch 0 and a wildcard (Bitcoin Core, 2026). BIP329's label export format even defines a record type whose reference is an extended public key as defined by BIP32 (Raw, 2022).

The derivation it permits is the public function of the previous group, and the limits are exact. Normal children can be derived, hardened children cannot, and no private key is reachable; BIP32 states the identity that makes this work and the failure for hardened indices (Wuille, 2012). The chapter also notes what is unchanged: the chain code inside the xpub is the same as the one inside the matching xprv, which is what allows the two to produce the same public keys by different routes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012).

An extended public key must be protected even though it cannot spend. BIP32 says that leaking a public key can mean loss of privacy, that more care must be taken with extended keys because they correspond to a whole subtree, and warns of the leak that a non-hardened child private key makes possible; the chapter repeats the practical version of that, that a leaked child private key with a parent chain code reveals all the children and even the parent private key (Wuille, 2012) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The defence is to derive the shared xpub below a hardened step, which is what the standard paths of the next branch do.

nodes.example: 111 characters of base58check
nodes.definition: An extended public key is a public key with its chain code: it derives all the normal public keys of its branch and none of the private ones, and is written with the prefix xpub.

nodes.label: Extended key encoding
nodes.body: The encoding is how an extended key becomes a string a person can copy. The chapter says that extended keys are encoded using base58check to make them easy to export and import between compatible wallets, and that the encoding uses a special version number that results in the prefixes xprv and xpub when encoded in base58 characters, to make them easily recognisable; it adds that because an extended key contains many more bytes than a regular address, the string is much longer than the base58check strings seen earlier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Base58check itself is the encoding chapter 4 of the book explains.

paras.text: The encoding is how an extended key becomes a string a person can copy. The chapter says that extended keys are encoded using base58check to make them easy to export and import between compatible wallets, and that the encoding uses a special version number that results in the prefixes xprv and xpub when encoded in base58 characters, to make them easily recognisable; it adds that because an extended key contains many more bytes than a regular address, the string is much longer than the base58check strings seen earlier (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Base58check itself is the encoding chapter 4 of the book explains.

A readable encoding with a checksum is what makes the key transferable at all. The checksum catches typing errors before any derivation is attempted, and the version prefix tells the reader and the software what kind of object they have, which matters because an extended public and an extended private key are otherwise the same length and shape. The fixed length of 111 characters is itself a check: a string of another length is not a mainnet extended key (Wuille, 2012).

The worked example decodes the chapter's own xpub with base58 arithmetic and a double SHA-256: the checksum holds, the version bytes are 0488b21e, and the key data begins with the byte 2, the prefix of a compressed public key with an even y coordinate (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012). The claims of this chapter decode the matching xprv in the same way and show that the two strings differ only in the version bytes and the key data, having the same depth, parent fingerprint, index and chain code.

The layout and the constants are given by BIP32: four version bytes, which on mainnet are 0x0488B21E for public and 0x0488ADE4 for private and on testnet 0x043587CF and 0x04358394; one byte of depth; four bytes of parent fingerprint; four bytes of child number; 32 bytes of chain code; and 33 bytes of key data; the 78-byte structure is then encoded like other Bitcoin data in base58 by adding 32 checksum bits derived from the double SHA-256 and converting, which results in exactly 111 characters (Wuille, 2012). Because of the choice of version bytes the string begins xprv or xpub on mainnet and tprv or tpub on testnet (Wuille, 2012).

The prefixes are a convention about display, not a statement about derivation, and this has caused real confusion. BIP49 and BIP84 define alternative version bytes producing ypub and zpub for their script types, and BIP43 argues against the whole practice, suggesting that 0x0488B21E and 0x0488ADE4 always be used because a scheme may generate nodes for several currencies or for something unrelated to currencies at all (Weigl, 2016) (Rusnak, 2017) (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a). BIP380 makes the same criticism of version-byte tricks, calling them a layer violation because key derivation should be separate from script type meaning (Wuille and Chow, 2021). A learner should therefore read the prefix as a hint and the descriptor or the path as the truth.

nodes.example: the book's xpub, decoded
nodes.definition: An extended key is written in base58check with four version bytes, which is what produces the recognisable xprv and xpub prefixes and a fixed length of 111 characters.

nodes.label: Key fingerprint
nodes.body: A key fingerprint is a four-byte label for an extended key. BIP32 defines it in two steps: extended keys can be identified by the hash of the serialised public key, that is RIPEMD-160, another hash function, applied after SHA-256, ignoring the chain code, which is exactly the data used in traditional Bitcoin addresses; and the first 32 bits of that identifier are called the key fingerprint (Wuille, 2012). The worked example counts those bits: eight hexadecimal digits, four bits each, make the 32 bits of the fingerprint.

paras.text: A key fingerprint is a four-byte label for an extended key. BIP32 defines it in two steps: extended keys can be identified by the hash of the serialised public key, that is RIPEMD-160, another hash function, applied after SHA-256, ignoring the chain code, which is exactly the data used in traditional Bitcoin addresses; and the first 32 bits of that identifier are called the key fingerprint (Wuille, 2012). The worked example counts those bits: eight hexadecimal digits, four bits each, make the 32 bits of the fingerprint.

The fingerprint exists so that software can match a child with its parent quickly. BIP32 says that it serves only as a fast way to detect parent and child nodes in software, that software must be willing to deal with collisions, and that internally the full 160-bit identifier could be used (Wuille, 2012). It is therefore a convenience, not an identity, and a design that treats it as unique is wrong.

A reader meets the fingerprint in two places. It is one of the fields inside every serialised extended key, where it records the parent: the chapter's own example xprv and xpub both carry the parent fingerprint 0a2683ed, which the claims of this chapter read out of the decoded bytes (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And it is the first element of the key origin of a descriptor, where BIP380 requires exactly eight hexadecimal characters for the fingerprint of the key where the derivation starts; the evidence of this chapter shows Bitcoin Core writing such origins, for example the fingerprint 6d8c4b8f followed by the path 84h/0h/0h (Wuille and Chow, 2021) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The computation is the hash160 of chapter 4 applied to the compressed public key and truncated. One consequence is that a fingerprint can be computed from a public key alone, so a wallet holding only an xpub can state the origin of the keys it derives. Another is that it cannot be computed in the course's browser pages, because the Python available there has no RIPEMD-160 implementation, which is why the fingerprints in this chapter's examples are given as data read from real wallets and standards rather than recomputed in the page.

BIP32 warns against reading too much into the identifier, and the warning has two parts. The first is the collision risk already mentioned: four bytes are not an identity. The second concerns the full identifier: it is not advised to represent that data in base58 format, because it may be interpreted as an address, and wallet software is not required to accept payment to the chain key itself (Wuille, 2012). The practical rule for a student is that a fingerprint is a lookup hint recorded for convenience, and that the authority for which key is meant is the full extended key or the descriptor that contains it.

nodes.example: the first 32 bits of an identifier
nodes.definition: A key fingerprint is the first four bytes of the hash identifier of an extended key, used as a short, non-unique label for the parent a derivation started from.

nodes.label: Navigating the tree
nodes.body: This group is about saying which key of the tree is meant. The chapter introduces the notation first: keys in an HD wallet are identified using a path naming convention, with each level of the tree separated by a slash, where private keys derived from the master private key start with m and public keys derived from the master public key start with M (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It then presents the two standards that give the levels a meaning, BIP43, which reserves the first level for a purpose, and BIP44, which defines five levels for multi-account wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group is about saying which key of the tree is meant. The chapter introduces the notation first: keys in an HD wallet are identified using a path naming convention, with each level of the tree separated by a slash, where private keys derived from the master private key start with m and public keys derived from the master public key start with M (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It then presents the two standards that give the levels a meaning, BIP43, which reserves the first level for a purpose, and BIP44, which defines five levels for multi-account wallets (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because the tree is unmanageably large without a convention. The chapter sets out the problem: each parent extended key can have four billion children, each of those another four billion, the tree can be as deep as one likes, and with all that flexibility it becomes quite difficult to navigate, and especially difficult to transfer wallets between implementations, because the possibilities for internal organisation are endless (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Two standards narrow that down to a handful of paths every wallet understands.

The notation works as an address within the tree, read from the root outwards. The letter m stands for the master key; each slash descends one level; the number after the slash is the index given to the derivation function at that level; and an apostrophe, or the letter h, marks an index taken from the hardened half. The conventions built on top of it give each level a meaning so that two programs reading the same path agree on what they are looking at: the first level says which standard is in use and therefore which kind of address the branch holds, the second which coin, the third which account, the fourth whether the branch is for receiving or for change, and the fifth which address in sequence. Nothing in the arithmetic requires any of this - the meanings are a convention, which is precisely why the next branch of the chapter is about what happens when a wallet does not follow it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012) (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a) (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b).

The reader meets paths everywhere once they are recognised. A hardware device shows one before it signs; a node's descriptor carries one in its key origin and another as its ranged child path; this course's own material quotes them in the standard paths of the next branch and in the derivations it checks against the published vectors. They are met in the chapter's two tables, whose rows are the paths of the four standards, and in the single line a restoration may need if the wallet used a path of its own (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is that a path is metadata and is not in the code. The recovery code restores the keys of the tree and says nothing about which branch of it a wallet used, so a code restored into software that assumes a different convention finds an empty wallet while the funds sit on a branch nobody looked at. That is the whole problem the next branch exists to solve. A smaller caution: the apostrophe and the letter h mean the same thing, and so do the two ways of writing a hardened index, which matters when a path is copied between programs that accept only one spelling (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Chow, 2022).

nodes.label: Key path
nodes.body: A key path is the name of one key, written as the route from the root to it. The chapter gives the rules: each level is separated by a slash; private keys derived from the master private key start with m and public keys from the master public key with M; so the first child private key of the master private key is m/0 and the first child public key is M/0, while the second grandchild of the first child is m/0/1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 uses the same shorthand and notes the identity that lets a path be read either way: neutering at any level and then deriving publicly gives the same keys as deriving privately and neutering at the end (Wuille, 2012).

paras.text: A key path is the name of one key, written as the route from the root to it. The chapter gives the rules: each level is separated by a slash; private keys derived from the master private key start with m and public keys from the master public key with M; so the first child private key of the master private key is m/0 and the first child public key is M/0, while the second grandchild of the first child is m/0/1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32 uses the same shorthand and notes the identity that lets a path be read either way: neutering at any level and then deriving publicly gives the same keys as deriving privately and neutering at the end (Wuille, 2012).

The notation is what makes a backup complete. A recovery code gives the seed, but the chapter's whole next branch exists because the seed does not say which paths a wallet used, and a path written down removes that ambiguity. A path is also the unit in which wallets and devices talk to each other: a signing device is asked for a signature at a path, and a descriptor records the path by which an extended key was reached (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

A reader meets paths everywhere in this course from here on, and the worked example converts one of them into the numbers a derivation function actually uses: m/84h/0h/0h/0/2 is the five indices 2147483732, 2147483648, 2147483648, 0 and 2, where the first three are hardened, being 2 to the 31 plus 84, 0 and 0 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The evidence files of this chapter show a real wallet reporting such a path for its first address, m/84h/0h/0h/0/0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Reading a path is mechanical: start at the root, apply the derivation function once for each element, choosing the hardened variant where the element carries a prime or an h, and the key named is the one left at the end. The chapter gives the rule for reading the other way, which is how its table is written: the ancestry of a key is read from right to left until the master key is reached, so m/x/y/z is the z-th child of m/x/y, which is the y-th child of m/x, which is the x-th child of m (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The claims of this chapter check every row of the chapter's own table of path examples against the derivations the notation implies.

Three details trip readers up. The capital M means only that the key named is public; it is not a different tree, and M/0 is the public key of m/0 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A hardened step cannot be taken from a public parent, so a path that contains a prime after an M is meaningless unless the prime comes above the point at which the public key was taken (Wuille, 2012). And a path alone does not say which script type the key is for, which is why the two paths m/44h/0h/0h and m/84h/0h/0h, differing only in the purpose level, mean different kinds of address (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b) (Rusnak, 2017).

nodes.definition: A key path names a key by the sequence of indices from the root, written with slashes, beginning m for private or M for public keys, with a prime or h for hardened steps.

nodes.label: Purpose level (BIP43)
nodes.body: The purpose level is the first level of the tree, used as a label for the structure below it. The chapter says that BIP43 proposes the use of the first hardened child index as a special identifier that signifies the purpose of the tree structure, and that an HD wallet should use only one level-1 branch, with the index number identifying the structure and namespace of the rest of the tree by defining its purpose, so that a wallet using only the branch m/i followed by a prime signifies a specific purpose identified by that number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP43 writes the pattern as m / purpose' / and notes that the apostrophe indicates hardened derivation (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a).

paras.text: The purpose level is the first level of the tree, used as a label for the structure below it. The chapter says that BIP43 proposes the use of the first hardened child index as a special identifier that signifies the purpose of the tree structure, and that an HD wallet should use only one level-1 branch, with the index number identifying the structure and namespace of the rest of the tree by defining its purpose, so that a wallet using only the branch m/i followed by a prime signifies a specific purpose identified by that number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP43 writes the pattern as m / purpose' / and notes that the apostrophe indicates hardened derivation (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a).

The level exists because BIP32 alone does not make wallets interoperable. BIP43's motivation says this bluntly: although the hierarchical structure of BIP32 is an important step, the specification offers implementers too many degrees of freedom, so multiple implementations may claim to be BIP32 compatible while in fact producing wallets with different logical structures, which renders the statement BIP32 compatible rather useless (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a). A purpose number turns a claim about an algorithm into a claim about a layout.

A reader meets purpose numbers as the first element of every standard path: 44 for the multi-account hierarchy, 49 for segwit nested in a script hash, 84 for native segwit and 86 for single-key taproot, each a hardened index (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b) (Weigl, 2016) (Rusnak, 2017) (Chow, 2021). The worked example converts the first of them: 2 to the 31 plus 44 is 0x8000002c, which is exactly the value BIP43 gives when it says that the scheme described in BIP44 should use 44 with a prime, or 0x8000002C, as purpose (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a).

The convention is a request rather than a mechanism, and BIP43 states how it is meant to be followed: different schemes are encouraged to apply for a separate BIP number and use the same number for the purpose field, so that addresses are not generated from overlapping BIP32 spaces; purpose codes from 10001 to 19999 are reserved for the SatoshiLabs improvement proposals; and the branch m/0' is already taken by BIP32's default account, which preceded the proposal (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a). The standard also suggests that software needing only a limited structure should describe it in another BIP with a different purpose value rather than claim partial compatibility (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a).

Two points are easy to miss. The first is that the purpose level is hardened, so nothing above it can be shared as an extended public key and the purpose cannot be read off a shared xpub. The second is that the number is a namespace and not a feature list: a wallet that finds a tree under 44' knows which document describes the layout, but still has to support that document, which is exactly the forward-compatibility problem Electrum's version numbers were designed to solve from the other end (Electrum Technologies, 2026) (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a).

nodes.example: 44 hardened is 0x8000002c
nodes.definition: BIP43 reserves the first hardened level of a BIP32 tree for a purpose number that says which scheme the rest of the tree follows, and recommends using the scheme's own BIP number.

nodes.label: BIP44 structure
nodes.body: BIP44 is the layout that gives a tree its familiar shape. The chapter says that, extending BIP43, BIP44 proposes a multi-account structure as purpose number 44 with a prime, that all wallets following the structure are identified by using only the branch m/44', and that the structure consists of five predefined tree levels: purpose, coin type, account, change and address index (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example counts them in the chapter's own line: five levels below m.

paras.text: BIP44 is the layout that gives a tree its familiar shape. The chapter says that, extending BIP43, BIP44 proposes a multi-account structure as purpose number 44 with a prime, that all wallets following the structure are identified by using only the branch m/44', and that the structure consists of five predefined tree levels: purpose, coin type, account, change and address index (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example counts them in the chapter's own line: five levels below m.

The structure answers the two questions a wallet has to answer before it can scan anything: which currency and which account. BIP44's motivation says the hierarchy is comprehensive, allowing the handling of multiple coins, multiple accounts, external and internal chains per account and millions of addresses per chain (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b). Because the layout is fixed, a wallet restored from a code knows where to look, which is the whole point of what the next branch calls an implicit path.

A reader meets the structure in the chapter's own examples and in real wallets. The chapter explains the first two levels: the purpose is always 44 with a prime; the coin type specifies the type of cryptocurrency, allowing multi-currency wallets where each currency has its own subtree, with Bitcoin at m/44'/0' and Bitcoin testnet at m/44'/1' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP44 registers exactly those two values and refers to SLIP-0044 for the rest, whose table gives 0 for Bitcoin, 1 for testnet and 2 for Litecoin, the coin in the chapter's third table row (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b) (Rusnak and Palatinus, 2014). Bitcoin Core's own descriptor wallets use the same shape, and its documentation records BIP44 as used by default since version 0.21.0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The division of hardened and normal levels is the part worth learning by heart. BIP44 says hardened derivation is used at the purpose, coin type and account levels, and public derivation at the change and index levels (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b); the chapter explains why: the change level uses normal derivation to allow this level of the tree to export extended public keys for use in a non-secured environment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). An account's extended public key can therefore be given to a server, which can derive both the receive and the change branches, while the account itself is hardened so that a leak below it cannot reach the master key (Wuille, 2012).

BIP44 adds rules about discovery that a reader should know before trusting a restoration. Software should prevent the creation of an account if the previous account has no transaction history, and after importing a seed it should discover accounts by deriving the first account, scanning its external chain while respecting the gap limit, and continuing only while transactions are found; the standard sets that gap limit at 20 addresses and says wallets should warn when a user exceeds it (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b). The chapter's own sidebar on the gap limit, in the next branch, shows how production systems stretch that number.

nodes.example: five predefined levels
nodes.definition: BIP44 defines the five levels purpose, coin type, account, change and address index under purpose 44 hardened, with the first three hardened and the last two normal.

io.code: len('m / purpose / coin_type / account / change / address_index'.split(' / ')) - 1

nodes.label: Account branch
nodes.body: The account branch is the third level of a BIP44 path. The chapter says that the third level of the tree is the account, which allows users to subdivide their wallets into separate logical subaccounts for accounting or organisational purposes, and gives the example of a wallet containing two Bitcoin accounts, m/44'/0'/0' and m/44'/0'/1', each the root of its own subtree (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example writes the second of those paths from its index.

paras.text: The account branch is the third level of a BIP44 path. The chapter says that the third level of the tree is the account, which allows users to subdivide their wallets into separate logical subaccounts for accounting or organisational purposes, and gives the example of a wallet containing two Bitcoin accounts, m/44'/0'/0' and m/44'/0'/1', each the root of its own subtree (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example writes the second of those paths from its index.

Accounts are the level at which a wallet becomes usable by an organisation. BIP44 says the level splits the key space into independent user identities so that the wallet never mixes coins across accounts, and suggests the same uses the chapter does, organising funds as bank accounts are organised, for donations where all addresses are considered public, for savings, or for common expenses (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b). BIP32's use cases add the per-office case, in which several offices use wallets derived from one master while headquarters keeps a super-wallet that sees all of them (Wuille, 2012).

A reader meets accounts as the third element of a path and as the unit a wallet exports. The extended public key a wallet hands to a server or an auditor is normally the account key, which is why the descriptors of the Bitcoin Core wallet in the evidence of this chapter each name an account, such as the origin 6d8c4b8f followed by 84h/0h/0h, and then the branch and index below it (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021). BIP32's audit use case describes sharing all account public extended keys so that an auditor sees all transactions but no secret key (Wuille, 2012).

The level is hardened, and that is the design decision that makes it safe to export. Because the account key is derived with a hardened step, its extended public key cannot be used to work back to the master key even if a private key below it leaks, which BIP32 gives as the reason hardened keys are used at the account level: a leak of account-specific or lower private keys never risks compromising the master or other accounts (Wuille, 2012). Accounts are numbered from zero and increase sequentially, and the number is the child index of the derivation (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b).

The word account here means a branch of a key tree and nothing more: it is not an account in the sense of a balance held somewhere, and no one but the wallet's owner can tell that two addresses belong to the same account. A reader should also note the discovery rule that goes with the level: because software is told not to create an account unless the previous one has history, a wallet restored from a code stops looking after the first account with no transactions, so an account created out of order can be missed (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b).

nodes.example: the second account of a BIP44 wallet
nodes.definition: The account level is the third level of a BIP44 path, hardened, which splits a wallet into independent subaccounts that never mix coins.

nodes.label: Change branch
nodes.body: The change branch is the fourth level of a BIP44 path, and it has only two values. The chapter says that on the fourth level, change, an HD wallet has two subtrees, one for creating receiving addresses and one for creating change addresses, and notes that whereas the previous levels used hardened derivation, this level uses normal derivation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP44 fixes the numbers: the constant 0 is used for the external chain and 1 for the internal chain, also known as change addresses (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b).

paras.text: The change branch is the fourth level of a BIP44 path, and it has only two values. The chapter says that on the fourth level, change, an HD wallet has two subtrees, one for creating receiving addresses and one for creating change addresses, and notes that whereas the previous levels used hardened derivation, this level uses normal derivation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP44 fixes the numbers: the constant 0 is used for the external chain and 1 for the internal chain, also known as change addresses (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b).

The split exists because the two kinds of address have different audiences. BIP32 explains the distinction when it describes the default layout: the external keychain is used to generate new public addresses while the internal keychain is used for all other operations, change addresses and anything that does not need to be communicated, and clients that do not support separate chains should use the external one for everything (Wuille, 2012). Chapter 2 of the book explained why change exists at all: a payment usually spends more than it sends and returns the remainder to its own wallet.

The worked example writes one of the chapter's own table rows: M/44'/0'/3'/1/14, which the chapter describes as the fifteenth change-address public key for the fourth Bitcoin account (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same structure appears in every descriptor pair of the Bitcoin Core wallet in this chapter's evidence, where two descriptors share an account key and differ only in that branch, one marked internal and one not (Bitcoin Core, 2026). BIP389's multipath notation, in the next branch, exists precisely to write those two descriptors as one (Chow, 2022).

Normal derivation at this level is what makes an account's extended public key useful, and the chapter says so: this is to allow this level of the tree to export extended public keys for use in a non-secured environment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A server given the account xpub can derive both branches, so it can recognise change as well as receipts; BIP44 notes the asymmetry that follows for scanning, saying that only external chains need be scanned because internal chains receive only coins that come from the associated external chains (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b).

Two cautions. The first is that change addresses are addresses of the same wallet, so a tool that scans only branch 0 will under-report a balance, and one that hands out addresses from branch 1 will leak which outputs are change. The second is that the numbering is a convention of BIP44 and its successors, not a rule of BIP32: a wallet is free to use another layout, and BIP32's own default simply calls the two chains internal and external without fixing the indices in the same words (Wuille, 2012) (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b).

nodes.example: the fifteenth change address of the fourth account
nodes.definition: The fourth level of a BIP44 path is 0 for the external chain, whose addresses are given out, and 1 for the internal chain, which receives change; both use normal derivation.

nodes.label: Address index
nodes.body: The address index is the last level of a BIP44 path. The chapter says that usable addresses are derived by the wallet as children of the fourth level, making the fifth level the address index, and gives an example: the third receiving address for payments in the primary account would be M/44'/0'/0'/0/2 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example writes exactly that path from the ordinal, since the third address has index 2. BIP44 adds that addresses are numbered from index 0 in sequentially increasing manner and that public derivation is used at this level (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b).

paras.text: The address index is the last level of a BIP44 path. The chapter says that usable addresses are derived by the wallet as children of the fourth level, making the fifth level the address index, and gives an example: the third receiving address for payments in the primary account would be M/44'/0'/0'/0/2 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example writes exactly that path from the ordinal, since the third address has index 2. BIP44 adds that addresses are numbered from index 0 in sequentially increasing manner and that public derivation is used at this level (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b).

This level is where privacy is won or lost. The chapter's web store section explains the gain: a unique address for every customer order immediately improves privacy and gives each order a unique identifier for tracking which invoices have been paid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's first branch made the opposite case, that using a single key severely reduces the privacy of that user and of everyone they transact with (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Advancing the index is the cheap way to avoid that.

A reader meets the index as the number at the end of every descriptor and every reported path. The wallet created by Bitcoin Core 31.1 for this chapter reports its first address at m/84h/0h/0h/0/0, and its descriptors end in a wildcard with a range from 0 to 999, which is the pool of indices it has prepared (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter's table of BIP44 examples gives three more rows, which the claims of this chapter reproduce by derivation (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Because the level uses normal derivation, the whole sequence of addresses can be produced from the account's extended public key, which is what the web store does. The consequence for software is that a wallet must decide how many indices to prepare in advance: Bitcoin Core calls this a keypool and sets it to 1,000 pre-generated keys or scripts by default, describing it as part of the look-ahead process used to detect payments (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The next branch's section on the gap limit explains what happens when a user runs past that pool.

The index is not visible to anyone else, and that cuts both ways. Nobody can tell from an address that it is the third of an account, which is good for privacy; but neither can a restored wallet tell how far a user had gone, which is why scanning stops after a run of unused indices and why a payment to a far-away index can be missed (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A reader should also not confuse the index with the number of addresses a wallet has used: indices may be skipped when an address is given out and never paid.

nodes.example: the third receiving address of an account
nodes.definition: The fifth level of a BIP44 path is the address index, counted from zero with normal derivation, and it is the level a wallet advances each time it needs a new address.

nodes.label: Backing up derivation paths
nodes.body: This branch is about the part of a backup that a recovery code does not contain. The chapter states the problem at the head of its section on backing up key derivation paths: in a BIP32 tree there are approximately four billion first-level keys, each of which can have its own four billion children, and so on, so it is not possible for a wallet to generate even a small fraction of every possible key, which means that recovering from data loss requires knowing more than the recovery code, the algorithm for obtaining the seed and the derivation algorithm, it also requires knowing what paths in the tree the wallet used for the keys it distributed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch is about the part of a backup that a recovery code does not contain. The chapter states the problem at the head of its section on backing up key derivation paths: in a BIP32 tree there are approximately four billion first-level keys, each of which can have its own four billion children, and so on, so it is not possible for a wallet to generate even a small fraction of every possible key, which means that recovering from data loss requires knowing more than the recovery code, the algorithm for obtaining the seed and the derivation algorithm, it also requires knowing what paths in the tree the wallet used for the keys it distributed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch matters because this is the gap through which money is actually lost. A user who holds a perfectly good recovery code and enters it into the wrong software may see an empty wallet, not because the keys are gone but because the software looked in a different part of the tree. The chapter says that two solutions to this problem have been adopted, and the whole branch is the comparison of those two: standard paths that every wallet knows, which it calls implicit paths, and paths recorded beside the code, which it calls explicit paths (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets the two solutions in the two kinds of wallet the chapter describes at the end of the section: it has long been the trend for wallets designed only for single-signature scripts to use implicit paths, while wallets designed for multiple signatures or other advanced scripts increasingly support explicit paths using descriptors, and applications that do both usually conform to the implicit standards and also provide descriptors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The evidence of this chapter shows the second kind in use: Bitcoin Core 31.1 described every key of a fresh wallet by a descriptor that states the script type, the key origin and the path (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The branch has two groups. The path conventions group explains the implicit and the explicit approach, then the four standard paths the chapter tabulates, one for each script type, and finally multisignature, which is the case the chapter uses to show why implicit paths are not enough. The descriptors group covers the standard that explicit paths are written in: what an output script is, what a descriptor says about one, the checksum that protects it, the key origin that records where its keys came from, the multipath form that writes a receive and a change descriptor as one, and miniscript, which describes the spending conditions themselves.

One caution frames the whole branch: neither solution removes the need for the recovery code, and neither is complete on its own. Implicit paths leave a wallet guessing which features were used; explicit paths require more to be written down. The chapter's own judgement is that the advantage of explicit paths is that they can describe exactly what keys should be used with what scripts, with no need to support outdated scripts and no compatibility problems, while their disadvantage is that they require users to back up additional information, which usually cannot compromise security but can reduce privacy and does require some protection (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Implicit and explicit paths
nodes.body: This group covers the two ways of knowing which paths a wallet used. The first, which the chapter calls implicit paths, is to use standardised paths that every implementation of the standard knows, so that nothing has to be recorded; the second, explicit paths, is to back up the path information with the recovery code, making it clear which path is used with which scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group also covers the standardised paths themselves and the case, multisignature, in which no standard path can be enough.

paras.text: This group covers the two ways of knowing which paths a wallet used. The first, which the chapter calls implicit paths, is to use standardised paths that every implementation of the standard knows, so that nothing has to be recorded; the second, explicit paths, is to back up the path information with the recovery code, making it clear which path is used with which scripts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The group also covers the standardised paths themselves and the case, multisignature, in which no standard path can be enough.

The choice between the two is the chapter's main argument in this part, and it is a trade-off rather than a verdict. Implicit paths are convenient and inflexible; explicit paths are flexible and demand more of the user. Since the recovery code is the only thing many users keep, the question of what else must be kept beside it is a practical one, and a course that leaves it unanswered leaves the reader with an incomplete backup.

The two approaches work by putting the convention in different places. An implicit path puts it in the standard: the wallet derives at the levels the standard prescribes, so a restoring program that knows which standard was used can reconstruct the paths from nothing but the code, and the backup is the code alone. An explicit path puts the convention in the backup: the wallet may derive wherever it likes and records the path it used, so the backup is the code plus a written description, and a restoring program follows the description instead of guessing. The cost of each is the other's benefit. Implicit paths need no extra record and allow no deviation; explicit paths allow any arrangement, including ones no standard anticipated, and fail completely if the record is lost. Multisignature is the case that settles the argument, because the public keys of the other signers are neither standard nor derivable from one seed, so they must be recorded whatever approach is chosen (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a) (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b) (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

The reader meets implicit paths as the reason a code from one wallet usually restores in another, and explicit paths as the descriptor a modern node gives out. Bitcoin Core is the clearest case of the second: its wallets are descriptor wallets, so every path it uses is written down in a descriptor rather than assumed, and the fresh wallet saved with this chapter's evidence reports eight of them, a receiving and a change branch for each of four script types. The four standard paths of the chapter's table are met in their own proposals, each with test vectors this course runs (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b) (Weigl, 2016) (Rusnak, 2017) (Chow, 2021).

The caution is about the coin-type level, where the chapter's own table is uneven for a real reason. Three of its four rows use the coin type for Bitcoin and the fourth uses the coin type that the registry assigns to test networks, because that proposal's own test vectors are on a test network; a learner who reads the table as four parallel cases will derive the wrong branch. The second caution is that an explicit record is only as good as its own integrity, which is why a descriptor carries a checksum of its own and why that checksum should be kept with it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Rusnak and Palatinus, 2014) (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

nodes.label: Implicit path
nodes.body: An implicit path is a path that does not have to be recorded because it is fixed by a standard. The chapter introduces the term through its mechanism: every time there is a change related to the addresses that wallets might want to generate, someone creates a BIP defining what derivation path to use, as BIP44 defines m/44'/0'/0' as the path for keys in pay-to-public-key-hash scripts, and a wallet implementing that standard uses the keys in that path both when it is first started and after a restoration from a recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An implicit path is a path that does not have to be recorded because it is fixed by a standard. The chapter introduces the term through its mechanism: every time there is a change related to the addresses that wallets might want to generate, someone creates a BIP defining what derivation path to use, as BIP44 defines m/44'/0'/0' as the path for keys in pay-to-public-key-hash scripts, and a wallet implementing that standard uses the keys in that path both when it is first started and after a restoration from a recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The gain is that a user needs to keep only the words. The chapter states it in one sentence: the advantage of implicit paths is that users do not need to keep a record of what paths they use, because if the code is entered into the same wallet application as before, of the same version or higher, it will automatically regenerate keys for the same paths it previously used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For the large majority of users, who hold one single-signature wallet, this is the whole of path management.

A reader meets implicit paths as the four rows of the chapter's table of implicit script paths, and as the behaviour of any wallet that asks only for words when restoring (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP44's own account discovery algorithm is the implicit approach written out: derive the first account, derive its external chain, scan its addresses respecting the gap limit, and stop when an account has no transactions (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b). Bitcoin Core's descriptor wallets use the standard paths by default too, which its documentation records for BIPs 43, 44, 49, 84 and 86 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The mechanism is a convention plus a search. On restoration a wallet derives the keys for every path it supports and scans the blockchain for transactions involving those keys; the chapter names that as the disadvantage, saying that this is wasteful in wallets that support many features, each with its own path, if the user tried only a few of them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The search is bounded in two directions, by the set of paths the software knows and by the gap limit at each path's address index, and anything outside those bounds is not found.

The chapter lists three consequences a reader should be able to state. For codes without a version number, such as BIP39 and SLIP39, a new version of a wallet that drops support for an older path cannot warn users during the restore that some funds may not be found, and the same happens in reverse when a code is entered into older software that does not know the newer paths; codes that carry version information, such as Electrum version 2 and Aezeed, can detect this and direct the user to appropriate resources (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And implicit paths can only carry information that is either universal or derived from the seed, so important non-deterministic information specific to a user cannot be restored from a code at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the path a wallet assumes
nodes.definition: An implicit path is a standardised derivation path that a wallet uses without being told, so that nothing has to be backed up beside the recovery code - at the price of inflexibility.

nodes.label: Explicit path
nodes.body: An explicit path is path information that is written down. The chapter defines it by contrast with the first solution: the second solution is to back up the path information with the recovery code, making it clear which path is used with which scripts, and the chapter calls this explicit paths (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In practice the information is written in a standard notation: the chapter says that almost all wallets that use explicit paths use the output script descriptors standard, specified in BIPs 380 to 386 and 389 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: An explicit path is path information that is written down. The chapter defines it by contrast with the first solution: the second solution is to back up the path information with the recovery code, making it clear which path is used with which scripts, and the chapter calls this explicit paths (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In practice the information is written in a standard notation: the chapter says that almost all wallets that use explicit paths use the output script descriptors standard, specified in BIPs 380 to 386 and 389 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The gain is exactness, and the chapter sets out what that buys: explicit paths can describe exactly what keys should be used with what scripts, there is no need to support outdated scripts, there are no problems with backward or forward compatibility, and any extra information, such as the public keys of other users, can be included directly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP380's motivation makes the same argument from the wallet author's side, saying that a backup of private keys alone is insufficient, especially since segregated witness added new output types, because a restored wallet cannot know which kinds of output script and address to produce (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

A reader meets explicit paths wherever a wallet shows or asks for a descriptor. Bitcoin Core is the clearest example: the wallet in this chapter's evidence lists eight descriptors, four script types with a receive and a change branch each, every one carrying its key origin and path, and the command that lists them is documented as listing all descriptors present in a wallet (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The chapter's own sample table of descriptors is taken from Bitcoin Core's documentation, whose text this chapter's claims read (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The mechanism is that the derivation information travels with the key rather than being assumed. A descriptor contains the script function, the key or extended key, the key origin, which records the fingerprint and the path above that key, and the path below it, so a restoring wallet needs to guess nothing (Wuille and Chow, 2021). Because the information is not secret in the way a key is, it can be kept with less protection than the recovery code, which the chapter notes when it says the additional information usually cannot compromise a user's security (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The cost is the obvious one and the chapter states it: explicit paths require users to back up additional information along with their recovery code, and although that information usually cannot compromise security it can reduce privacy and does require some protection (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The privacy point is worth taking seriously, since an extended public key in a descriptor reveals every address of its branch (Wuille, 2012). A second caution is that a descriptor is not a substitute for the code: it contains public information, and without the seed it can only watch.

nodes.example: the path written down with the code
nodes.definition: An explicit path is derivation information backed up alongside the recovery code, which says exactly which keys go with which scripts and can carry extra data such as other people's public keys.

nodes.label: BIP44 path for legacy scripts
nodes.body: The BIP44 path is the oldest of the standard implicit paths. The chapter's table of implicit script paths gives it in one row: the standard BIP44, the script P2PKH, the BIP32 path m/44'/0'/0' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The text explains the row before the table, saying that BIP44 defines m/44'/0'/0' as the path to use for keys in pay-to-public-key-hash scripts, which it glosses as a legacy address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example writes the path from its purpose number.

paras.text: The BIP44 path is the oldest of the standard implicit paths. The chapter's table of implicit script paths gives it in one row: the standard BIP44, the script P2PKH, the BIP32 path m/44'/0'/0' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The text explains the row before the table, saying that BIP44 defines m/44'/0'/0' as the path to use for keys in pay-to-public-key-hash scripts, which it glosses as a legacy address (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example writes the path from its purpose number.

The path matters because it is what a wallet tries first when a code is restored, and because it defines what legacy means in this context. Pay-to-public-key-hash is the address type chapter 4 of the book described as the legacy form, beginning with the digit 1, and a wallet that supports only BIP44 will find only those addresses. Since many wallets created before segregated witness used this path, it remains the path on which old funds are found.

A reader meets the path in the chapter's table, in BIP44's own examples, where the first receiving address of the first Bitcoin account is m/44'/0'/0'/0/0, and in real software: the fresh Bitcoin Core wallet of this chapter's evidence has a descriptor pair under the origin 6d8c4b8f followed by 44h/0h/0h, written with the function pkh, which is the descriptor name for this script type (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021). Bitcoin Core's documentation records BIP44 as used by default in descriptor wallets since version 0.21.0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The path is BIP44's five-level structure with the purpose set to 44 and the coin type to 0 for Bitcoin, which the previous branch explained; the levels below the account are the change branch and the address index (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b). The script type is not part of the path arithmetic: the same keys could be used to make any kind of address, and it is the standard alone that says this path's keys belong in pay-to-public-key-hash scripts, which is exactly the layer violation BIP380 complains about and descriptors remove (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

Two points of care. The first is that the chapter's table prints m/44'/0'/0' for BIP44 but m/49'/1'/0' for BIP49, whose second level is 1, the coin type for testnet, because BIP49's own test vectors are on testnet; the table is faithful to the standards but a reader should not read the 1 as part of the scheme (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Weigl, 2016) (Rusnak and Palatinus, 2014). The second is that a wallet supporting only this path will not find segwit or taproot funds, which is the whole reason the other three rows of the table exist.

nodes.definition: BIP44's account path for pay-to-public-key-hash scripts is the first of the standard implicit paths and the one the chapter's table gives for legacy addresses.

nodes.label: BIP49 path for nested segwit
nodes.body: The BIP49 path is the standard path for pay-to-witness-public-key-hash nested in pay-to-script-hash, which the chapter's table calls nested P2WPKH and gives as m/49'/1'/0' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard's own title is a derivation scheme for P2WPKH-nested-in-P2SH based accounts, and it says it uses the same account structure as BIP44 but a different purpose value to indicate the different transaction serialisation method (Weigl, 2016). The worked example gives the hardened purpose index, 2 to the 31 plus 49, as 0x80000031.

paras.text: The BIP49 path is the standard path for pay-to-witness-public-key-hash nested in pay-to-script-hash, which the chapter's table calls nested P2WPKH and gives as m/49'/1'/0' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard's own title is a derivation scheme for P2WPKH-nested-in-P2SH based accounts, and it says it uses the same account structure as BIP44 but a different purpose value to indicate the different transaction serialisation method (Weigl, 2016). The worked example gives the hardened purpose index, 2 to the 31 plus 49, as 0x80000031.

The reasoning behind a separate path is the clearest statement in these standards of why implicit paths need discipline. BIP49 lists the alternatives it rejected, in which the same account would carry both legacy and segwit addresses, and gives its reason: those approaches share a common disadvantage, that if a user imports or recovers a BIP49-compatible master seed in a wallet that is not BIP49-compatible, the account might show up but might also miss some unspent outputs; the chosen approach fails in a more visible way, since either the account shows up or it does not at all, so the user does not have to check the balance after using the same seed in different wallets (Weigl, 2016).

A reader meets this path as the wrapped segwit addresses that begin with the digit 3, and in the descriptors of the Bitcoin Core wallet in this chapter's evidence, where the pair under the origin 6d8c4b8f followed by 49h/0h/0h is written with the nested functions sh and wpkh (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The claims of this chapter reproduce BIP49's own test vector from its recovery code: the first receiving key of the testnet account at m/49'/1'/0'/0/0 has the public key the standard prints, and the address derived from it is the 2Mww8d address of the standard (Weigl, 2016).

The mechanism of the address is the encapsulation the standard sets out: the witness holds the signature and the public key, the input script holds a push of the version-zero witness program, and the output script is a hash-160 of that program followed by an equality check (Weigl, 2016). The path is the BIP44 structure with purpose 49, and the standard also defines alternative version bytes for extended keys, giving the prefixes ypub and yprv, with testnet upub and uprv (Weigl, 2016). The claims of this chapter compute the address from the public key by hashing the input script, which is why the example reproduces the standard exactly.

The chapter's table row for this standard uses coin type 1, which is testnet, and the standard's vectors are on testnet as well, so a reader working on mainnet should use m/49'/0'/0' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Weigl, 2016) (Rusnak and Palatinus, 2014). The deeper caution is the one the standard itself gives: this scheme is not backward compatible by design, so a wallet that does not know it will simply not see the account; that is intended, and it is better than silently showing part of a balance (Weigl, 2016).

nodes.example: 49 hardened is 0x80000031
nodes.definition: BIP49 gives segregated witness keys wrapped in a script hash their own account path, so that an incompatible wallet finds nothing rather than finding part of the funds.

nodes.label: BIP84 path for native segwit
nodes.body: The BIP84 path is the standard path for native pay-to-witness-public-key-hash keys. The chapter's table gives it as m/84'/0'/0' for the script P2WPKH (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard says the same as BIP49 with a different number: it uses the account structure of BIP44 and BIP49 with the purpose level set to 84, and the address is derived by the native encapsulation of segregated witness, where the input script is empty and the output script is a zero followed by the twenty-byte key hash (Rusnak, 2017).

paras.text: The BIP84 path is the standard path for native pay-to-witness-public-key-hash keys. The chapter's table gives it as m/84'/0'/0' for the script P2WPKH (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard says the same as BIP49 with a different number: it uses the account structure of BIP44 and BIP49 with the purpose level set to 84, and the address is derived by the native encapsulation of segregated witness, where the input script is empty and the output script is a zero followed by the twenty-byte key hash (Rusnak, 2017).

This is the path most wallets use today, so a reader restoring a modern wallet is most likely to need it. The addresses it produces are the bech32 addresses beginning bc1q that chapter 4 of the book explained, and they are cheaper to spend than the nested form, which is why the nested scheme was transitional. For this course it is also the path the evidence of a real node shows in use: the wallet created by Bitcoin Core 31.1 reported its first address at m/84h/0h/0h/0/0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example reproduces the standard's own first test vector in full. From the recovery code of twelve repetitions of the word abandon ending in about, the standard derives the account m/84'/0'/0' and gives its first receiving public key and the address bc1qcr8te4kr609gcawutmrza0j4xv80jy8z306fyu (Rusnak, 2017). The example takes the hash of that public key as data, because the course's browser pages have no RIPEMD-160, and performs the whole bech32 encoding, checksum included, to arrive at the same address. The claims of this chapter derive the key itself from the code with this chapter's library, and Bitcoin Core 31.1 produced the same address from a descriptor built on the same account key (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The derivation is the familiar one: the recovery code gives a seed through PBKDF2, the seed gives the master key through HMAC-SHA512, three hardened steps give the account, and two normal steps give the address key. The encoding of the address is bech32, which takes the witness version and the twenty-byte key hash, converts them to groups of five bits, appends a six-character checksum computed over the human-readable part and the data, and writes the result in the thirty-two-character alphabet (Rusnak, 2017). The example's output is checked against the string the standard prints and against the address the real node derived.

Two cautions. The standard defines its own extended key prefixes, zpub and zprv, and the chapter's example descriptor from the Core evidence uses an ordinary xpub with an explicit path instead, which is BIP43's and BIP380's preference; a reader who meets a zpub should recognise it as the same key with different version bytes (Rusnak, 2017) (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014a) (Wuille and Chow, 2021). And the test vector's recovery code is the well-known abandon sequence, which is valid and public: it must never be used for funds, which is exactly why a standard can print it.

nodes.example: the first address of the standard's test vector
nodes.definition: BIP84 gives native segregated witness keys their own account path, and its test vector's first address is the bech32 address the course can recompute from the key hash.
