nodes.label: BIP86 path for single-key taproot
nodes.body: The BIP86 path is the standard path for taproot outputs with a single key. The chapter's table gives it as m/86'/0'/0' for the script P2TR single-key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard describes itself as suggesting a derivation scheme for wallets whose keys are involved in single-key pay-to-taproot outputs as the taproot internal key, and says it largely uses the same approach as BIPs 49 and 84 for ease of implementation (Chow, 2021).

paras.text: The BIP86 path is the standard path for taproot outputs with a single key. The chapter's table gives it as m/86'/0'/0' for the script P2TR single-key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard describes itself as suggesting a derivation scheme for wallets whose keys are involved in single-key pay-to-taproot outputs as the taproot internal key, and says it largely uses the same approach as BIPs 49 and 84 for ease of implementation (Chow, 2021).

The standard exists because seed backups are still poorer than descriptors. Its motivation says that with single-key taproot transactions it is useful to have a common derivation scheme so that wallets which have only a backup of the seed can be likely to recover such outputs, and adds, candidly, that although there are now solutions which obviate the need for fixed derivation paths for specific script types, many software wallets and hardware signers still use seed backups that lack derivation path and script information (Chow, 2021). That sentence is the whole argument of this branch in miniature.

A reader meets this path as the taproot addresses beginning bc1p and in the fourth descriptor pair of the Bitcoin Core wallet in this chapter's evidence, written with the function tr under the origin 6d8c4b8f followed by 86h/0h/0h (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The worked example computes the first step of the standard's own address derivation: the tagged hash of the test vector's internal key cc8a4bc6..., which begins 2ca01ed85cf6b652. The claims of this chapter carry the derivation through to the output key a60869f0... and the address bc1p5cyxnuxmeuwuvkwfem96lqzszd02n6xdcjrs20cac6yqjjwudpxqkedrcr that the standard prints (Chow, 2021).

The mechanism adds one step to the pattern of the other standards. The derived key becomes the internal key, and the standard quotes the taproot specification's rule that if the spending conditions do not require a script path, the output key should commit to an unspendable script path instead of having none, which is achieved by computing the output key as the internal key plus the tagged hash of the internal key times the generator point (Chow, 2021). The tag is the string TapTweak, and a tagged hash is the hash of the tag's hash twice followed by the message, which is what the worked example computes; the output script is then a one followed by the thirty-two-byte output key (Chow, 2021).

The address cannot be recomputed in the course's browser pages beyond this step, because the addition of a point to the curve needs the elliptic curve arithmetic of chapter 4 and the address uses the bech32m checksum rather than bech32; both are checked in the claims of this chapter instead (Chow, 2021). The standard also warns, as the others do, that it is not backward compatible by design, so an incompatible wallet will not discover these accounts at all (Chow, 2021).

nodes.example: the tweak of the test vector's internal key
nodes.definition: BIP86 gives single-key taproot outputs their own account path and says how the output key is computed from the derived key by a tagged hash.

nodes.label: Multisignature
nodes.body: Multisignature means that spending needs signatures from more than one key. The book's glossary defines it as requiring more than one key to authorise a Bitcoin transaction, and chapter 7 states the general form: multisignature scripts set a condition in which a number of public keys are recorded in the script and at least a threshold of those must provide signatures to spend the funds, so that a two-of-three arrangement lists three potential signers of whom at least two must sign (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example counts the ways that condition can be met: three pairs out of three keys.

paras.text: Multisignature means that spending needs signatures from more than one key. The book's glossary defines it as requiring more than one key to authorise a Bitcoin transaction, and chapter 7 states the general form: multisignature scripts set a condition in which a number of public keys are recorded in the script and at least a threshold of those must provide signatures to spend the funds, so that a two-of-three arrangement lists three potential signers of whom at least two must sign (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example counts the ways that condition can be met: three pairs out of three keys.

In this chapter multisignature is the argument that implicit paths cannot be enough. The chapter gives the case in full: Alice, Bob and Carol receive funds that can only be spent with signatures from two out of three of them, and although Alice needs only Bob's or Carol's signature to spend, she needs both of their public keys in order to find their joint funds on the blockchain, which means each of them must back up the public keys for all three; and it adds that as multisignature and other advanced scripts become more common, the inflexibility of implicit paths becomes more significant (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets multisignature in three places in this chapter. It is the reason the Muun wallet's recovery code is accompanied by a document, since that wallet defaults to requiring that spending transactions be signed by multiple keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is the case in which a wallet database holds only some of the private keys that a spending transaction needs, which the first branch described as external signing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And it is one of the script types a descriptor can express, which the chapter's sample table shows as a script-hash multisignature requiring two signatures corresponding to two given keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The mechanism that matters here is not the script but the information each participant must keep. The seed of one participant derives that participant's keys and nothing else, so the arrangement itself, which keys, how many signatures, in what order, is non-deterministic information that no recovery code can reproduce. Descriptors record exactly that: BIP383 defines the multi and sortedmulti expressions, and Bitcoin Core's documentation shows them with several extended public keys and their paths, so that one descriptor describes the whole arrangement (Wuille and Chow, 2021) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Two distinctions keep the subject clear. The threshold and the number of keys are different numbers, and chapter 7 notes that earlier editions of the book used m-of-n for what it now writes as t-of-k, so a reader comparing texts should check which letter means which (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). And a multisignature wallet is not more recoverable for having several keys: it is less recoverable, because every participant needs the public keys of all the others, which is why this is the case that pushed wallets towards descriptors.

nodes.example: two of three signatures
nodes.definition: A multisignature arrangement requires several of a set of keys to sign; its participants cannot restore the arrangement from their own seeds alone, because they also need the others' public keys.

nodes.label: Output script descriptors
nodes.body: This group covers the notation in which explicit paths are written. The chapter introduces it in one sentence: almost all wallet applications that use explicit paths use the output script descriptors standard, called descriptors for short, as specified in BIPs 380, 381, 382, 383, 384, 385, 386 and 389, and descriptors describe a script and the keys, or key paths, to be used with it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP380 is the general specification, and the others define the individual script expressions (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

paras.text: This group covers the notation in which explicit paths are written. The chapter introduces it in one sentence: almost all wallet applications that use explicit paths use the output script descriptors standard, called descriptors for short, as specified in BIPs 380, 381, 382, 383, 384, 385, 386 and 389, and descriptors describe a script and the keys, or key paths, to be used with it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP380 is the general specification, and the others define the individual script expressions (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

The group matters because descriptors are now how wallets talk about keys. Bitcoin Core's wallets are descriptor wallets, so every example in this course that comes from a real node is a descriptor; the chapter's own sample table is taken from Bitcoin Core's documentation; and the standard's motivation is exactly the problem this branch is about, that a backup of keys alone cannot say which output scripts and addresses to produce (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille and Chow, 2021) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

A descriptor works as a small expression that names a script type and supplies its keys, so that one line says everything a program needs in order to recognise and later spend a whole family of outputs. The outermost function says which kind of output script to build; its argument is a key, written either directly or as an extended key followed by the path to derive along, with a star standing for every index in a range so that one line covers an unbounded sequence of addresses. In front of the key, in brackets, the key origin records the fingerprint of the master key and the path already taken to reach this point, which is what lets a signer decide whether the key is one of its own. Eight characters of checksum close the line, computed over the text so that a copying mistake is refused rather than acted on, and the whole thing is text, which is why it can be written in a backup beside the recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille and Chow, 2021) (Chow, 2022).

The reader meets descriptors in any current node. The run of release 31.1 saved with this chapter printed the descriptors of a fresh wallet, each with its key origin, its ranged child path and its checksum, and answered with the same four checksums that this course computes from the standard's own algorithm; the account descriptor of one branch derived the address that the proposal's test vector names. They are met again wherever a watching wallet or a payment processor is set up, because a descriptor is now the usual way of telling such a program what to watch (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

The caution is that a descriptor is a backup and must be treated as one. It is not secret in the private sense when it carries only public keys, but it is the record without which an explicit arrangement cannot be restored, so storing it in the wallet it describes is no backup at all. And a descriptor carrying an extended public key discloses the whole branch to whoever reads it, with the privacy consequence the previous branch described. A learner should also expect the notation to grow: the spending conditions a descriptor can carry are a language of their own, and this chapter opens it only far enough to read the common forms (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

nodes.label: Output script
nodes.body: An output script is the piece of a transaction output that states the condition for spending it. Chapter 4 of the book introduced output and input scripts for the address types this course has met, and this chapter meets them again as the thing a descriptor describes: BIP380's title is output script descriptors, and it says that descriptors are a simple language that can be used to describe collections of output scripts (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The worked example measures one: a native segwit output script is a zero byte, a push of twenty bytes and the twenty-byte key hash, twenty-two bytes in all (Rusnak, 2017).

paras.text: An output script is the piece of a transaction output that states the condition for spending it. Chapter 4 of the book introduced output and input scripts for the address types this course has met, and this chapter meets them again as the thing a descriptor describes: BIP380's title is output script descriptors, and it says that descriptors are a simple language that can be used to describe collections of output scripts (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The worked example measures one: a native segwit output script is a zero byte, a push of twenty bytes and the twenty-byte key hash, twenty-two bytes in all (Rusnak, 2017).

The script is the thing that actually decides whether a payment can be spent, which is why a backup that does not record the script type is incomplete. BIP380 makes the argument: wallets have traditionally stored keys which are later serialised and mutated to produce the output scripts the wallet watches and the addresses it provides, but given just the private keys it is not possible for a restored wallet to know which kinds of output script and address to produce, which has led to incompatibilities between wallets when restoring a backup or exporting data for a watch-only wallet (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

A reader meets output scripts in the standards of this branch, each of which prints the script its path's keys belong in: BIP49 gives an input script that pushes a witness program and an output script that hashes it; BIP84 gives an empty input script and an output script of a zero and a key hash; BIP86 gives an output script of a one and a thirty-two-byte output key (Weigl, 2016) (Rusnak, 2017) (Chow, 2021). The same three forms appear in the descriptor functions sh, wpkh and tr that Bitcoin Core used in the wallet of this chapter's evidence (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

For this chapter the mechanism worth noting is the relation between a key and a script. One key can appear in several kinds of script, and each kind gives a different address, which is why the standards of this branch assign a different path to each: the key itself does not say which script it belongs in. Bitcoin Core's descriptor documentation lists the functions for each script type, among them pk, pkh, wpkh, sh and tr, with the rules about where each may appear (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The word script is used for several things in Bitcoin and a reader should keep them apart: the output script in the output being spent, the input script in the spending input, and the witness, which segregated witness moved out of the input script. This chapter needs only the first, and only as the object a descriptor describes; the details belong to the later chapters of the book on transactions and on authorisation.

nodes.example: twenty-two bytes for a native segwit output
nodes.definition: An output script is the program in a transaction output that says what must be presented to spend it; a descriptor is a description of a family of such scripts.

nodes.label: Output script descriptor
nodes.body: A descriptor is an expression that describes a set of output scripts. The chapter says descriptors describe a script and the keys, or key paths, to be used with it, and prints three examples from Bitcoin Core's documentation: a script-hash multisignature requiring two signatures for two given keys, a pay-to-public-key-hash script for a given public key, and a ranged descriptor whose extended public key is reached by a path from a master with a given fingerprint (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP380 gives the grammar: script types are specified explicitly through script expressions, and key derivation paths explicitly in key expressions (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

paras.text: A descriptor is an expression that describes a set of output scripts. The chapter says descriptors describe a script and the keys, or key paths, to be used with it, and prints three examples from Bitcoin Core's documentation: a script-hash multisignature requiring two signatures for two given keys, a pay-to-public-key-hash script for a given public key, and a ranged descriptor whose extended public key is reached by a path from a master with a given fingerprint (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP380 gives the grammar: script types are specified explicitly through script expressions, and key derivation paths explicitly in key expressions (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

The notation solves the problem this branch opened with, and it does so in one line of text. A descriptor records the script type, the keys, the origin of each key and the paths below it, so a wallet given a descriptor needs to guess nothing and a wallet given only a seed must guess everything. That is why Bitcoin Core's modern wallets are built on descriptors and why the chapter says applications that support advanced scripts increasingly adopt them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The worked example takes one real descriptor apart: the one Bitcoin Core 31.1 produced for the native segwit receive branch of the wallet created for this chapter. Its function is wpkh; its key origin is the fingerprint 6d8c4b8f with the path 84h/0h/0h; and it ends with the branch and wildcard /0/*, which stands for every index of the receive branch (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The chapter's own table and Bitcoin Core's documentation give many more forms, from a single public key to a taproot output with script paths (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The syntax is a function applied to arguments, which may themselves be functions. BIP380 says a key expression consists of optional key origin information in brackets, then the key itself, which may be a hexadecimal public key, a key in wallet import format, or an extended public or private key, followed by zero or more path elements and optionally a final wildcard (Wuille and Chow, 2021). Script expressions wrap key expressions: Bitcoin Core's documentation lists which may appear at the top level and which only inside others, so that for example wpkh is allowed at the top level or inside sh (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Two things a descriptor is not. It is not a secret by default: a descriptor with an extended public key lets its holder compute every address of the branch, which is useful for a watching wallet and a privacy loss if it leaks (Wuille, 2012). And it is not a wallet state: the range of indices a wallet has prepared is separate, which is why the descriptors in this chapter's evidence carry a range from 0 to 999 and a next index alongside the descriptor itself (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: a descriptor split into function and argument
nodes.definition: A descriptor is a short expression naming a script type as a function and its keys as arguments, so that it says exactly which scripts and addresses a wallet should produce.

nodes.label: Descriptor checksum
nodes.body: The descriptor checksum is the eight characters that follow a hash sign at the end of a descriptor. BIP380 describes it exactly: following the top-level script expression is a single octothorpe followed by the eight-character checksum, which is an error-correcting checksum similar to bech32 and uses the same character set, the thirty-two characters of the bech32 alphabet (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The worked example counts them in the standard's own smallest example, raw(deadbeef) with the checksum 89f8spxm.

paras.text: The descriptor checksum is the eight characters that follow a hash sign at the end of a descriptor. BIP380 describes it exactly: following the top-level script expression is a single octothorpe followed by the eight-character checksum, which is an error-correcting checksum similar to bech32 and uses the same character set, the thirty-two characters of the bech32 alphabet (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The worked example counts them in the standard's own smallest example, raw(deadbeef) with the checksum 89f8spxm.

A descriptor is a long string that a user may have to type, and a single wrong character would point a wallet at the wrong keys. The checksum turns that silent failure into a refusal. BIP380 states its guarantees in terms of symbol errors: any one symbol error is always detected; any two or three symbol errors in a descriptor of up to 49,154 characters are always detected; any four in up to 507 characters and any five in up to 77 characters; and random errors have a chance of one in 2 to the 40 of going undetected (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

A reader meets the checksum on every descriptor a wallet prints: all eight descriptors of the Bitcoin Core wallet in this chapter's evidence end in one, and the node's own command for inspecting a descriptor returns the checksum as a separate field, which the evidence of this chapter records for four descriptors including the three the chapter prints in its sample table (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The claims of this chapter recompute all four checksums from the standard's algorithm and obtain the values the real node returned.

The mechanism is a linear code over the alphabet, computed in two stages. The characters of the descriptor are mapped into an input alphabet and grouped so that each group of three characters contributes an extra symbol, then a polynomial remainder is computed with five generator constants and the result is written as eight characters of the bech32 alphabet; checking recomputes the same remainder and compares it with a constant (Wuille and Chow, 2021). BIP380 notes which substitutions count as one symbol error, including any character of the set used by hexadecimal keys and any case error, and observes that extended keys have their own checksum as well (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

The checksum protects the descriptor, not the keys: a descriptor with a valid checksum may still name the wrong account, and a descriptor whose extended key is wrong will usually fail the key's own base58check instead. A reader should also note that the checksum is part of the string a wallet expects: Bitcoin Core accepts a descriptor without one in some commands and will compute it, but the canonical form includes it, which is why the evidence files of this chapter show the node returning descriptors with the checksum appended (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

nodes.example: eight characters after a hash sign
nodes.definition: A descriptor carries an eight-character error-detecting checksum after a hash sign, which catches any one or two symbol errors in a descriptor of ordinary length.

nodes.label: Key origin
nodes.body: The key origin is the bracketed part at the start of a key expression. BIP380 specifies it: optionally, key origin information, consisting of an open bracket, exactly eight hexadecimal characters for the fingerprint of the key where the derivation starts, then zero or more path elements written as a number with or without an h to indicate hardened steps, then a closing bracket (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The chapter's third sample descriptor shows one: it specifies that the extended public key is a child of a master with fingerprint d34db33f derived using the path 44'/0'/0' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The key origin is the bracketed part at the start of a key expression. BIP380 specifies it: optionally, key origin information, consisting of an open bracket, exactly eight hexadecimal characters for the fingerprint of the key where the derivation starts, then zero or more path elements written as a number with or without an h to indicate hardened steps, then a closing bracket (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The chapter's third sample descriptor shows one: it specifies that the extended public key is a child of a master with fingerprint d34db33f derived using the path 44'/0'/0' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The origin is what lets a public descriptor be matched with a private key held elsewhere. A hardware signing device given a descriptor can compare the fingerprint with its own master key and then derive exactly the key the descriptor names; without the origin it would have to guess the path. BIP380's motivation lists this among the problems it solves, noting that the lack of derivation path information in backups and exports leads to incompatibilities between wallets (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

The worked example reads the origin out of a real descriptor: the native segwit receive descriptor of the wallet Bitcoin Core 31.1 created for this chapter begins with the fingerprint 6d8c4b8f and the path 84h/0h/0h, and the program recovers both (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The same structure appears in the chapter's sample table, in the BIP84 account descriptor built for this chapter's evidence, and in BIP329's label format, where the optional origin property must contain an abbreviated descriptor with all key origin information but no keys, paths or checksum (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Raw, 2022).

Mechanically the origin is metadata: it takes no part in deriving anything below the key, and the path it records is the path above the key, which has already been applied. That is why the path in the brackets is usually the hardened part, down to the account, and the path after the key is the normal part, the branch and the index. Because the fingerprint is only four bytes, BIP32 warns that software must be willing to deal with collisions, so the origin is a hint for selecting a device, not a proof of identity (Wuille, 2012).

Two details to keep straight. The origin is written with h or with an apostrophe for hardened steps, and the chapter recommends h in contexts such as descriptors where an apostrophe has a special meaning in a shell, which is what Bitcoin Core writes in the evidence of this chapter (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026). And the fingerprint belongs to the master key, not to the key that follows: it is the fingerprint of the key where the derivation starts, so two descriptors from the same seed share it (Wuille and Chow, 2021).

nodes.example: a fingerprint and three hardened steps
nodes.definition: The key origin of a descriptor records, in brackets, the fingerprint of the master key and the path from it to the key that follows, so that a signing device can find the right key.

nodes.label: Multipath descriptor
nodes.body: A multipath descriptor is a descriptor in which one derivation step is a tuple of values. BIP389 specifies the modification: a key expression may contain one path element of the form of several numbers separated by semicolons inside angle brackets, indicating a tuple of derivation steps to be taken after the extended key (Chow, 2022). The worked example expands such a descriptor by hand: the element containing 0 and 1 becomes two descriptors, one for each value, in the order written.

paras.text: A multipath descriptor is a descriptor in which one derivation step is a tuple of values. BIP389 specifies the modification: a key expression may contain one path element of the form of several numbers separated by semicolons inside angle brackets, indicating a tuple of derivation steps to be taken after the extended key (Chow, 2022). The worked example expands such a descriptor by hand: the element containing 0 and 1 becomes two descriptors, one for each value, in the order written.

The form exists because wallets almost always need two descriptors that differ in one digit. BIP389's motivation says that wallets typically have one descriptor for producing receiving addresses and another for change addresses, that these are extremely similar, producing the same types of script and deriving from the same master key with almost identical paths, and that it is therefore useful to have a notation representing both as a single descriptor where one of the derivation steps is a pair of values (Chow, 2022).

A reader meets the need for this form directly in the evidence of this chapter: the Bitcoin Core wallet created for it has eight descriptors that are four pairs, each pair sharing an account key and differing only in the branch, 0 or 1, with one of each pair marked internal (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Bitcoin Core's own descriptor documentation shows the multipath notation in use, in a two-of-three multisignature whose keys each carry the element for the receive and change paths (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The standard's status in the BIPs repository is Draft (Chow, 2022).

The expansion is purely textual and the standard fixes its order: the descriptor is equivalent to the list of descriptors obtained by replacing the tuple with each of its values in turn, so the first descriptor of the list is the receive branch and the second the change branch when the tuple is written 0 and 1. Because the expansion happens before any derivation, nothing else about the descriptor changes, and the checksum is computed over the multipath form itself.

The notation is a convenience and not a new capability: a wallet that does not support it can be given the two descriptors separately, which is what Bitcoin Core's own listing shows. A reader should also notice that the tuple is a path element, not a wildcard: the wildcard star at the end still stands for the whole range of address indices, so a multipath descriptor with a wildcard describes two infinite families of scripts rather than two scripts (Wuille and Chow, 2021) (Chow, 2022).

nodes.example: one descriptor expanded into two
nodes.definition: A multipath descriptor writes a tuple of derivation steps in angle brackets, so that one descriptor stands for the receive and the change descriptor of a wallet.

nodes.label: Miniscript
nodes.body: Miniscript is a language for writing a subset of Bitcoin scripts in a structured way. Its specification describes it as enabling analysis, composition, generic signing and more (Wuille et al., 2023). The chapter mentions it once, among the newer technologies that the Muun wallet's unusual recovery arrangement supports, beside the Lightning Network and output script descriptors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); it belongs in this group because a descriptor can contain a miniscript expression, which is how an arbitrary spending condition is written down in a backup.

paras.text: Miniscript is a language for writing a subset of Bitcoin scripts in a structured way. Its specification describes it as enabling analysis, composition, generic signing and more (Wuille et al., 2023). The chapter mentions it once, among the newer technologies that the Muun wallet's unusual recovery arrangement supports, beside the Lightning Network and output script descriptors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); it belongs in this group because a descriptor can contain a miniscript expression, which is how an arbitrary spending condition is written down in a backup.

The reason such a language exists is that raw Bitcoin script is hard to reason about. The specification lists what is highly non-trivial even though the language is limited: finding the most economical script for a combination of spending conditions, composing two scripts into one, finding out what conditions a script permits, and constructing a satisfying witness given enough private keys (Wuille et al., 2023). For backups the consequence is direct: a condition that cannot be analysed cannot be safely recorded or restored.

A reader meets miniscript in Bitcoin Core's descriptor documentation, which shows a policy of four keys and three time locks that the documentation describes as starting as four-of-four and decaying to three-of-four, two-of-four and finally one-of-four at each future halving height, written as a threshold expression inside a witness-script descriptor with multipath keys (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example is that sequence of thresholds. The specification's status in the BIPs repository is Draft (Wuille et al., 2023).

The mechanism that matters here is that miniscript is a notation for the same scripts, with enough structure that a tool can compute properties of them. Because a descriptor can carry such an expression, one line of text can record a condition involving several parties and several times, together with the key origins needed to find each participant's keys; that is the extreme case of the explicit path, and it is the case the chapter says is driving wallets towards descriptors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2023).

Miniscript is beyond what this chapter needs, and a learner should take only two points from it. The first is that the explicit approach scales to conditions that no implicit path could express. The second is that it is a draft, like several standards in this chapter, so a course should present it as a direction of travel and not as a settled part of the stack; the chapter's own treatment, one mention in a list, is the right weight for a first course (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille et al., 2023).

nodes.example: a policy that decays from four of four to one of four
nodes.definition: Miniscript is a structured language for a subset of Bitcoin scripts, so that spending conditions can be analysed, composed and signed for; descriptors can contain it.

nodes.label: Backing up data that is not keys
nodes.body: This branch is about everything in a wallet that a seed cannot reproduce. The chapter opens its section on backing up non-key data by granting the obvious: the most important data in a wallet database is its private keys, and deterministic derivation with recovery codes provides a reasonably robust solution for backing up and recovering the keys and the bitcoins they control; but it is important to consider that many wallet databases store more than just keys, since they also store user-provided information about every transaction they sent or received (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch is about everything in a wallet that a seed cannot reproduce. The chapter opens its section on backing up non-key data by granting the obvious: the most important data in a wallet database is its private keys, and deterministic derivation with recovery codes provides a reasonably robust solution for backing up and recovering the keys and the bitcoins they control; but it is important to consider that many wallet databases store more than just keys, since they also store user-provided information about every transaction they sent or received (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch matters because a restored wallet with the right balance can still be useless. The chapter asks the reader to imagine reviewing a bank or credit card statement from a year ago that had the date and amount of every transaction listed but a blank entry for the description field, and says that because address and transaction labels are stored only in each user's wallet database and are not deterministic, they cannot be restored by using just a recovery code: all the user will see is a list of approximate transaction times and bitcoin amounts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For a user with tax obligations or an accountant, that is a real loss.

A reader meets the problem in two forms. The first is labels, which the chapter illustrates with Bob adding a label to an address when he sends Alice an invoice and Alice labelling the transaction as paying Bob, and with a small table of Alice's own transaction history (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The second is data belonging to protocols built on Bitcoin: the chapter notes that an increasing number of applications support sending and receiving over the Lightning Network, whose recovery mechanism cannot guarantee results (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch has two groups. The wallet notes group covers the labels themselves, on addresses and on transactions, and the standard proposed for exporting them, BIP329. The other protocol data group covers the data that other protocols add, with the Lightning Network and its static channel backups as the chapter's example, and the one solution the chapter describes for backing up everything at once: a complete, automatic backup of the wallet database encrypted by a key derived from the seed, which also requires a section on what encryption is.

The branch's conclusion is the chapter's own, and it is a warning about habits rather than about software: again, this means that users and wallet applications need to do more than just back up a recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter also notes that wallets should provide a convenient way to back up label data, which it says seems obvious, and yet a number of widely used applications make it easy to create and use recovery codes while providing no way to back up or restore label data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A learner should test a restoration before relying on one.

nodes.label: Labels and notes
nodes.body: This group covers the information a user adds to a wallet by hand. The chapter's examples are the two kinds that nearly every wallet keeps: a label attached to an address, so that the payment received there can be told apart from others, and a label attached to a transaction, so that the user can remember what it was for; it adds that some wallets store other useful information with a transaction, such as the exchange rate at the time, which can be useful for calculating taxes in some jurisdictions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group covers the information a user adds to a wallet by hand. The chapter's examples are the two kinds that nearly every wallet keeps: a label attached to an address, so that the payment received there can be told apart from others, and a label attached to a transaction, so that the user can remember what it was for; it adds that some wallets store other useful information with a transaction, such as the exchange rate at the time, which can be useful for calculating taxes in some jurisdictions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because this information is private in a way the keys are not. The chapter notes that labels are stored entirely within their own wallets and not shared with the network, which protects the users' privacy and keeps unnecessary personal data out of the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The same property that protects them, that they exist in one place only, is what makes them easy to lose, so privacy and fragility have the same cause.

Labels work in the opposite direction from everything else in this chapter. A key is derived, so one record reproduces it; a label is assigned, so nothing reproduces it. The wallet stores a short piece of text against a reference - an address, a transaction, an output - and the pairing exists only in that store, because the chain records the payment and knows nothing about what the payer called it. That is why moving labels between applications needs a format rather than a derivation: the proposal this section names writes one record per line, each a small object giving the kind of thing being labelled, the reference that identifies it and the text itself, so that an export from one wallet is a file another can read. The mechanism is deliberately plain, because the difficulty here is not the encoding but the fact that this information has no other source (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Raw, 2022).

The reader meets labels as the first thing they lose and the last thing they think of. A wallet restored from its code shows the right balance and the right history with every description gone, which is the moment the distinction in this section becomes concrete. They are met in the export and import menus of wallets that implement the format, and in this course's own account of what a complete backup contains, where the labels are one of the five items and the only one that no amount of derivation can rebuild (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Raw, 2022).

The caution is about privacy rather than loss. A label file is the most revealing document a wallet can produce: it ties addresses to names, purposes and counterparties, which is exactly the linkage that using a fresh address for each payment was meant to prevent. So a label backup needs the protection a key backup needs, for a different reason, and the encrypted backup of the next section is the mechanism the chapter offers for it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Raw, 2022).

nodes.label: Address label
nodes.body: An address label is a name a user gives to one of their own addresses. The chapter's example is the natural one: when Bob creates a new address as part of sending an invoice to Alice, he adds a label to the address he generates so that he can distinguish her payment from other payments he receives (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The label is a note about the wallet's own address, not about the payer, and nothing about it leaves the wallet.

paras.text: An address label is a name a user gives to one of their own addresses. The chapter's example is the natural one: when Bob creates a new address as part of sending an invoice to Alice, he adds a label to the address he generates so that he can distinguish her payment from other payments he receives (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The label is a note about the wallet's own address, not about the payer, and nothing about it leaves the wallet.

The label is what makes a fresh address per payment practical. The branch on deploying keys shows a web store giving every order its own address so that each order has a unique identifier; without a note recording which address belonged to which order, that identifier would be useless (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Labelling is therefore not a nicety but the bookkeeping that privacy-preserving address use requires.

A reader meets address labels in every wallet interface that asks for a name when an address is created, and in BIP329's record types, where the type addr takes an address in base58 or bech32 format as its reference (Raw, 2022). Bitcoin Core keeps labels for addresses as well, which is why its own address information command reports a label field; the evidence of this chapter shows the fields a fresh wallet reports for its first address, among them the descriptor and the key path (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

Mechanically a label is a row in the wallet database keyed by the address, and that is all. Because the address is derived from the seed and the label is not, a restoration reproduces the address and loses the label, which is the asymmetry this branch is about. BIP329 adds one refinement for the case of several wallets from one seed: a record may carry an origin property describing the originating wallet, to disambiguate labels from different wallets contained in the same export (Raw, 2022).

Labels look harmless and are not. Because they connect an address to a person or a purpose, a leaked label file can undo the privacy that fresh addresses provide, and BIP329 says so plainly: care should be taken when exporting due to the privacy-sensitive nature of the data, encryption in transit over untrusted networks is highly recommended, encryption at rest should be considered, and unencrypted exports should be deleted as soon as possible (Raw, 2022).

nodes.example: a name on an address at the time it is created
nodes.definition: An address label is a note a user attaches to an address they hand out, so that payments arriving there can be recognised; it exists only in that user's wallet.

nodes.label: Transaction label
nodes.body: A transaction label is a note on a payment. The chapter's example continues the one before it: when Alice pays Bob's address, she labels the transaction as paying Bob, for the same reason Bob labelled the address, and the chapter prints her transaction history with each transaction labelled, two rows, one for bitcoins bought from Joe and one for a payment to Bob for a podcast (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example adds the two amounts of that table, a receipt of 0.001 and a payment of 0.00075, and gets the 0.00025 bitcoin left.

paras.text: A transaction label is a note on a payment. The chapter's example continues the one before it: when Alice pays Bob's address, she labels the transaction as paying Bob, for the same reason Bob labelled the address, and the chapter prints her transaction history with each transaction labelled, two rows, one for bitcoins bought from Joe and one for a payment to Bob for a podcast (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example adds the two amounts of that table, a receipt of 0.001 and a payment of 0.00075, and gets the 0.00025 bitcoin left.

Transaction labels are the user's own record of what their money did, and nothing else records it. The blockchain holds the amounts and the times; it holds no field for a description, which the chapter notes in its web store section when it says that the only metadata chosen by the receiver of a typical transaction are the amount and the payment address, with no subject or message field to hold a unique invoice number (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The label fills that gap privately.

A reader meets transaction labels in the history view of any wallet, in the chapter's table, and in BIP329, whose type tx takes a transaction identifier in hexadecimal format as its reference and whose motivation observes that labels have even become mandatory when spending in several Bitcoin wallets (Raw, 2022). The standard also allows labels on inputs and outputs, with a reference of a transaction identifier and an index, and notes that the model Bitcoin uses makes these labels particularly valuable because they may indicate the source of funds (Raw, 2022).

The mechanism is the same as for an address label, a row in the local database, and so is the consequence for recovery. The chapter spells out what a seed-only restoration shows: a list of approximate transaction times and bitcoin amounts, which can make it quite difficult to figure out how the money was used in the past (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The amounts and times come from the blockchain, which is why they survive; the words do not.

Two cautions. The arithmetic of a wallet's balance is not the arithmetic of its labels: the worked example's subtraction uses rounded decimal figures as the chapter prints them, whereas a real wallet works in satoshis, the integer unit chapter 2 introduced, precisely to avoid the rounding that decimal fractions invite. And a label is an assertion by the user, not evidence: it is as reliable as the person who typed it, which is worth remembering when labels are used for tax records.

nodes.example: Alice's two labelled payments
nodes.definition: A transaction label is a note a user attaches to a payment they made or received, which a seed-based restoration cannot reproduce.

nodes.label: Label export format (BIP329)
nodes.body: BIP329 is the proposal for writing labels down in a portable way. The chapter mentions it in one sentence: it may be useful for wallet applications to provide a standardised format to export labels so that they can be used in other applications, such as accounting software, and a standard for that format is proposed in BIP329 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard itself says it specifies a format for the export of labels that may be attached to various common types of records in a wallet (Raw, 2022).

paras.text: BIP329 is the proposal for writing labels down in a portable way. The chapter mentions it in one sentence: it may be useful for wallet applications to provide a standardised format to export labels so that they can be used in other applications, such as accounting software, and a standard for that format is proposed in BIP329 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard itself says it specifies a format for the export of labels that may be attached to various common types of records in a wallet (Raw, 2022).

The reason given is lock-in. The standard's motivation says that the export and import of funds across different wallets is well defined through standards such as BIP39, BIP32 and BIP44, which are well supported and allow users to move easily between wallets, but that there is no defined standard to transfer the labels a user may have applied; allowing users to import and export labels in a standardised way ensures that they do not experience lock-in to a particular wallet application (Raw, 2022). The argument is exactly the one BIP380 makes about scripts, applied to notes.

The worked example writes one record in the shape the standard defines: a JSON object with a type, a reference and a label, here an address record for the address of the BIP84 test vector with one of the chapter's own labels (Raw, 2022) (Rusnak, 2017) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The standard's full set of types is wider: a transaction, an address, a public key, an input, an output, an extended public key or a scan key of a newer payment scheme, each with a defined form of reference, plus optional origin and spendable properties (Raw, 2022).

The format is deliberately plain. The standard uses JSON lines, also called newline-delimited JSON, so that a document can be split, streamed or incrementally added to, and so that a formatting error cannot invalidate an entire import; an export must be a UTF-8 text file with one JSON object per line, separated by a newline, with no multiline values, and each object must carry the type and the reference while the label, origin and spendable properties are optional (Raw, 2022). It also includes the frozen state of an output, because that wallet-related metadata is similar to labels and is not captured elsewhere (Raw, 2022).

Three limits are worth stating. The standard is a Draft and informational, so support varies; it defines no private key types, for security reasons; and the data it carries is privacy-sensitive, which is why it recommends encryption in transit and at rest (Raw, 2022). The chapter's own complaint stands beside it: a format helps only if wallets implement it, and the chapter notes that a number of widely used wallets still provide no way to back up label data at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: one record as a line of JSON
nodes.definition: BIP329 proposes a line-based JSON format for exporting wallet labels, so that labels can be moved between applications instead of locking a user into one.

nodes.label: Other data a wallet keeps
nodes.body: This group covers the data that protocols built on top of Bitcoin add to a wallet, and the one general solution the chapter offers for backing everything up. The chapter introduces the subject by saying that wallet applications implementing additional protocols beyond basic Bitcoin support may also need or want to store other data, and gives the Lightning Network as its example, noting that although the protocol provides a method to recover funds in the event of a data loss, called static channel backups, it cannot guarantee results (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group covers the data that protocols built on top of Bitcoin add to a wallet, and the one general solution the chapter offers for backing everything up. The chapter introduces the subject by saying that wallet applications implementing additional protocols beyond basic Bitcoin support may also need or want to store other data, and gives the Lightning Network as its example, noting that although the protocol provides a method to recover funds in the event of a data loss, called static channel backups, it cannot guarantee results (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because the consequences here are worse than losing a label. The chapter states them: if the node a wallet connects to realises that data has been lost, it may be able to steal bitcoins; and if that node loses its own database at the same time and neither party has an adequate backup, both lose funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Data loss in such a protocol is therefore not only a loss of records but a loss of money.

The difficulty works like this. A protocol built on top of Bitcoin keeps state that changes with every payment, and the newest state is the only safe one, because an old state is a claim the counterparty can prove to be out of date and penalise. A backup is therefore stale the moment it is taken, which is a different problem from the one a recovery code solves - the code is correct for ever, and this data is correct for one moment. The two answers in this section attack it from opposite ends. A static backup gives up on restoring the state and keeps only what is needed to ask the counterparty to close out and return the funds, which recovers the money and loses the channel. An encrypted wallet backup gives up on deriving the data and simply copies all of it, keys and labels and protocol state together, under a key that the seed itself produces - which is the one mechanism in the chapter that backs up everything (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lightning Labs, 2026b).

The reader meets this group only if they use a second-layer protocol, and then immediately. Setting up a payment channel produces a backup file within minutes and a warning about restoring old copies of it; the same warning appears in the documents of the implementations, which this course fetched and saved. The encrypted backup is met in the handful of wallets that offer it, and its idea is met again in chapter 4's passphrase protection, because both derive a protecting key from something the user already has (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lightning Labs, 2026b).

The caution is that restoring the wrong copy here is worse than restoring nothing. With keys, an old backup is simply incomplete; with channel state, an old backup can be a provably stale claim, and acting on it can cost the funds it was meant to protect. The second caution is that an encrypted backup moves the problem to the key that encrypts it: if that key is derived from the seed, the backup is only as safe as the seed, and if it is not, it is one more secret to keep (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Lightning Network
nodes.body: The Lightning Network is a protocol layered on Bitcoin for making payments without putting each of them on the blockchain. The book's glossary describes it as an implementation of hashed timelock contracts, which the same glossary defines as payments that require the receiver either to acknowledge the payment before a deadline by producing cryptographic proof of it or to forfeit the right to claim it, with bidirectional payment channels, which allows payments to be securely routed across multiple peer-to-peer channels, so that any peer can pay any other even without a direct channel between them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 14 of the book develops the idea from a one-directional channel for a metered service to bidirectional channels joined end to end into a routed network first proposed under that name (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The Lightning Network is a protocol layered on Bitcoin for making payments without putting each of them on the blockchain. The book's glossary describes it as an implementation of hashed timelock contracts, which the same glossary defines as payments that require the receiver either to acknowledge the payment before a deadline by producing cryptographic proof of it or to forfeit the right to claim it, with bidirectional payment channels, which allows payments to be securely routed across multiple peer-to-peer channels, so that any peer can pay any other even without a direct channel between them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 14 of the book develops the idea from a one-directional channel for a metered service to bidirectional channels joined end to end into a routed network first proposed under that name (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

For this chapter the protocol matters because of where the money sits. The lnd recovery document explains that a node's funds can be in one of two pools, on-chain funds, which are outputs under the node's control that can be spent immediately and without any auxiliary data, and off-chain funds, which exist within a two-of-two multisignature output usually called a payment channel (Lightning Labs, 2026b). A seed recovers the first pool; the second needs the channel's state, which is not derivable from the seed.

A reader meets the protocol in this chapter three times: as the reason the chapter says wallets may need to store other data; as one of the newer technologies the Muun wallet's recovery arrangement supports; and in the lnd documentation, where recovery needs both the 24-word cipher seed and the encrypted static channel backup file (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lightning Labs, 2026b). Chapter 1 of the book introduced it among the ways Bitcoin is used, and chapter 14 gives the mechanism.

The part of the mechanism this chapter needs is short. A channel is opened by a transaction that pays an output requiring both parties' signatures, which chapter 14 describes for a related construction as assigning funds to an output that requires signatures from both parties; the parties then sign successive versions of a settlement that divides the balance, and only the last of them is meant to be published (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because only the latest version is valid in the parties' agreement, a wallet that restores an old version is in a dangerous position, which is the next section's subject.

The protocol is outside the scope of this chapter and a reader should take only the recovery consequence from it: a Lightning-capable wallet's backup problem is strictly harder than a Bitcoin wallet's, because part of its state changes with every payment and cannot be recomputed. The chapter's conclusion applies with full force here: users and wallets need to do more than back up a recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a channel as a shared output
nodes.definition: The Lightning Network is a protocol of payment channels built on Bitcoin, in which funds live in outputs that two parties control jointly, so a wallet must keep state that no seed can reproduce.

nodes.label: Static channel backup
nodes.body: A static channel backup is the recovery mechanism the Lightning Network provides for the off-chain pool. The chapter names it: although the protocol provides a method to recover funds in the event of a data loss, called static channel backups, it cannot guarantee results (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The lnd documentation explains the word static: the backups need to be obtained only once, when the channel is created, and from then on a backup is good until the channel is closed (Lightning Labs, 2026b).

paras.text: A static channel backup is the recovery mechanism the Lightning Network provides for the off-chain pool. The chapter names it: although the protocol provides a method to recover funds in the event of a data loss, called static channel backups, it cannot guarantee results (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The lnd documentation explains the word static: the backups need to be obtained only once, when the channel is created, and from then on a backup is good until the channel is closed (Lightning Labs, 2026b).

The mechanism exists because the obvious alternative is dangerous. The document explains why copying the channel database periodically is worse: those methods can be dangerous because one never knows whether one has the latest state of a channel, whereas the static backup aims to provide a simple, safe method to let users recover the settled funds in their channels in the case of partial or complete data loss (Lightning Labs, 2026b). It also says what the backup contains and what it triggers: all the information needed to initiate the protocol's data loss protection feature, which ultimately leads to recovering the channel's funds on-chain (Lightning Labs, 2026b).

A reader meets static channel backups as a file beside the chain data, which the lnd documentation describes as a special file containing backup state, and as the second of the two things its recovery procedure requires beside the cipher seed (Lightning Labs, 2026b). The chapter's own warning about the relationship with the other node belongs here: if the node a wallet connects to realises that data has been lost, it may be able to steal bitcoins, and if both parties lose their databases at the same time with no adequate backup, both lose funds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mechanism connects to the rest of this chapter through its encryption. The lnd documentation says that the backup file is encrypted using a key derived from the user's seed, so that it cannot be used in isolation, and gives the reason: this protects the privacy of the user's channels in the backup state and ensures that a random node cannot attempt to import another user's channels (Lightning Labs, 2026b). That is the same construction as the encrypted wallet backup two sections below, and it is why the seed remains the single root of a recovery even for data that is not derived from it.

The limits are stated by both sources and should be quoted rather than softened. The chapter says the method cannot guarantee results (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The documentation is more precise about what is recoverable: given a valid backup a user will be able to recover funds that are fully settled within their channels, meaning funds in the base commitment outputs, the outputs of the transaction that records the channel's current division, and not those in the payments still in flight, because the backup is made right after the channel is created, when the future payments are not yet known (Lightning Labs, 2026b). A learner should therefore read static as once per channel, not as complete.

nodes.example: one backup per channel, not per payment
nodes.definition: A static channel backup records what is needed to recover a channel's settled funds and is taken once, when the channel is created; it allows recovery of those funds but cannot guarantee the result.

nodes.label: Encryption
nodes.body: Encryption is the operation that turns readable data into a form from which only a holder of the key can recover it. The chapter uses the idea without defining it, in the sentence that matters most for this branch: a few wallet applications frequently and automatically create complete backups of their wallet database encrypted by one of the keys derived from their seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example shows the shape of such an operation at its simplest: a key is derived from a seed by hashing, a note is combined with it by exclusive-or so that it becomes unreadable bytes, and combining the result with the same key again returns the original text.

paras.text: Encryption is the operation that turns readable data into a form from which only a holder of the key can recover it. The chapter uses the idea without defining it, in the sentence that matters most for this branch: a few wallet applications frequently and automatically create complete backups of their wallet database encrypted by one of the keys derived from their seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example shows the shape of such an operation at its simplest: a key is derived from a seed by hashing, a note is combined with it by exclusive-or so that it becomes unreadable bytes, and combining the result with the same key again returns the original text.

Encryption is what lets a backup be stored in a place the user does not control. The chapter draws exactly that conclusion: because Bitcoin keys must be unguessable and modern encryption algorithms are considered very secure, nobody should be able to open the encrypted backup except someone who can generate the seed, which makes it safe to store the backup on untrusted computers such as cloud hosting services or even random network peers (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The hard problem of backups, finding a safe place, is thereby replaced by the problem already solved, keeping the seed.

A reader meets encryption in several places in this chapter. The Muun recovery code decrypts the private keys contained in the user's kit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The lnd static channel backup file is encrypted with a key derived from the seed (Lightning Labs, 2026b). SLIP39 encrypts the master secret with the user's passphrase before splitting it, and Aezeed enciphers its whole plaintext seed, which is why its words are a ciphertext (Rusnak et al., 2017) (Lightning Labs, 2026a). In each case the same pattern appears: a secret the user already keeps protects data the user cannot otherwise protect.

The example in the worked example is a one-time pad and is shown only for its shape; real schemes use a block cipher or an authenticated cipher, as Aezeed does with aez and SLIP39 does with a Feistel network whose round function is PBKDF2 (Lightning Labs, 2026a) (Rusnak et al., 2017). What the example does show correctly is the structure a reader needs: the key comes from the seed by a one-way function, so it never has to be stored, and decryption is the same operation run again, so nothing else needs to be remembered.

Three cautions. A one-time pad reused on two messages is broken, which is why real schemes never derive one key for two purposes; the example's key is derived with a purpose string for exactly that reason. Encryption without authentication hides data but does not detect tampering, which is why Aezeed's designers chose a cipher with a built-in checksum (Lightning Labs, 2026a). And encryption does not reduce the number of secrets a user must keep: it moves the whole backup's safety onto the seed, so a lost seed now loses the labels as well as the keys.

nodes.example: a note hidden and recovered with a derived key
nodes.definition: Encryption turns data into a form that only a holder of the key can read back; a wallet can therefore store a backup where anyone can see it, as long as the key stays secret.
