nodes.label: Encrypted wallet backup
nodes.body: An encrypted wallet backup is the chapter's one solution for backing up everything at once. It describes the practice: one solution implemented by a few wallet applications is to frequently and automatically create complete backups of their wallet database, encrypted by one of the keys derived from their seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The backup therefore contains the keys, the labels and whatever protocol data the wallet keeps, and its safety rests on the seed the user already has.

paras.text: An encrypted wallet backup is the chapter's one solution for backing up everything at once. It describes the practice: one solution implemented by a few wallet applications is to frequently and automatically create complete backups of their wallet database, encrypted by one of the keys derived from their seed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The backup therefore contains the keys, the labels and whatever protocol data the wallet keeps, and its safety rests on the seed the user already has.

The attraction is that it restores the whole wallet from one secret. The chapter describes the recovery: if the original database is lost, the user enters their recovery code into the wallet application to restore the seed, and the application can then retrieve the latest backup file, regenerate the encryption key, decrypt the backup and restore all of the user's labels and additional protocol data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Nothing else has to have been written down, which is what makes this the only mechanism in the chapter that closes the gap the branch opened with.

A reader meets the same construction in the lnd static channel backup, encrypted with a key derived from the user's seed so that it cannot be used in isolation (Lightning Labs, 2026b). Bitcoin Core offers the plain version of the idea without the encryption: its backupwallet command, whose help text this chapter's claims read, safely copies the current wallet file to a destination, leaving the protection of that copy to the user (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The worked example shows the first step of the scheme: a backup key derived from the seed by hashing it together with a purpose string.

The mechanism has three parts, each already covered. A key is derived from the seed, as the chapter says, by one of the keys derived from it; the database is encrypted under that key; and the encrypted file is stored somewhere the user does not need to trust (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The derivation is what makes the scheme work without a second secret: the same seed that proves ownership of the coins also opens the backup, so the recovery code remains the single thing to keep.

Two limits deserve emphasis. The scheme concentrates risk on the seed: a leaked seed now exposes the user's complete transaction history and labels as well as their money, which is a privacy loss on top of a financial one. And the backup is only as current as its last copy, so a wallet that encrypts and uploads rarely leaves a gap; the chapter's phrase frequently and automatically is part of the design, not a detail (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Few wallets implement it, which is why the chapter's closing advice is again that users must do more than back up a recovery code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: a backup key derived from the seed
nodes.definition: An encrypted wallet backup is a complete copy of the wallet database, encrypted under a key derived from the seed, which a user can restore from a recovery code alone.

nodes.label: Deploying keys in practice
nodes.body: This branch is the chapter's extended worked example and its practical advice. The chapter's section on using an extended public key on a web store follows a merchant, Gabriel, from a single address on a hobby page to a shop that derives a fresh address for every order from an extended public key held on the server, and the surrounding sections give the other half of that arrangement, the keys kept offline on a device or on paper (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This branch is the chapter's extended worked example and its practical advice. The chapter's section on using an extended public key on a web store follows a merchant, Gabriel, from a single address on a hobby page to a shop that derives a fresh address for every order from an extended public key held on the server, and the surrounding sections give the other half of that arrangement, the keys kept offline on a device or on paper (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The branch matters because it shows what the machinery of the previous branches is for. Everything the chapter has built, the tree, the extended public key, the hardened step above it, the standard path, exists so that a person can take payments without putting the power to spend on an exposed computer. The branch also introduces one new concept that only appears when the arrangement is used in earnest, the gap limit, which is the practical boundary of a deterministic wallet's ability to find its own payments.

The reader meets the arrangement in the chapter's narrative, in the public-key-only wallet of the first branch, and in real software: the chapter has Gabriel export an extended public key from a Trezor device using its web application, noting that the device must be plugged in for the public keys to be exported and that most hardware signing devices will never export private keys, and then copy that key into his payment processing software, such as the widely used open-source BTCPay Server (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (BTCPay Server contributors, 2026).

The branch has two groups. The web store group covers the deployment of an extended public key, the gap limit that limits how far a wallet will look for payments, and the payment processor that puts the two together. The offline keys group covers cold storage, the hardware signing device and the written backup, which are the three ways the chapter describes of keeping the private side out of reach.

The branch is practice rather than protocol, and two of its lessons are organisational. The first is that the safety of the arrangement comes from the hardened step above the shared key, not from the secrecy of the extended public key, which must still be protected for privacy (Wuille, 2012). The second is the chapter's closing sentence for the whole chapter: one of the leading causes of lost bitcoins, perhaps the leading cause, is data loss, and it is up to the user to actually use the systems available to make good backups and regularly test them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: An extended key on a web store
nodes.body: This group follows the chapter's web store example and the one new idea it needs. The story is told in stages: Gabriel starts with a hosted page and a single Bitcoin address, which works well enough with a few orders a week even though it weakens the privacy of Gabriel, his clients and the people he pays; then the shop becomes successful and he is overwhelmed, because with all the orders paying the same address it becomes difficult to match orders and transactions, especially when several orders for the same amount arrive close together (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group follows the chapter's web store example and the one new idea it needs. The story is told in stages: Gabriel starts with a hosted page and a single Bitcoin address, which works well enough with a few orders a week even though it weakens the privacy of Gabriel, his clients and the people he pays; then the shop becomes successful and he is overwhelmed, because with all the orders paying the same address it becomes difficult to match orders and transactions, especially when several orders for the same amount arrive close together (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because it is the chapter's answer to a question students ask: why would anyone want a tree of keys? The answer is in the chapter's own words: Gabriel's wallet offers a much better solution through the ability to derive public child keys without knowing the private keys, so he can load an extended public key on his website and derive a unique address for every customer order, which immediately improves privacy and gives each order a unique identifier for tracking which invoices have been paid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The arrangement works by putting a parent public key where the risk is and keeping its private counterpart away. The store's server holds an extended public key and a path to derive along; for each visitor it derives the next index and shows the address that comes out, so every customer is given a fresh address and the server never holds anything that can spend. Watching for payment is then the same derivation run ahead of time: the program derives a run of addresses it has not yet handed out and watches them all, and the length of that run is the gap limit. The limit exists because the watching program cannot tell an unused address from an address that was used while it was not looking, so if addresses are handed out faster than they are paid, a payment can land beyond the end of the watched run and go unnoticed until the limit is raised and the branch is rescanned (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012).

The reader meets this arrangement in the chapter's own story of a store that grows from one address to a tree, and in any payment processor that is configured with an extended public key rather than with a wallet file. The gap limit is met as a number in the settings of such a program and in a node's own look-ahead, which the run saved with this chapter shows as a ranged child path over a thousand indices, a range the source describes as the look-ahead used to detect payments (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The caution is that this arrangement protects the money and not the privacy. The extended public key on the server is enough to derive every address the store will ever use, so whoever reads it - an attacker, a hosting provider, a subpoena - obtains the store's whole turnover, past and future. And it does not protect the money completely either: a server that can be altered can be made to show an attacker's addresses instead, which costs the store its takings without any key being stolen at all (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Extended public key deployment
nodes.body: Deploying an extended public key means installing the public half of a branch on a machine that needs to receive but not to spend. The chapter describes the case: one common application of this solution is to install an extended public key on a web server that serves an e-commerce application, so that the server can use the public key derivation function to create a new Bitcoin address for every transaction, for example for a customer shopping cart, without having any private keys that would be vulnerable to theft (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example writes the first three paths such a server would use.

paras.text: Deploying an extended public key means installing the public half of a branch on a machine that needs to receive but not to spend. The chapter describes the case: one common application of this solution is to install an extended public key on a web server that serves an e-commerce application, so that the server can use the public key derivation function to create a new Bitcoin address for every transaction, for example for a customer shopping cart, without having any private keys that would be vulnerable to theft (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example writes the first three paths such a server would use.

The gain is stated twice in the chapter, once in general and once in the story. In general: that kind of deployment can produce an infinite number of public keys and addresses but cannot spend any of the money sent to them, while on another, more secure machine the extended private key can derive the corresponding private keys and spend (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the story: using the HD wallet allows Gabriel to spend from his personal wallet while the extended public key on the website can only generate addresses and receive funds, which the chapter calls a great security feature, because Gabriel's website contains no private keys and any hack of it can only steal the funds he would have received in the future, not those he received in the past (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets the deployment in the chapter's narrative, where Gabriel exports the key from his hardware device and copies it into his payment software, and in the alternative the chapter mentions for comparison: without HD wallets the only way to do this is to generate thousands of addresses on a separate secure server and preload them on the shop's server, an approach the chapter calls cumbersome and in need of constant maintenance to ensure the shop does not run out of keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP32's own use case for an unsecure money receiver describes the same arrangement and its limits (Wuille, 2012).

The mechanism is the public derivation of the previous branch applied at the two normal levels of a standard path. The server holds the account's extended public key, derives the branch and then each index, and never needs a private key; the chapter notes that the branch structure itself can carry meaning, with one branch for incoming payments and another for change (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Because the account level is hardened, nothing the server holds can be used to work back to the master key, which is the design rule the chapter gives as best practice (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012).

Two risks remain and the sources name both. The first is privacy: BIP32 says that someone who illegally obtains access to the web server can at most see all incoming payments, and that is already a serious loss, since the extended public key reveals every address of the branch (Wuille, 2012). The second is substitution: a compromised server can be made to show the attacker's own addresses rather than the merchant's, which no amount of key separation prevents; the chapter's claim is only that past funds are safe (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.definition: Deploying an extended public key means putting the watching half of a wallet on an exposed computer, which can then derive a fresh address for every order and spend nothing.

nodes.label: Gap limit
nodes.body: The gap limit is how far a wallet keeps looking after it stops finding payments. The chapter introduces it in a sidebar: an extended public key can generate approximately four billion direct child keys, far more than any store should need, but it would take an unreasonable amount of time to generate all of them and scan the blockchain for transactions involving them, so most wallets generate only a few keys at a time, scan for payments involving those keys, and generate more as the previous ones are used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The maximum number of unused keys in a row that can fail to receive a payment without causing problems is what it calls the gap limit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: The gap limit is how far a wallet keeps looking after it stops finding payments. The chapter introduces it in a sidebar: an extended public key can generate approximately four billion direct child keys, far more than any store should need, but it would take an unreasonable amount of time to generate all of them and scan the blockchain for transactions involving them, so most wallets generate only a few keys at a time, scan for payments involving those keys, and generate more as the previous ones are used (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The maximum number of unused keys in a row that can fail to receive a payment without causing problems is what it calls the gap limit (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The limit matters because exceeding it loses money in the most confusing possible way: the funds are on the blockchain, the keys are derivable, and the wallet still shows nothing. The chapter explains how a gap arises in ordinary use: sometimes a wallet distributes a key to someone who later decides not to pay, creating a gap in the key chain, which is fine as long as the wallet has already generated keys after the gap so that it finds later payments and continues generating more (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The worked example is a scan with the standard limit. BIP44 sets the address gap limit at 20, saying that if the software hits twenty unused addresses in a row it expects there are no used addresses beyond that point and stops searching the chain (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b). The example scans a branch in which indices 0, 3 and 25 received payments: it finds 0 and 3, stops after examining index 23, and never sees the payment at 25. Bitcoin Core avoids the situation by preparing many keys in advance, 1,000 by default, which its source calls the look-ahead process used to detect payments, and the wallet in this chapter's evidence shows that range from 0 to 999 (Bitcoin Core, 2026) (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

The chapter lists the three choices a wallet has when it has handed out keys up to its limit and none has been paid, and each has a cost: it can refuse further requests, which is unpalatable although simplest and prevents any further payments; it can generate keys beyond the limit, which gives every payer a unique key and preserves privacy but means that a restoration, or other software loaded with the same extended public key, will not see payments received after the extended gap; or it can hand out keys it has already distributed, which ensures a smooth recovery but reduces the privacy of the owner and of the people they transact with (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The chapter's note on how production systems cope is the practical lesson, and so is its note on what has not been solved. Open-source production systems for online merchants, such as BTCPay Server, attempt to dodge the problem by using very large gap limits and limiting the rate at which they generate invoices; other solutions have been proposed, such as asking the spender's wallet to construct but not broadcast a transaction paying a possibly reused address before a fresh address is given out, but these have not been used in production as of the chapter's writing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP44 adds the rule a wallet should follow in the meantime: warn the user when they are about to exceed the gap limit (Palatinus and Rusnak, 2014b).

nodes.label: Payment processor
nodes.body: A payment processor, in the chapter's story, is the software that turns an extended public key into a working shop. The chapter says that Gabriel copies the extended public key to his web store's Bitcoin payment processing software, such as the widely used open-source BTCPay Server (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That project describes itself in the same terms: a free and open-source, self-hosted Bitcoin payment processor that lets merchants accept Bitcoin directly, without fees or intermediaries (BTCPay Server contributors, 2026).

paras.text: A payment processor, in the chapter's story, is the software that turns an extended public key into a working shop. The chapter says that Gabriel copies the extended public key to his web store's Bitcoin payment processing software, such as the widely used open-source BTCPay Server (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That project describes itself in the same terms: a free and open-source, self-hosted Bitcoin payment processor that lets merchants accept Bitcoin directly, without fees or intermediaries (BTCPay Server contributors, 2026).

The processor matters because it is where the bookkeeping of the previous branch actually happens. Somebody has to derive the next address, show it to the customer, watch the blockchain for a payment of the right amount to that address, mark the invoice paid and keep the association for later; the chapter's point about the unique identifier only becomes real inside such a program (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The self-hosted kind is also the one that fits the rest of the chapter, because an intermediary would hold the keys and the whole arrangement would be unnecessary.

A reader meets the processor at the end of the web store story and in the gap limit sidebar, where the chapter names BTCPay Server as one of the open-source production systems for online merchants that use very large gap limits and limit the rate at which they generate invoices (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The project's own documentation is organised for the roles the chapter implies, with separate guides for users, operators and developers, and it is released under a permissive licence (BTCPay Server contributors, 2026).

The mechanism from this chapter's point of view is a loop over the address index. The processor holds the account's extended public key, keeps a record of the next unused index, derives an address for each new invoice and watches for payments to the addresses it has derived; because it holds no private key, the worst a compromise can do is divert future payments, as the deployment section explained (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012). Its interaction with the gap limit is the subject of the previous section.

Two cautions. The chapter names one product as an example and this course should not read that as a recommendation; what matters is the property, self-hosted and holding no private keys. And a processor is a piece of infrastructure with its own backup problem: the association between invoices and addresses is exactly the non-key data of the previous branch, so a merchant who restores only the seed recovers the money and loses the order book (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Raw, 2022).

nodes.example: the software the extended public key is loaded into
nodes.definition: A payment processor is the program that watches for payments and matches them to orders; a self-hosted one lets a merchant accept bitcoins with the extended public key as its only key material.

nodes.label: Keys kept offline
nodes.body: This group covers the other half of every arrangement in the chapter: where the private keys are when they are not in use. The chapter names the cases together: another common application of public derivation is for cold storage or hardware signing devices, in which the extended private key can be stored on a paper wallet or hardware device while the extended public key is kept online, so that the user can create receive addresses at will while the private keys are safely stored offline, and spending is done with the extended private key on an offline wallet or the hardware device (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This group covers the other half of every arrangement in the chapter: where the private keys are when they are not in use. The chapter names the cases together: another common application of public derivation is for cold storage or hardware signing devices, in which the extended private key can be stored on a paper wallet or hardware device while the extended public key is kept online, so that the user can create receive addresses at will while the private keys are safely stored offline, and spending is done with the extended private key on an offline wallet or the hardware device (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because the whole chapter's reasoning about which key is where becomes a decision about physical objects. A seed written on paper, a device in a drawer, a code memorised: each is a different trade-off between the risk of loss and the risk of theft, which the first branch examined in the abstract. The group also closes the chapter's advice, which is to write the recovery code down and to test the backup.

Keeping keys offline works by making a boundary that the secret never crosses. The unsigned transaction is built on the connected machine and carried over the boundary; the signature is produced on the other side and carried back; the key stays where it was. A hardware signing device is that boundary built into an object - it holds the seed, derives what it needs, shows the path and the amount on its own screen so that the connected machine cannot lie about what is being signed, and returns only the signature. A written record of the recovery code is the same boundary in its simplest form: paper has no interface at all, which is exactly its security property and exactly its weakness, since it cannot check anything either and is lost to fire, water and tidying up (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets this group as the physical half of every arrangement earlier in the chapter. The device is met as the thing the wallet application asks to sign; the written code is met once, when it is copied down, and then ideally never; cold storage is met as a decision about where an object lives rather than as software. They are met again in chapter 4's section on the same device, and in this chapter's record of what goes wrong, where the risks to a physical object are documented rather than assumed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lopp, 2026).

The caution is that offline is a property of the key and not of the device. A device used to restore a code that was typed into a connected computer has an online key in an offline box, and a paper record photographed once is online for ever. The second caution is that the device's screen is the whole of its advantage: a signature approved without reading the path and the amount on that screen is a signature the connected machine chose, and the boundary has bought nothing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Cold storage
nodes.body: Cold storage is the practice of keeping keys where no connected computer can read them. The book's glossary defines it as keeping a reserve of bitcoin offline, achieved when the private keys are created and stored in a secure offline environment, and adds that it is important for anyone with bitcoin holdings because online computers are vulnerable to attackers and should not be used to store a significant amount (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter names cold storage as one of the two common applications of public child derivation, beside hardware signing devices (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Cold storage is the practice of keeping keys where no connected computer can read them. The book's glossary defines it as keeping a reserve of bitcoin offline, achieved when the private keys are created and stored in a secure offline environment, and adds that it is important for anyone with bitcoin holdings because online computers are vulnerable to attackers and should not be used to store a significant amount (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter names cold storage as one of the two common applications of public child derivation, beside hardware signing devices (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reason is the asymmetry between receiving and spending. Receiving needs only public information, which the deployment section showed can live on an exposed machine; spending needs the private key, and spending happens rarely. Keeping the private side offline therefore costs little convenience and removes the largest class of attack, which is why the chapter's arrangement, extended public key online and extended private key offline, is the standard shape of a careful setup (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets cold storage in this chapter as the destination of an extended private key, on a paper wallet or a hardware device, and in chapter 4 of the book, which treats the paper wallet as an older form of the same idea (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The arrangement in the chapter's web store story is cold storage in practice: Gabriel's keys are on a Trezor device and the shop sees only the extended public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mechanism is the separation of the two halves of the tree, which this chapter has now described from three directions: public derivation makes the receiving side possible without secrets; a hardened step above the shared key makes the leak of a child harmless to the master; and an offline device or a written seed holds the private side (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012). Spending is then a transfer of an unsigned transaction to the offline side and of a signature back, which is the external signing of the chapter's first branch (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Cold storage moves risk rather than removing it, and the direction it moves is towards loss. An offline key cannot be stolen over a network and cannot be recovered if the paper burns, which is why the chapter's advice about recovery codes applies with full force to cold storage: the code, not the device, is the backup. A reader should also note that cold does not mean unused: a device that is never tested is a backup whose condition is unknown, which is the chapter's final point about testing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: keys that never touch a connected computer
nodes.definition: Cold storage means keeping keys offline, created and stored in a secure environment that is not connected to a network, so that an attack on a connected computer cannot reach them.

nodes.label: Hardware signing device
nodes.body: A hardware signing device is a small purpose-built computer that holds private keys and signs with them. The chapter introduces it in its first branch, where it says that a user can provide the key tweaks she used to a hardware signing device, sometimes confusingly called a hardware wallet, that securely stores her original private key, and that the device uses the tweaks to derive the necessary child private keys and sign the transactions, returning them to the less secure frontend for broadcast (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's parenthesis about the name is worth keeping: the device signs, and the wallet is the database and the application.

paras.text: A hardware signing device is a small purpose-built computer that holds private keys and signs with them. The chapter introduces it in its first branch, where it says that a user can provide the key tweaks she used to a hardware signing device, sometimes confusingly called a hardware wallet, that securely stores her original private key, and that the device uses the tweaks to derive the necessary child private keys and sign the transactions, returning them to the less secure frontend for broadcast (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's parenthesis about the name is worth keeping: the device signs, and the wallet is the database and the application.

The device exists because a general-purpose computer cannot be trusted with a key that cannot be replaced. By keeping the key inside and exposing only a signing operation, the device reduces what an attacker on the connected computer can do to proposing transactions, which the user is asked to confirm on the device's own screen. This is the arrangement the chapter calls the separation of wallet frontends, which do not require private keys, from signing operations, which do (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader meets the device in the chapter's web store story, where Gabriel exports an extended public key from his Trezor device using the web-based wallet application, with the device plugged in, and where the chapter notes that most hardware signing devices will never export private keys, since those always remain on the device (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The reader also meets its influence on the standards of this chapter: BIP39 was proposed by the company behind the Trezor device, and the chapter says BIP39's weak key-stretching parameters are likely a consequence of being designed for compatibility with such devices and their low-powered processors (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The mechanism that matters here is what crosses the boundary. Out of the device come public keys, extended public keys and signatures; into it go transactions to sign and the derivation information needed to find the right key, which is why descriptors carry a key origin with a master fingerprint and a path (Wuille and Chow, 2021). The device's own backup is a recovery code, which it shows once when it is initialised, so the device is replaceable while the code is not.

Three cautions. The name hardware wallet invites the belief that the coins are in the device, which the chapter's first branch corrected: the device holds keys, and the coins are outputs on the blockchain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A device protects the key from a compromised computer, not the user from a mistaken confirmation. And a device is a thing that can be lost, which is why the chapter's advice about writing the code down is the real backup, as the next section explains.

nodes.example: a device that signs but does not export
nodes.definition: A hardware signing device stores private keys and produces signatures on request without revealing the keys, so a less secure computer can build transactions it cannot sign.

nodes.label: Written backup
nodes.body: A written backup is the recovery code recorded on a physical medium. The chapter's recommendation is explicit: even if a type of recovery code designed for easy memorisation is used, the authors very strongly encourage the reader to consider writing it down (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example compares what is written in the two encodings the chapter prints for the same 128 bits: thirty-two hexadecimal digits against twelve English words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: A written backup is the recovery code recorded on a physical medium. The chapter's recommendation is explicit: even if a type of recovery code designed for easy memorisation is used, the authors very strongly encourage the reader to consider writing it down (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example compares what is written in the two encodings the chapter prints for the same 128 bits: thirty-two hexadecimal digits against twelve English words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reason is the list of failure modes the first branch gave. Memory fails, so a forgotten code with a lost database means the bitcoins are lost forever; memory cannot be inherited, so heirs without access to the database cannot inherit; and a memorised code can be the reason a person is coerced (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Paper fails differently, and the two failure modes are largely independent, which is why holding both is better than holding either.

A reader meets the written backup as the card a hardware device ships with, as the chapter's own table of a code in hexadecimal and in words, and in the owner's course notes for this chapter, which include a slide showing an example paper backup of the code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Altunel, 2021). The schemes of the first branch differ in how well they suit paper: codex32 was designed so that codes can be created and validated with printed instructions and simple tools, while Muun's arrangement requires a printed kit beside the code (Olsson Curr et al., 2023) (Muun, 2026).

What is written is the code and, where used, a note that a passphrase exists, though the chapter warns against keeping the passphrase in the same place (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For explicit-path wallets the descriptor should be written too, which is the previous branch's conclusion; for multisignature arrangements each participant must record the other participants' public keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's three technologies, a BIP39 code, BIP32 derivation and a BIP44-style path, are exactly the three things a complete written backup records, two of them implicitly (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

Paper has its own risks, and a course should name them: it burns, it fades, it can be photographed, and a code lying in a drawer is a bearer instrument that anyone in the house can carry away. The chapter's answer is not to choose between paper and memory but to plan: it recommends using a passphrase only together with a carefully planned process for backup and recovery that considers surviving the owner, and it closes the chapter by saying that it is up to the reader to actually use the systems available to make good backups and regularly test them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: twelve words instead of thirty-two hexadecimal digits
nodes.definition: A written backup is the recovery code on paper, which the chapter recommends even for schemes designed to be memorised, because memory fails and cannot be inherited.

nodes.label: Foundations the chapter relies on
nodes.body: This last branch collects the ideas that the rest of the chapter uses as though they were already known. Some of them the earlier chapters of the book have introduced: the private key, the public key, the elliptic curve, the address and its encodings belong to chapter 4, and the transaction, the output and the blockchain to chapters 1 and 2. The ones gathered here are the remainder, the terms that this chapter's own explanations lean on most heavily and that no earlier chapter of this course defines in its own right.

paras.text: This last branch collects the ideas that the rest of the chapter uses as though they were already known. Some of them the earlier chapters of the book have introduced: the private key, the public key, the elliptic curve, the address and its encodings belong to chapter 4, and the transaction, the output and the blockchain to chapters 1 and 2. The ones gathered here are the remainder, the terms that this chapter's own explanations lean on most heavily and that no earlier chapter of this course defines in its own right.

The branch exists for a reason of method rather than of subject. A teaching text should not use a word it has not explained, and an audit of the explanations written for this chapter found several terms used as though they were self-evident: the hash function on which every derivation in the chapter rests, the particular algorithms SHA-256 and SHA-512 that the standards name, the digital signature that the keys exist to produce, and the secret sharing that two of the recovery schemes are built on. Each is now a concept of this chapter with its own section.

The reader has met all four already. The hash function appeared in the chapter's first demonstration of deterministic key generation and in every derivation since; SHA-256 computes the BIP39 checksum and SHA-512 the keyed hash of BIP32 and of PBKDF2; the signature is what a hardware device returns and what the private keys of the whole chapter exist for; and secret sharing is the mathematics behind SLIP39 and codex32 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Palatinus et al., 2013) (Wuille, 2012) (Rusnak et al., 2017) (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

The branch has two groups. The cryptographic primitives group gives the four ideas just named, each with a worked example small enough to check by hand or in the page. The recovery practice group closes the chapter with the two statements the chapter itself ends on: that data loss, not theft, is perhaps the leading cause of lost bitcoins, and that a backup is worth only as much as the test that shows it works (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A warning about the level of treatment. These sections are summaries sufficient for this chapter and no more: the design of hash functions, the security proofs of signature schemes and the algebra of secret sharing are each a subject of their own, and the course's later chapters and the book's chapters 7 and 8 go further. What a reader should take from this branch is enough precision to read the standards of this chapter without hand-waving.

nodes.label: Cryptographic primitives
nodes.body: A cryptographic primitive is a basic operation out of which protocols are built: this group covers the four that chapter 5 uses. The hash function is the one-way, repeatable function behind every derivation in the chapter. The SHA family provides the two particular hash functions the standards name. The digital signature is the operation that a private key exists to perform. And secret sharing is the construction that lets one secret be split so that a subset of the parts recovers it.

paras.text: A cryptographic primitive is a basic operation out of which protocols are built: this group covers the four that chapter 5 uses. The hash function is the one-way, repeatable function behind every derivation in the chapter. The SHA family provides the two particular hash functions the standards name. The digital signature is the operation that a private key exists to perform. And secret sharing is the construction that lets one secret be split so that a subset of the parts recovers it.

The group matters because the properties of these primitives are the reasons the chapter's claims are true. That a child key cannot be used to find its parent is a property of the hash function; that a recovery code's checksum detects an error but cannot correct it is a property of SHA-256 used as a compressor; that a server can hold an extended public key safely is a property of the signature scheme's key pair; and that three of five codes can recover a seed while two cannot is a property of polynomial interpolation.

The four primitives work together as a chain of guarantees, and each statement in this chapter rests on one of them. A hash function gives a short value that depends on all of its input, cannot be run backwards and changes completely when the input changes, which is what makes a checksum, a fingerprint and a commitment possible. The named family of hash functions supplies the particular functions the standards call for, and the keyed form of one of them is the splitter behind every derivation in this chapter. A digital signature turns control of a private key into a number anybody can check, which is what proves a spend is authorised without revealing the key. Secret sharing distributes one secret into several pieces so that any agreed number of them restores it and fewer reveal nothing, which is how one of the recovery-code schemes turns a single point of failure into a threshold (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Wuille, 2012) (Rusnak et al., 2017) (Krawczyk et al., 1997).

The reader meets these four throughout the course rather than only here. The hash function gave the transaction identifier of chapter 2, the block identifier of chapter 3 and the address commitment of chapter 4; its keyed form gives the master keys and every child of this chapter; the signature authorised every payment of chapter 2 and is the proof of control of chapter 4. Secret sharing is met only in this chapter, and the worked example for it is a toy over a small prime field rather than the field the real scheme uses, so that the arithmetic can be read (Rusnak et al., 2017).

The caution is that these are the assumptions of the chapter and not its results. Every claim that a child key cannot be traced to its parent, that a code cannot be guessed, or that a signature cannot be forged, is a claim about the present strength of one of these primitives, which is the state of the art rather than a theorem. A learner should also resist treating them as interchangeable: a keyed hash and a signature both prove that somebody knew a secret, but only the signature can be checked by a party who does not know it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Krawczyk et al., 1997).

nodes.label: Hash function
nodes.body: A hash function maps an input of any length to an output of fixed length. The chapter gives the two properties it needs in one sentence: a hash function will always produce the same output when given the same input, but if the input is changed even slightly the output will be different, and if the function is cryptographically secure nobody should be able to predict the new output, not even if they know the new input (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example computes the beginning of the SHA-256 hash of the three letters abc, which is the standard's own best-known test value.

paras.text: A hash function maps an input of any length to an output of fixed length. The chapter gives the two properties it needs in one sentence: a hash function will always produce the same output when given the same input, but if the input is changed even slightly the output will be different, and if the function is cryptographically secure nobody should be able to predict the new output, not even if they know the new input (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The worked example computes the beginning of the SHA-256 hash of the three letters abc, which is the standard's own best-known test value.

Every mechanism in this chapter rests on those properties. Repeatability is what makes a seed a backup, since the same seed gives the same keys; unpredictability is what makes the derived keys unguessable; and the one-way direction is what makes a child key useless for finding its parent, which the chapter states when it says that because the derivation function is a one-way function the child key cannot be used to find the parent key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's opening demonstration makes the same point positively: a hash function lets one take one random value and transform it into a practically unlimited number of seemingly random values (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

A reader has met hash functions at every stage. The chapter's first example hashes a random value with a counter to produce a sequence of private keys (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP39 takes the first bits of a SHA-256 hash as a checksum and runs 2,048 rounds of a keyed hash to produce a seed (Palatinus et al., 2013). BIP32 derives every key with a keyed hash and identifies extended keys by a hash of the public key (Wuille, 2012). Chapter 4 of the book used hashes to commit to a public key in an address, and chapter 2 used them to identify transactions.

What a hash function does not do is as important as what it does, and two limits matter here. It is not encryption: nothing can be recovered from the output, which is why BIP39 notes that the conversion from a sentence to a seed is one-way only and an arbitrary BIP32 seed cannot be written as a BIP39 sentence (Palatinus et al., 2013). And it is not a random oracle in practice: its output is fully determined by its input, so a hash of a guessable value is guessable, which is the brainwallet lesson of the first branch.

Two cautions for a learner. A hash is not a signature and proves nothing about who produced the data; proving that requires the keyed hash or the signature of the next sections. And collisions exist in principle, since a long input is mapped to a short output; the security claim is only that finding one is infeasible, which is why chapter 4 of the book discusses collision and preimage attacks on the shorter hashes used in addresses.

nodes.example: the hash of three letters
nodes.definition: A hash function maps data of any size to a fixed-size value, always the same for the same input and unpredictable for a changed one, and cannot be run backwards.

nodes.label: SHA-256 and SHA-512
nodes.body: SHA-256 and SHA-512 are two members of the second family of secure hash algorithms, producing outputs of 256 and 512 bits. The worked example measures both: 32 bytes and 64 bytes. The chapter names them where its standards do: the BIP39 checksum is taken from a SHA-256 hash, and the key-stretching function uses HMAC-SHA512, which produces a 512-bit value (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Python's standard library provides both, and the documentation of its hashing module describes the constructors and the derivation function this chapter uses (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

paras.text: SHA-256 and SHA-512 are two members of the second family of secure hash algorithms, producing outputs of 256 and 512 bits. The worked example measures both: 32 bytes and 64 bytes. The chapter names them where its standards do: the BIP39 checksum is taken from a SHA-256 hash, and the key-stretching function uses HMAC-SHA512, which produces a 512-bit value (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Python's standard library provides both, and the documentation of its hashing module describes the constructors and the derivation function this chapter uses (Python Software Foundation, 2026).

The choice of algorithm fixes the sizes everything else is built around, and a reader who notices this will stop finding the numbers arbitrary. A BIP39 seed is 512 bits because HMAC-SHA512 produces 64 bytes in one block; a BIP32 derivation yields a 256-bit key and a 256-bit chain code because the same 64 bytes are split in half; an extended key's 78 bytes include those 32 bytes of chain code and 33 of key data (Palatinus et al., 2013) (Wuille, 2012). Change the hash and every one of those numbers changes.

A reader meets SHA-256 in the BIP39 checksum, in the double hash of base58check that protects an extended key, and in the tagged hash of BIP86's taproot tweak; SHA-512 in BIP32's master key generation and child derivation and in PBKDF2's pseudorandom function (Palatinus et al., 2013) (Wuille, 2012) (Chow, 2021). codex32's criticism of BIP39 names the choice explicitly, listing the use of SHA-512 to derive seeds among the design decisions it considers unhelpful (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

For this chapter the mechanism can be taken as given: both functions process their input in blocks and produce a fixed digest, and both are available as single calls. What matters is which is used where, and the sizes that follow. The claims of this chapter check those sizes directly, and also check that the two functions are not interchangeable: the same input gives unrelated outputs, which is why a standard must name the function and not merely say a hash.

Two points of care. The names are easy to confuse with SHA-1 and with the third family, SHA-3, which are different algorithms; the course's browser pages provide SHA-2 and SHA-3 but not the RIPEMD-160, a different hash function, that Bitcoin addresses also use, which is why some values in this chapter are given as data (Python Software Foundation, 2026). And a longer digest is not automatically more secure for a given purpose: BIP39 uses 512 bits for a seed whose entropy is at most 256, which the chapter's sidebar on security strength explains (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: 32 bytes and 64 bytes
nodes.definition: SHA-256 and SHA-512 are the two secure hash algorithms this chapter's standards name, producing 32 and 64 bytes; the choice of one or the other fixes the sizes in every scheme.

nodes.label: Digital signature
nodes.body: A digital signature is the proof that the holder of a private key authorised a particular message. In Bitcoin the message is a transaction and the key is the one that controls the output being spent; the chapter assumes this throughout, beginning with its first sentence about wallet databases, which says that simple databases contain both the public keys to which bitcoins are received and the private keys that allow creating the signatures necessary to authorize spending those bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 4 of the book introduced the key pair, and the book's chapters 7 and 8 treat the signature itself.

paras.text: A digital signature is the proof that the holder of a private key authorised a particular message. In Bitcoin the message is a transaction and the key is the one that controls the output being spent; the chapter assumes this throughout, beginning with its first sentence about wallet databases, which says that simple databases contain both the public keys to which bitcoins are received and the private keys that allow creating the signatures necessary to authorize spending those bitcoins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Chapter 4 of the book introduced the key pair, and the book's chapters 7 and 8 treat the signature itself.

The signature is why the whole chapter is about keys. Losing a key does not lose data, it loses the ability to produce a signature, and the chapter's opening states the consequence: losing access to a private key can make it impossible for anyone ever to spend the bitcoins received to the corresponding public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Conversely, the ability to sign is the whole of ownership, which is why a copied key is a stolen coin and why the separation of signing from the rest of a wallet is the chapter's central practical idea.

A reader meets signatures in this chapter mostly by their absence. A wallet with public keys only cannot make them; external signing is the arrangement in which someone else does; a hardware signing device is named for the operation it performs, and the chapter describes it returning the signed transactions to the less secure frontend for broadcast (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A multisignature arrangement needs several of them, and BIP32 calls the extended public key the neutered version of an extended private key because neutering removes the ability to sign transactions (Wuille, 2012) (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

For this chapter the mechanism needs only its shape: a signature is computed from the message and the private key, it can be verified with the public key, and it cannot be produced without the private key. The claims of this chapter include a small signing and verification with the curve of chapter 4, which show the shape: a signature over one message does not verify over another. The details of the scheme, including the nonce whose reuse is catastrophic, belong to the book's chapter on signatures.

Two confusions to avoid. A signature is not encryption and nothing in a Bitcoin transaction is hidden; the blockchain is public, as chapter 2 made clear. And a signature authorises one message only, which is why a signing device must show what it is signing: possession of the key is necessary and consent to the particular transaction is what the user is actually giving.

nodes.example: what a signing device returns
nodes.definition: A digital signature is a value computed from a message and a private key that anyone can check against the matching public key, which is how spending a Bitcoin output is authorised.

nodes.label: Secret sharing
nodes.body: Secret sharing is a way of splitting one secret into several parts with a threshold. SLIP39's description is the clearest: the scheme splits a secret into a number of unique parts, of which any threshold-many are required to reconstruct it, and knowledge of fewer than the required number does not leak information about the secret (Rusnak et al., 2017). The chapter meets the idea through the schemes that use it, saying of SLIP39 that a single seed can be distributed using multiple recovery codes stored in different places or by different people, with the number required specified when they are created (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Secret sharing is a way of splitting one secret into several parts with a threshold. SLIP39's description is the clearest: the scheme splits a secret into a number of unique parts, of which any threshold-many are required to reconstruct it, and knowledge of fewer than the required number does not leak information about the secret (Rusnak et al., 2017). The chapter meets the idea through the schemes that use it, saying of SLIP39 that a single seed can be distributed using multiple recovery codes stored in different places or by different people, with the number required specified when they are created (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The construction answers a problem no single backup can solve, which the first branch described: one copy can be lost, and many copies can be stolen. SLIP39 states the trade-off and the resolution: the usual approach is redundant backups, but when the asset is valuable there is a substantial risk of a backup holder absconding with it, and secret sharing distributes custodianship in a manner that can prevent loss even if one or a few parties are compromised (Rusnak et al., 2017). codex32's motivation puts the same tension as security against resilience (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

The worked example is the mathematics in miniature. A secret and two coefficients define a polynomial whose arithmetic is carried out modulo a large prime, so that every value stays in a fixed range; five points on it are the shares; any three of them recover the secret, as the example shows for the first three and for the last three; and two of them do not, which the example's third value reports as false. SLIP39's own description is the same construction with the shared secret stored at the value 255 and a digest at 254, over the field of 256 elements, applied to each byte separately (Rusnak et al., 2017).

Why a threshold reveals nothing below it is worth one sentence: a polynomial of degree less than the threshold is not determined by fewer points than its coefficients, so every candidate secret remains possible, which is the sense in which fewer shares leak no information (Rusnak et al., 2017). The two standards that use the construction differ in their packaging rather than in this core: SLIP39 encrypts the master secret with the passphrase first and supports two levels of groups, while codex32 works in the bech32 alphabet so that the arithmetic can be done by hand and supports up to 31 shares with a threshold between 2 and 9 (Rusnak et al., 2017) (Olsson Curr et al., 2023).

Three cautions. The toy in the worked example is not a secure implementation: it uses fixed coefficients where a real scheme draws them from a secure random source, and it works on one integer rather than on a byte string. A threshold is a policy decision with two failure modes, as the first branch said: too low invites theft, too high invites loss. And the shares are secrets: distributing them is a plan for who is trusted with what, which is why SLIP39 provides two levels of grouping to express uneven trust (Rusnak et al., 2017).

nodes.example: three of five points recover the secret
nodes.definition: Secret sharing splits a secret into parts so that any sufficient number of them recovers it and any smaller number reveals nothing; it is the mathematics behind SLIP39 and codex32.

nodes.label: Recovery as a practice
nodes.body: This last group turns the chapter's technical content into two statements about practice. The chapter's closing paragraph makes both: many people focus on securing their bitcoins against theft and other attacks, but one of the leading causes of lost bitcoins, perhaps the leading cause, is data loss, and if the keys and other essential data required to spend are lost, those bitcoins will forever be unspendable, with nobody able to get them back; and it is up to the reader to actually use the systems available to make good backups and regularly test them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: This last group turns the chapter's technical content into two statements about practice. The chapter's closing paragraph makes both: many people focus on securing their bitcoins against theft and other attacks, but one of the leading causes of lost bitcoins, perhaps the leading cause, is data loss, and if the keys and other essential data required to spend are lost, those bitcoins will forever be unspendable, with nobody able to get them back; and it is up to the reader to actually use the systems available to make good backups and regularly test them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The group matters because the chapter's whole argument is practical. Every mechanism it describes, from the word list to the descriptor, exists to make a recovery possible, and none of them acts on its own. A course that taught the mechanisms without the two statements above would leave a student able to explain a recovery code and unable to keep one.

The practice works by turning the chapter's technical content into a list and then checking the list. A complete backup is the recovery code, the passphrase if one is used, the derivation paths or the descriptors that record them, the public keys of any other signers, and the data that is not keys; each item is one of this chapter's own branches, and each is a separate way for a restoration to fail. Testing is what converts that list from a belief into a fact, and a test means a real restoration into software that did not create the wallet, because only that catches the failures that matter - a word copied wrongly, a passphrase remembered imperfectly, a path nobody wrote down, a label file never exported. Nothing about this is automatic: data loss is not an attack that defences prevent but an accident that only a tested backup survives (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The reader meets this group at the end of the chapter and, if the chapter has done its work, before anything has gone wrong. It is met in the chapter's own closing sentences, which name loss rather than theft as the leading cause of lost bitcoins and put the responsibility on the holder; and it is met in the design of this course's material, where every chapter's figures are recomputed rather than copied for the same reason a backup is restored rather than assumed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The caution is that a test can give false comfort. Restoring into the same application that made the wallet proves that the application can read its own file and nothing more; restoring the code without the passphrase proves that the words are right and leaves the wallet still unreachable; checking that a balance appears proves the receiving branch and says nothing about the change branch. A test is worth what it covers, which is why the list above has five items rather than one, and why the chapter asks for the test to be repeated rather than performed once (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.label: Data loss
nodes.body: Data loss, in this chapter, means losing the information needed to spend rather than having it stolen. The chapter's closing paragraph puts it first among causes: many people focus on securing their bitcoins against theft and other attacks, but one of the leading causes of lost bitcoins, perhaps the leading cause, is data loss, and if the keys and other essential data required to spend are lost, those bitcoins will forever be unspendable, and nobody can get them back (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's first sentence said the same of a single key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

paras.text: Data loss, in this chapter, means losing the information needed to spend rather than having it stolen. The chapter's closing paragraph puts it first among causes: many people focus on securing their bitcoins against theft and other attacks, but one of the leading causes of lost bitcoins, perhaps the leading cause, is data loss, and if the keys and other essential data required to spend are lost, those bitcoins will forever be unspendable, and nobody can get them back (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The chapter's first sentence said the same of a single key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

The emphasis is a correction of intuition. Theft is vivid and loss is dull, and so users protect against the first and neglect the second, while the chapter's examples of loss are mundane: a corrupted database, a wallet application whose labels were never exported, a passphrase that only the deceased owner knew, a payment beyond the gap limit, a path a newer wallet no longer tries (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each of those is a loss of data rather than an attack, and each has appeared in this chapter with its own section.

A reader meets the forms of loss throughout the chapter. Independent key generation loses funds received to keys that had not yet been backed up (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A forgotten passphrase makes a seed useless and the funds lost forever (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A seed-only restoration loses every label (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A wallet restored into software that does not know its path finds nothing (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A Lightning channel whose state is lost may be unrecoverable even with a static channel backup (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023) (Lightning Labs, 2026b).

The mechanism common to all of them is the one the chapter keeps returning to: Bitcoin has no authority that can reissue a key or reverse a payment, which chapter 1 of the book described as irreversibility and decentralisation. The remedy is therefore always the same in form, to hold enough information in enough places, and the chapter's branches are the list of what that information is: the recovery code, the passphrase if any, the derivation paths or descriptors, and the data that is not keys.

Two things should not be inferred. That data loss is the leading cause does not make theft unimportant, and the chapter's own treatment of coercion shows that the two interact: a backup held in many places is easier to find. And a loss is not always immediately visible, which is the chapter's warning about a mistyped passphrase that shows a zero balance the user may not question for years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The practical conclusion is the next section's.

nodes.example: the loss the chapter calls the leading cause
nodes.definition: Data loss is the loss of the keys or of the information needed to use them, which the chapter names as perhaps the leading cause of lost bitcoins, and which no one can reverse.

nodes.label: Testing a backup
nodes.body: Testing a backup means performing the recovery while it is still optional. It is the action the chapter's last sentence asks for: it is up to the reader to actually use the systems available to make good backups and regularly test them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The test is the only evidence that the backup is complete, because every other check verifies a part: a checksum says the code was typed correctly, not that the code is the right one; a descriptor's checksum says the descriptor is intact, not that it describes the wallet.

paras.text: Testing a backup means performing the recovery while it is still optional. It is the action the chapter's last sentence asks for: it is up to the reader to actually use the systems available to make good backups and regularly test them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The test is the only evidence that the backup is complete, because every other check verifies a part: a checksum says the code was typed correctly, not that the code is the right one; a descriptor's checksum says the descriptor is intact, not that it describes the wallet.

The reason a test is needed is that this chapter has produced a list of things that can each be individually right and jointly insufficient. A valid code with the wrong passphrase gives an empty wallet; a valid code in software that does not know the path gives an empty wallet; a complete key recovery with no labels gives an unreadable history; a recovered single-signature wallet says nothing about a multisignature arrangement's other participants (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Only an attempted recovery exercises all of them at once.

A reader meets the need for a test in several of the chapter's own warnings. The chapter notes that a user who enters a slightly wrong passphrase may use the wallet for years before discovering the mistake, and that novice users seeing a zero balance may think their money is permanently lost and do something foolish, such as giving up and throwing away the code (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Both are failures that a test would have caught. Bitcoin Core's own warning about its key pool points the same way, saying that smaller sizes may increase the risk of losing funds when restoring from an old backup (Bitcoin Core, 2026).

What a complete test covers follows from the branches of this chapter, and it can be stated as a short list: restore the recovery code, with the passphrase if one is used, into software other than the one that created it; check that the balance and the transaction history are as expected, which tests the paths or the descriptors; check that labels and any protocol data are present, which tests the non-key backup; and for a multisignature or descriptor wallet, check that the other participants' public keys or the descriptor itself were recorded. Each item is one of the chapter's sections.

A test is itself a risk and should be done carefully: entering a recovery code into software or a device exposes it, so a test belongs on a machine the user would trust with the wallet itself, and a code should never be typed into a web page. Two further cautions: a test proves the backup worked on that day, which is why the chapter says regularly; and a test of the recovery code is not a test of the kit, the descriptor or the label export unless those are included (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

nodes.example: the one action the chapter asks for
nodes.definition: Testing a backup means carrying out a recovery before it is needed, which is the only way to learn that a code, a path and the non-key data are all sufficient.

findings: Background

Chapter 5 is about preventing the loss of data from becoming a loss of money. It moves from what a wallet database holds, only keys, through the history of how keys are made, independently, then from a seed, then with key tweaks, then as a BIP32 tree, to the recovery codes that record a seed, the data a code cannot record, and the derivation paths a restoration needs; it then works one stack in detail, BIP39 codes, BIP32 derivation and BIP44-style implicit paths, and ends with an extended public key deployed on a web store and the closing advice to make good backups and test them regularly.
Comparative analysis

Every number the chapter prints in this stack reproduces exactly from the standards, computed with Python's standard library alone: the three SHA-256 values of its deterministic-generation example; the 12 words of the entropy 0c1e24e5917779d297e14d45f14e1a1a and the 24 words of its 256-bit example; all 64 bytes of each of the three seeds its tables give, with no passphrase, with the passphrase SuperDuperSecret, and for the 24-word code; the whole entropy-and-word-length table from the standard's two formulas; and the extended public key printed beside its extended private key, which is the neutered form of it, both 111 characters with the version bytes 0488ade4 and 0488b21e, depth 1 and parent fingerprint 0a2683ed.
Comparative analysis

The chapter states that each parent key can have 2,147,483,647 children and gives 2 to the 31 as that value. The two are not equal: 2 to the 31 is 2,147,483,648, and BIP32 says that each extended key has 2 to the 31 normal child keys, using indices 0 through 2 to the 31 minus 1, and as many hardened ones. The chapter's figure is the largest normal index, not the number of children.
Comparative analysis

The chapter lists the inputs of the child key derivation function as a parent private or public key with the parenthesis uncompressed key. BIP32 serialises the parent public key in the 33-byte compressed form for normal derivation and pads the 32-byte private key with a zero byte for hardened derivation. Running the normal derivation with the 65-byte uncompressed form instead gives a different child private key, which an executed claim of this chapter shows, so the parenthesis is a slip rather than an option.
Comparative analysis

The published test vectors of the standards the chapter names all reproduce with the chapter's own library: BIP32's test vectors 1 and 2, every chain of both, as serialised xprv and xpub strings found verbatim in the BIP text; the BIP39 English test vectors of trezor/python-mnemonic, entropy to words, words to seed with the passphrase TREZOR, seed to master extended private key and words back to entropy; BIP49's testnet vector down to the address 2Mww8dCYPUpKHofjgcXcBCEGmniw9CoaiD2; BIP84's first and second receiving addresses, including bc1qcr8te4kr609gcawutmrza0j4xv80jy8z306fyu, which Bitcoin Core 31.1 also derived from the account descriptor; BIP86's internal key, output key and address bc1p5cyxnuxmeuwuvkwfem96lqzszd02n6xdcjrs20cac6yqjjwudpxqkedrcr; BIP380's descriptor checksums, which agree with the four checksums Bitcoin Core 31.1 returned; and codex32's first test vector with its checksum and 16-byte payload.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's table of implicit script paths is faithful to the standards and uneven in one respect that a reader should notice: it gives m/44'/0'/0', m/84'/0'/0' and m/86'/0'/0' with the coin type 0, Bitcoin, but m/49'/1'/0' with the coin type 1, which SLIP-0044 registers as testnet for all coins, because BIP49's own test vectors are on testnet. The purpose numbers themselves are those of the four standards, hardened: 0x8000002c, 0x80000031, 0x80000054 and 0x80000056.
Comparative analysis

Two statements of the chapter about the other schemes were checked against those schemes' own documents and hold, with their figures: Aezeed's plaintext is one byte of internal version, two bytes of timestamp and sixteen bytes of entropy, its two-byte timestamp counts days since the genesis block and its document says this reaches 2188, which is 2009 plus 65,536 divided by 365; and its key derivation is scrypt with n equal to 32,768, which is sixteen times BIP39's 2,048 rounds. Electrum's document gives the version-number rule the chapter describes, with the registered numbers 0x01, 0x100 and 0x101, and works the cost of the prefix out as 2 to the 135 hashes for a 12-word, 132-bit seed.
Conclusion

For the course, the chapter's lesson can be stated as a list of what a complete backup is, and every item of the list is one of this chapter's concepts: the recovery code, the passphrase if one is used, the derivation paths or the descriptors that record them, the public keys of any other signers, and the data that is not keys, which means the labels and whatever a protocol such as the Lightning Network adds. The chapter's own closing sentences are the reason the list matters: data loss is perhaps the leading cause of lost bitcoins, nobody can reverse it, and it is up to the holder to make the backups and test them.
Contemporary developments

Bitcoin Core 31.1, run offline for this chapter, is a descriptor wallet and implements the derivation side of the chapter's stack but not its recovery codes: the project's list of implemented proposals names BIP 32, 43, 44, 49, 84 and 86 and contains no entry for BIP 39, and the fresh wallet created for this chapter reports the sqlite format, descriptor support and eight descriptors, four script types with a receiving and a change branch each, every one carrying a key origin such as 6d8c4b8f with the path 84h/0h/0h and a ranged child path with the range 0 to 999; its first address was at m/84h/0h/0h/0/0. The source sets the pool behind that range, DEFAULT_KEYPOOL_SIZE, to 1000 and describes it as the look-ahead process used to detect payments.
Contemporary developments

The record the chapter cites for the risk of coercion has grown since the book was printed. The chapter says that Jameson Lopp has documented over 100 physical attacks against suspected owners of bitcoin and other digital assets; the saved copy of that list read for this chapter holds 364 table rows, which an executed claim of this chapter counts, and the list states that it is not comprehensive because many attacks are not publicly reported. The chapter's figure should therefore be read as a floor and dated.
Course notes

The owner's course notes for this chapter, written in 2021 after the 2nd edition, cover the same ground in the older vocabulary that the 3rd edition has renamed: nondeterministic or JBOK wallet, Type-0, Type-1 and Type-2 wallets, mnemonic code words rather than recovery codes, and figures numbered 5-1 to 5-13. Their topics that the 3rd edition keeps are all present in this ontology, among them the brainwallet comparison, the paper backup of the code, the Trezor export in Gabriel's case, hardened derivation, index numbers and the two path tables; the slides' own numbering of the book's figures and tables belongs to the 2nd edition and is not carried over.
Known limit

Known limit of the chapter page. The quality gate that governs this chapter's ontology is a SHACL shape file, sen0401_ch05_domain_shacl_v1_0_1.ttl, which states 4 node shapes: that every individual carries a label, that anything defined cites its source, and that a worked example carries exactly one input and one output. The chapter builder applies those shapes to the TBox and the ABox before it writes them, and the build fails if they are violated, so the gate does run; what it does not do is reach the student. The interactive page embeds the chapter's TBox, ABox, document and this research record as Turtle, and the shape file is not among them, so a reader who opens the page can read the ontology it teaches from but cannot read, query or re-run the gate that admitted it, and the page's own list of the triples in each corpus file never mentions the shapes. The limit is recorded here rather than repaired here because the list of files the page embeds is set by the page build chain, which this chapter does not own; repairing it means adding the shape file to that chain's corpus list, after which this finding should be revised to say that the gate is shipped.
Terms used without definition

An audit of the explanations written for this chapter listed every technical term they use and compared it with the concepts of chapters 1 to 4 and of this chapter. The terms used without a concept of their own were the hash function, the SHA-256 and SHA-512 algorithms, the digital signature, secret sharing, encryption, multisignature, the output script, the Lightning Network, entropy, the key-stretching function, PBKDF2, the salt, text normalisation, data loss and the testing of a backup. Each was added as a concept of this chapter with its own section, so that no term in the document is used before it is explained; the terms that chapters 1 to 4 do define, among them the private and public key, the elliptic curve and its generator point, base58check, bech32 and bech32m, the address, the transaction, the unspent output, the full node, the improvement proposal, the byte and the keyed hash, are used as they stand.

stories.title: Two guesses from 7,002 bitcoin
stories.who: Stefan Thomas, programmer (early bitcoin adopter, later Ripple's CTO)
stories.where: an IronKey USB drive in a safe - and the front page of the New York Times
stories.story: In 2011 Stefan Thomas was paid 7,002 BTC for making an animated explainer about bitcoin. He put the keys on an encrypted IronKey drive, wrote the password on a paper he later lost, and the drive allows ten guesses before locking forever. By January 2021, when the New York Times told the story, he had used eight. The chapter you are in - recovery codes, written backups, backup TESTING - is the discipline that makes this story impossible to repeat.
stories.lesson: Memory is not a backup; a recovery code you never test is barely one
stories.source: The New York Times, 2021-01-12, 'Lost Passwords Lock Millionaires Out of Their Bitcoin Fortunes': 7,002 BTC, ten guesses, eight used. Photo: Lift Conference 2015, CC BY 2.0 (the file page names Stefan Thomas).
