stories.title: Twelve words between you and 128 bits
stories.who: Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak (SatoshiLabs/Trezor), with Aaron Voisine and Sean Bowe
stories.where: BIP 39, in the public bips repository
stories.story: The team building the first hardware signing device faced a human problem: nobody transcribes 128 raw bits correctly. Their 2013 proposal, BIP 39, encodes entropy as ordinary words from a curated list of 2,048 - eleven bits a word, a checksum folded in, a key-stretching function from words to seed. The slides around this one do not describe that pipeline; they run it, word by word, against the standard's own test vectors.
stories.lesson: The recovery code is an interface standard between humans and entropy
stories.source: BIP 39, 'Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys', authors Palatinus, Rusnak, Voisine, Bowe, dated 2013-09-10, in bitcoin/bips. Photo: two Trezor One devices by Gage Skidmore, CC BY-SA 3.0.

stories.title: The 200,000 BTC in a forgotten wallet file
stories.who: Mt. Gox, weeks into its bankruptcy proceedings
stories.where: an old-format wallet file, unused since June 2011
stories.story: Chapter 1 told how Mt. Gox collapsed owing 850,000 BTC. Three weeks after the bankruptcy filing came a twist: the company reported finding about 200,000 BTC in an old-format wallet file that had sat unused since 2011. A file made by software two generations older still held spendable keys - backups do not expire. Those coins became the pool from which creditors, a decade later, began to be repaid.
stories.lesson: Wallet files hold keys forever - label, test, and never discard them blindly
stories.source: Mt. Gox announcement of 2014-03-20/21 reporting approximately 200,000 BTC found in an old-format wallet; summarized with the bankruptcy chronology at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mt._Gox.

resources.title: BIP 32: Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets (status: Deployed)
resources.why: The derivation this chapter performs: the master key from the seed, the child key derivation function, hardened and normal indices, and the extended-key encoding, with the test vectors it checks against.

resources.title: BIP 39: Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys (status: Deployed)
resources.why: The recovery code this chapter generates: the entropy and checksum table, the word list and the key-stretching step that turns words into a seed.

resources.title: BIP 43: Purpose Field for Deterministic Wallets (status: Deployed)
resources.why: Why a derivation path begins with a purpose number, which is what makes the implicit paths of this chapter readable at all.

resources.title: BIP 44: Multi-Account Hierarchy for Deterministic Wallets (status: Deployed)
resources.why: The five-level path - purpose, coin type, account, change, index - that most wallets still follow.

resources.title: BIP 84: Derivation scheme for P2WPKH based accounts (status: Deployed)
resources.why: The native-segwit path and its own test vector, one of the addresses this chapter derives and then confirms against Bitcoin Core.

resources.title: BIP 93: codex32: Checksummed SSSS-aware BIP32 seeds (status: Draft)
resources.why: A recovery code that is itself a share of a split secret, and carries a checksum a person can verify by hand; the most recent of the schemes this chapter compares.

resources.title: BIP 329: Wallet Labels Export Format (status: Draft)
resources.why: The format for the one thing a seed cannot reproduce: the labels and notes a user has attached to their own addresses and transactions.

resources.title: BIP 380: Output Script Descriptors General Operation (status: Deployed)
resources.why: What a descriptor is and how its checksum works; the explicit alternative to remembering a derivation path.

resources.title: SLIP-0039: Shamir's Secret-Sharing for Mnemonic Codes
resources.why: The scheme that splits a seed into shares, any threshold of which restores it; the secret-sharing option in this chapter's comparison.

resources.title: SLIP-0044: Registered coin types for BIP-0044
resources.why: The registry that says coin type 0 is Bitcoin and coin type 1 is testnet for every coin, which is what explains the one uneven row in the chapter's path table.

resources.title: BIP39 test vectors (trezor/python-mnemonic)
resources.why: The published vectors this chapter's recovery-code arithmetic is checked against, entropy to words to seed to master key; the English set alone holds 24 of them.

resources.title: aezeed cipher seed (lnd)
resources.why: A recovery code carrying a version byte and a birthday as well as entropy, which is why its holder need not scan the whole chain; one of the alternatives this chapter weighs.

resources.title: Electrum Seed Version System
resources.why: A code whose own words encode which wallet made it, and the cost of forging that prefix; the version-number scheme this chapter describes.

resources.title: RFC 8018: PKCS #5 Password-Based Cryptography Specification Version 2.1
resources.why: Where PBKDF2 is defined, with the salt and the iteration count whose purpose this chapter explains and whose cost it measures.

resources.title: RFC 7914: The scrypt Password-Based Key Derivation Function
resources.why: The memory-hard alternative to PBKDF2 that one of the compared schemes uses, and the parameters that set its cost.

resources.title: Physical Bitcoin Attacks - Interactive Map
resources.why: The running record behind this chapter's warning about coercion; its own page says the list is not comprehensive, so its count is a floor.
